items.title: Dutch Cabinet minister wants churches to help fill the thousands of healthcare vacancies
items.summary: Long-term Care Minister Mirjam Sterk wants churches to do more to relieve the burden on the healthcare system, she said during the Willibrord Lecture at the opening of the academic year o
items.body_text:
Dutch Cabinet minister wants churches to help fill the thousands of healthcare vacancies
Long-term Care Minister Mirjam Sterk wants churches to do more to relieve the burden on the healthcare system, she said during the Willibrord Lecture at the opening of the academic year of the Protestant Theological University in Utrecht on Monday. Churches can help fill the thousands of vacancies in the healthcare sector if they stop focusing on caring for the soul alone, she said, Trouw reports.
In recent decades, more and more of the care burden has fallen on the government, while churches turned to lobbying and criticising, Sterk said. She called on churches to focus less on “care for the soul” and commit themselves to the “caring society” - a society in which people help and support each other more so that they rely less on the overburdened healthcare sector.
The Dutch healthcare sector is facing massive shortages. In the coming decade, the number of open vacancies in the sector is expected to increase to over 300,000 care providers - more people than the residents of Eindhoven. “Now that you see the government can no longer provide all the care, I think churches need to think about how they can fill that gap, as they did in the past,” Sterk told Trouw.
“The churches have often degenerated into commenters on the government’s shortcomings in the areas of care, welfare, and asylum. Without truly stepping in themselves and thinking through how old concepts such as community, mercy, and justice can be developed into new concepts like self-reliance or compassion,” the Minister told Trouw.
“I don’t know if they did that consciously, but churches have really fallen back on caring for the soul. In my work as Healthcare Minister, I encounter spiritual caregivers in prisons and care institutions. But otherwise, I don’t see the church anywhere anymore.”
She added that she’s not asking churches to start providing medical care. “Healthcare reforms are also very much about how to shape caring communities together. Churches can certainly contribute to this by being more outward-looking than inward-looking. For example, by organizing activities that are very accessible. It is more about supporting people; think, for instance, of having coffee with people with mental health issues.”

items.title: Amsterdam taxi drivers launch app to rival Uber
items.summary: A group of Amsterdam taxi drivers has launched a rival booking app to try and loosen Uber’s grip on the...
items.body_text:
Amsterdam taxi drivers launch app to rival Uber
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
A group of Amsterdam taxi drivers has launched a rival booking app to try and loosen Uber’s grip on the city’s cab market, amid long-running disputes over employee status, wages and workers’ rights. The founders claim nearly 1,300 drivers have already signed up.
The app, NLCabs, was set up by driver Mostapha Ahidar and co-founder Ivo van Leeuwen, who told Het Parool they were tired of watching a US monopoly control the terms of their trade. It works the same as Uber: passengers order a ride through the app and nearby drivers pick them up.
The difference, the founders say, is the cut. NLCabs takes a 3% commission from drivers, which Ahidar said was only what the platform needs to keep running. Uber’s commission is variable and can rise beyond half the fare, according to the drivers, though the company does not publish its rates.
“We are treated like children by Uber,” one driver told the paper. “We have absolutely no room for negotiation.”
Years of friction
 The launch comes after years of conflict between Uber and Dutch drivers, much of which has gone through courts and regulators.
In August, the data protection authority (AP) fined Uber €825 million for deactivating drivers’ accounts through automated systems, without proper human review or explanation – the second-largest penalty ever issued under EU privacy law. Uber is appealing and has called the fine disproportionate.
That followed a €290 million fine in 2024 for sending drivers’ data to the US, a record at the time. Both cases originally stemmed from complaints by French drivers.
Employee or entrepreneur
 In January, an Amsterdam appeal court ruled that Uber drivers cannot all be treated as employees, overturning a 2021 judgment that had put them on the payroll. The FNV trade union, which launched the case, said it was weighing a Supreme Court appeal.
Many drivers work almost exclusively through Uber and have little way of finding fares without it.
NLCabs is live but has only a few hundred downloads on Google Play, and the founders said they know shifting a habit as ingrained as opening Uber will be hard. They plan to expand across the Netherlands.

Groningen University launches Frisian language degree
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Groningen University has launched a bachelor’s degree programme in the Frisian language, the first standalone course in the country’s second official language for 15 years.
Three students began the course this week, which covers linguistics, history and Frisian culture. Frisian was taught as a degree in its own right until 2012, when it was absorbed into a broader programme on Europe’s minority languages, Minorities & Multilingualism.
That programme drew too few students to survive and the university said it would phase it out from the 2025/26 academic year, leaving the academic study of Frisian at risk of vanishing altogether.
A rescue from The Hague
 The course was saved after the Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences (KNAW) recommended, in a report on the future of Frisian studies, that the state pay for a dedicated bachelor. The government agreed to put in €340,000 a year, with further provincial money.
For legal reasons the new degree sits as a Frisian track within the university’s Dutch Languages and Cultures programme, though the focus is now entirely on Frisian.
Professor of Frisian Arjen Versloot said he was happy with the intake, even though a course usually needs around 20 students to break even. “There are often only five students in French and German too, so as a small language we can’t complain,” he told regional broadcaster Omrop Fryslân.
Teachers in demand
 The degree is also meant to supply qualified teachers. Since August, schools in Friesland have been required to use more Frisian in the classroom under new curriculum rules, and Versloot expects strong demand for teachers able to deliver it at the highest level.
Frisian is spoken by around 470,000 people in Friesland and is the closest living relative of English.
Reading and writing proficiency in Frisian has risen sharply over the past two decades, despite fewer people speaking the language at home, according to a recent survey.
Around 58% of residents in Friesland now say they can read Frisian well or very well, up from 46% in 2007. Self-reported writing proficiency nearly doubled over the same period, from 9.6% to 18.9%.

items.title: Man cleared of plotting to kidnap princesses Amalia and Alexia
items.summary: A man has been cleared of plotting to kidnap princesses Amalia and Alexia, the eldest daughters of king Willem-Alexander and...
items.body_text:
Man cleared of plotting to kidnap princesses Amalia and Alexia
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
A man has been cleared of plotting to kidnap princesses Amalia and Alexia, the eldest daughters of king Willem-Alexander and queen Máxima, after a court ruled he was suffering from a psychosis at the time.
Anne Romke van der H., 33, believed he was in a relationship with Amalia, 22, and fantasised about marrying her before living in the wilds in Poland with her and her 21-year-old sister.
He bought items from a hardware store designed to use as a survival kit, including knives, cooking equipment and two hatchets, one of which he inscribed with Alexia’s name.
The prosecution service said he intended to abduct or attack the two princesses if they were unwilling to go along with his plans.
But a court in The Hague ruled there was no evidence that van der H., from Groningen, was preparing an actual attack on Amalia and Alexia or intended to threaten them.
A psychiatric assessment found he was schizophrenic and had become obsessed with the royal family, particularly the two princesses.
He was found guilty of insulting six police officers and smashing a window, but the court did not impose a fine or punishment because he was in psychosis at the time.
The court said the offences were not severe enough to justify a compulsory treatment regime (tbs), but Van der H. told the judges at an earlier hearing that he was willing to undergo voluntary treatment.

items.title: Poland investigates potential “foreign intelligence” involvement in fire at drone plant
items.summary: The fire broke out at a facility belonging to WB Electronics, Europe's largest drone maker.
items.body_text:
Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
After a fire at a facility belonging to WB Electronics, the EU’s largest drone maker, Polish prosecutors have launched an investigation into suspicions that the incident was a “crime of a terrorist nature” committed with the “participation of foreign intelligence”.
Prokurator z Małopolskiego Wydziału Zamiejscowego Departamentu do Spraw Przestępczości Zorganizowanej i Korupcji @PK_GOV_PL w Krakowie wszczął dziś śledztwo w sprawie brania udziału w działalności obcego wywiadu przeciwko Rzeczypospolitej Polskiej i dopuszczenia się przestępstwa… https://t.co/h6k4Fvv3CK
— Jacek Dobrzyński (@JacekDobrzynski) August 31, 2026
Shortly after midnight, a fire broke out in storage facilities at WB Electronics’ plant in the city of Skarżysko-Kamienna. The site is used to produce components for drones that are supplied to the Polish and Ukrainian armed forces, among others. The fire was soon extinguished with no injuries reported.
Speculation immediately emerged that the blaze could have been caused deliberately. Poland has been the primary target in Europe of sabotage activities carried out by operatives working on behalf of Russia.
While the Polish authorities initially refused to speculate on the cause of the fire, the provincial police headquarters in nearby Kielce confirmed that a burglar alarm had been triggered in the area around midnight. When the emergency services arrived, they confirmed that a fire had broken out.
Shortly before 5 p.m. local time on Monday afternoon, prosecutors announced that they had launched an investigation into the potential involvement of foreign intelligence and the committing of a terrorist offence.
“The offence consisted of intentionally starting a fire on the premises of WB Electronics in Skarżysko-Kamienna on 31 August 2026 by planting a charge containing flammable materials,” they wrote. The resultant fire destroyed the warehouse facilities, causing at least 15 million zloty (€3.46m) of damage.
Jacek Dobrzyński, the spokesman for Poland’s security services, revealed that the Internal Security Agency (ABW) was conducting the investigation in cooperation with prosecutors.
🔴 Pożar w Skarżysku-Kamiennej. "To było podpalenie"
Znamy nowe szczegóły w sprawie nocnego pożaru w zakładach w Skarżysku-Kamiennej. Coraz więcej wskazuje na to, że możemy mówić o przypadku dywersji lub sabotażu. W zakładzie dronowej firmy doszło do podpalenia.
✒️ @jodynaa…
— Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) August 31, 2026
The incident in Skarżysko-Kamienna came shortly after a separate fire on Sunday at a warehouse in another Polish city, Lublin, that belonged to a company that also supplies components for drones used in Ukraine, according to news website Wirtualna Polska.
Interior ministry spokeswoman Karolina Gałecka refused to confirm to Wirtualna Polska whether the authorities are treating the two fires as related, but said that “every aspect will be thoroughly investigated”.
Earlier this year, a report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism on Moscow’s growing campaign of sabotage in Europe found that Poland is the “primary focus of Russian activity”.
Last year, Poland confirmed that Russia was behind the fire that in 2024 destroyed Warsaw’s largest shopping centre. It is also seeking to detain two men believed to have sabotaged a rail line in Poland last year on Russian orders.

items.title: Fundraiser for baby orphaned by speeding driver in Polish city reaches 1 million zloty
items.summary: The accident has brought anger and calls for action from residents and local politicians.
items.body_text:
Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
A fundraiser for an eight-month-old baby who survived an accident in the Polish city of Kraków in which his parents were killed by a speeding driver has reached more than 1 million zloty (€231,000).
The tragedy has prompted widespread anger, with calls from residents and local politicians for the authorities to take action to deal with dangerous driving in the city.
To będzie jedna z najtrudniejszych zbiórek, jakie wspólnie przeprowadzimy.💔Proszę o RT🙏
Kilka dni temu rozpędzony kierowca w Krakowie wjechał w młode małżeństwo. Mateusz i Klaudia zginęli. Ich kilkumiesięczny synek, Oliwier, trafił do szpitala.
Mam dla Was dobrą wiadomość.… pic.twitter.com/R8L1xgEBPn
— Damian Żurawski (@damian_zurawski) August 26, 2026
On 22 August, a married couple, Mateusz and Klaudia, both 32, were walking with their baby on Solna Street, close to the southern bank of the Vistula river, when a car driven by 26-year-old Hubert B., whose surname is masked under Polish privacy law, mounted the pavement, killing both parents.
The child, eight-month-old Oliwier, survived the accident but was hospitalised. His condition is continuing to improve, reports broadcaster TVP Kraków.
According to prosecutors, the car was travelling around 40 km/h (25mph) faster than the speed limit in the area. Hubert B., has been charged with unintentionally causing a fatal accident, for which he could face up to eight years in prison.
“The suspect pleaded not guilty to the offence he was charged with, explaining, among other things, that the car skidded due to the uneven road surface,” prosecutors said, adding the suspect has been placed in pretrial detention.
An online fundraiser set up last week to provide Oliwier “with financial security for years to come” shared the news that the baby’s condition is now stable, although “his arm and leg are in plaster”.
“We can’t give Oliwier back his mum and dad,” reads the fundraiser’s description. “However, we can do everything we can to ensure he has the resources for his education and a peaceful start to adult life.”
At the time of writing, the fundraiser has reached more than 1.05 million zloty, over double its initial target. There have been more than 23,300 donations so far.
Meanwhile, Oliwier’s grandfather, Andrzej, told newspaper Fakt that the family had given its consent for the fundraiser and was very grateful for those who had donated. A court in Kraków has granted Mateusz’s brother custody of the child.
Wypadek w Krakowie. Dziadek Oliwiera przekazał wieść, na którą czekali wszyscy #krakow #wypadek #krakow #opiekanaddzieckiem https://t.co/idGGdA5uFe
— Fakt (@Fakt_pl) August 28, 2026
As well as sympathy for the victims, the accident aroused anger from residents. Several hundred people attended a protest at the site, holding signs reading “How many more people must die for something to change?” and “Stop road killers”. They installed their own mock-up pedestrian crossing and speed bumps.
“Such tragedies are not isolated incidents,” said the organisers, quoted by news website Interia. They cited police figures showing that Kraków had the most road accidents of all Poland’s provincial capitals in 2025. Its figure of 941 was over 100 more than in Łódź and over 250 more than in Warsaw.
Local councillor Rafał Zawiślak told news website Onet that he was filing a complaint with the prosecutor’s office, saying the city authorities had been negligent, failing to respond to warnings from 2024 that the site of the accident was dangerous.
Godzina ciszy w Krakowie. Mieszkańcy upamiętniają parę, która zginęła w sobotniej tragedii przy ulicy Solnej. Na miejsce przybyły tłumy. „Nie chcemy bać się chodzić po chodnikach” – apelują.@RadioKrakow pic.twitter.com

items.title: Polish student accused of planning Islamist terrorist attack on Christmas market to stand trial
items.summary: The 20-year-old was a first year at the Catholic University of Lublin but reportedly became "infatuated with Islam".
items.body_text:
Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
A Polish student is to stand trial accused of planning a terrorist attack on a Christmas market in Poland as an act of support for Islamic State.
On Monday, prosecutors announced that they have filed an indictment against the 20-year-old suspect, a student at the Catholic University of Lublin (KUL) who can be named only as Mateusz W. under Polish privacy law.
Jacek Dobrzyński, spokesman for Poland’s security services, confirmed that Mateusz W. had been “preparing a mass attack at a Christmas market, which he planned to carry out using explosive materials”.
Wracamy do sprawy 20-letniego Mateusza W. – studenta Katolickiego Uniwersytetu Lubelskiego podejrzewanego o przygotowywanie masowego zamachu na jednym z jarmarków świątecznych, którego planował dokonać z wykorzystaniem materiałów wybuchowych. Do Sądu Okręgowego w Koszalinie… https://t.co/6vGPcjiDnc pic.twitter.com/seFGV8nHMz
— Jacek Dobrzyński (@JacekDobrzynski) August 31, 2026
The suspect was detained late last year, when details of his alleged plot and plans to establish contact with Islamic State were first revealed. He has remained in custody since then.
Though the authorities have confirmed that Mateusz W. was a first-year student at KUL, a leading Catholic university that counts the late Pope John Paul II among its former students and lecturers, and that they have also searched premises in the province of Łódź, they have not revealed where his alleged attack was planned.
However, prosecutors reported today that the suspect had established contacts through which he could gain access to explosive materials and devices, had looked for bomb-making instructions, and had tried to recruit others to his terrorist cause.
“Mateusz W.’s actions were intended to further the policies of the terrorist organisation known as Islamic State and to seriously intimidate people with views contrary to the ideology espoused by the suspect,” wrote Katarzyna Calów-Jaszewska, a spokeswoman for the National Prosecutor’s Office.
In a separate statement, the Internal Security Agency (ABW) revealed that the suspect had “intended to join a terrorist organisation affiliated with the so-called Islamic State and sought people who could help him carry out this plan”.
Neither the security services nor prosecutors have indicated whether Mateusz W. denied or admitted to his alleged crimes or has offered any explanation for his actions. If convicted of preparing a mass attack, he could face up to ten years in prison.
Last year, after Mateusz W. was detained, Dobrzyński said that he came from a devoutly Catholic family but had become “deeply infatuated with Islam” and had “fallen in love with terrorism”.
In an appeal to parents, Dobrzyński said that, “if you see your children interested in Islam, communism, or fascism, and collecting all sorts of information and items on the subject, that’s the first sign. Take care of your own children, because things can only get worse from there”.
Poland has detained a man who was allegedly planning a terrorist attack on a Christmas market as an act of support for Islamic State.
The suspect, a 19-year-old Pole, had become "infatuated with Islam", say the security services https://t.co/N4WDVZdlai
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 16, 2025
After news of Mateusz W.’s detention emerged, KUL suspended his student status. The university’s spokesman, Wojciech Andrusiewicz, said that neither fellow students nor lecturers had noticed any unusual behaviour by the suspect.

items.title: Narva-Jõesuu eyes €10 million revival for historic resort hall
items.summary: Narva-Jõesuu is buying back its historic resort hall from private owners, with plans to redevelop it with EU support as a mixed-use cultural and community hub.
items.body_text:
Narva-Jõesuu eyes €10 million revival for historic resort hall
Narva-Jõesuu is buying back its historic resort hall from private owners, with plans to redevelop it with EU support as a mixed-use cultural and community hub.
Completed in 1912, the Art Nouveau-style resort hall, or kuursaal, is listed in Estonia's National Registry of Cultural Monuments. Much of the building was damaged during World War II.
More than two decades ago, a company linked to businessman Tiit Vähi bought the property with plans for a hotel and restaurant, but the project never materialized.
Mayor Maksim Iljin said those plans had once been realistic, but became unfeasible after the global financial crisis, Russia's annexation of Crimea and the ongoing war in Ukraine.
"And that's one of the reasons we've reached the point where we're buying the property back for the city," he said.
Events as soon as next year
Narva-Jõesuu City Council has agreed to pay €375,000 for the resort hall and nearly 3 hectares of adjoining properties, with the aim of seeking EU funding for the redevelopment.
The total investment could reach €10 million, Iljin said, noting that the city has already set aside up to €20,000 this year for basic safety work and plans to begin improving the surrounding grounds.
The city hopes to start holding events in the park behind the hall next year.
The redevelopment could also include a new concert hall, addressing a longstanding shortage of year-round venues in town big enough to host major events.
"Our plan is not only to restore the existing resort hall but also build a concert hall, because outside the summer season, we pretty much have no options for hosting large events," the mayor explained.
High hopes for EU funds
The city plans to finance preliminary work, including surveys, expert assessments and design work, from its own budget.
For the rest, the goal is to secure EU funding when the next Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) begins, with three specific funding measures already under consideration.
The completed complex is envisioned as a year-round hub and destination, combining conference and event facilities with a restaurant, youth center and tourist information center.
--
Editor: Karmen Rebane, Aili Vahtla

items.title: Local residents say drone that crossed into Estonia flew as far as Põlva
items.summary: According to local residents, the drone that crossed Estonia's southeastern border overnight reached the city of Põlva. Estonian Defense Forces has not commented on how far the drone traveled into Estonian territory.
items.body_text:
Local residents say drone that crossed into Estonia flew as far as Põlva
According to local residents, the drone that crossed Estonia's southeastern border overnight reached the city of Põlva. Estonian Defense Forces has not commented on how far the drone traveled into Estonian territory.
Two drones flew toward Estonia's eastern border overnight into Tuesday. According to the Estonian Defense Forces (EDF), the drone flying toward Narva turned back toward Russia and did not enter Estonian airspace. However, another drone crossed the border into Estonian airspace in the country's southeast. The Defense Forces said the drone remained close to the border zone.
Over the course of Tuesday, however, ERR received reports from several people living in the city of Põlva who said the drone that crossed the national border made it as far as Põlva. The city is about 35 kilometers (22 miles) from the border.
A local resident sent ERR an audio recording made at 3:48 a.m. in which a sound resembling a drone can be heard.
"I woke up at 3:48 a.m. when I received an EE-ALARM message warning of a possible drone threat. It was quiet outside. About 10 minutes after the message arrived, I began to hear a buzzing sound similar to a motor scooter," the person who made the audio recording told ERR.
"At first, I thought it was a vehicle and that the sound was coming from the highway, but it kept getting closer. Since there is a wooded area in front of the house, it couldn't have been coming from a vehicle on the ground," the person added.
The resident said they had heard that drones sound similar to motor scooters and began to feel increasingly afraid.
"The sound kept getting closer and then gradually began to fade away. A short while later, I heard the noise of a fighter jet, which could be heard repeatedly for about another hour. My 13-year-old daughter had been half-awake and recorded the sound coming from outside, which she shared with friends who had also been woken up by the noise. It was all very frightening," the resident added.
The resident said that when they read in the news that morning that the drone had crossed the Estonian border in southeastern Estonia but had not left the border zone, they were even more confused, as Põlva is not in the border zone. "It left me wondering whether the situation really was under control."
Another local resident said the drone flew over Põlva after 4 a.m. and was followed a couple of minutes later by a jet aircraft. A third source said a drone flew over a house in the village of Vardja at around 3:30 a.m. A person living in Põlva said they believed the drone could be heard over the lake in the city.
Responding to an ERR inquiry, the Defense Forces said that for security reasons it could not comment on the drones' exact flight paths or the locations and times at which the unmanned aerial vehicles were detected.
"Releasing such information would make it possible to draw conclusions about the capabilities and coverage of Estonia's air surveillance. Nor is it possible, based solely on an audio recording, to reliably determine whether the recorded sound came specifically from an unmanned aerial vehicle," the Defense Forces said.
Estonian Air Force Commander Brig. Gen. Riivo Valge confirmed Tuesday morning that one drone briefly headed toward Narva from Russia overnight, while another drone crossed the border in southeastern Estonia some time later.
The drone heading toward Narva veered back toward Russia and did not enter Estonia. About half an hour later, a second drone crossed the border in southeastern Estonia. "It also crossed the Estonian border and remained close to the border zone," Valge said.
In the early hours of September 1, the Estonian Defense Forces issued an alert about a potential aerial threat in Lääne-Viru and Ida-Viru counties. Half an hour later, the Defense Forces also issued an alert about a potential threat in Tartu, Jõgeva, Viljandi, Valga, Võru and Põlva counties. Drone alerts were also

items.title: Isamaa leader: Online casino tax break to cost state €31 million
items.summary: An online casino tax break put in place last December will cost the state €31 million in lost revenues, Isamaa chair Urmas Reinsalu said.
items.body_text:
Isamaa leader: Online casino tax break to cost state €31 million
An online casino tax break put in place last December will cost the state €31 million in lost revenues, Isamaa chair Urmas Reinsalu said.
The government introduced the gambling tax break late last year, aiming to attract new market players in the sector. The Riigikogu adopted the bill amending the Gambling Tax Act on December 3, 2025, with the aim of incrementally reducing the gambling tax rate by 0.5 percentage points per year, from 6 percent to 4 percent. Due to an oversight in the law, the Riigikogu had to reconsider and adopted it once more on February 10.
"We learned how much revenue the state is expected to lose, according to the Finance Ministry's forecast, compared with the previous assumption. From this year through 2029, it amounts to around €31 million," Reinsalu told ERR.
Taxes on casinos and gambling have long been a source of revenue for the culture sector, which is now suffering as a result of the cut. The Cultural Endowment will lose €4 million in 2026 and again in 2027 as a result of the tax break, it is estimated.
Cultural Endowment (Kultuurkapital) head Margus Allikmaa said the reverse of a planned hike and its replacement by a cut had been "unjustifiable."
"Estonia's tax rate is already the lowest in Europe, and that small increase would have meant nothing other than additional revenue, which it actually produced in previous years as well. When the tax rate was raised in 2024 for the first time in quite a while, state revenues and those of the Cultural Endowment rose sharply. So the tax cut was in no way justified or necessary — now we are paying the price, and both we and the state budget as a whole have less revenue," Allikmaa said.
Allikmaa noted Eesti 200 MP Tanel Tein and his party as a whole, which had strongly pushed for the tax break, "may have been entirely sincere and honest" in their desires, but "unfortunately it did not work out" and turned out to be "an empty hope."
"You still have to analyze the situation, look at the international picture and at what other countries are doing. I think in this case they simply put too much faith in the gambling operators," he added.
The Riigikogu's State Budget Control Select Committee held an extraordinary sitting Monday to discuss the impact of the remote gambling tax rate change on state revenues and the sectors it finances. Allikmaa attended, along with Tax and Customs Board (MTA) Director General Raigo Uukkivi, Finance Ministry Fiscal Policy Department state finances analyst Rait Kiveste, and Tax and Customs Policy Department senior specialist Maret Mets.
"Finance Ministry officials foresaw the drop in revenue when the law was passed but said it was a political decision, and they have received no government-level input to reverse it," Reinsalu said, adding he is convinced the decision must be reversed without delay.
"Finance Ministry representatives acknowledged that even if the change is reversed, a six‑month notice period must be taken into account. Since this involves a tax rate increase, every month or week of delay adds to the shortfall in budget and Cultural Endowment revenues. It makes sense for parliament to initiate the bill without delay and return things to the previous level," Reinsalu added.
Allikmaa said the lower remote gambling tax revenue is forcing the endowment to reduce grants and review its investment plan for cultural buildings.
"Nothing will actually be left undone outright, but the grants paid to cultural organizers, authors, performers and everyone else who receives support will simply be slightly more modest," Allikmaa said, adding that adjustments to cultural building financing are not yet large enough to require cancellations. However, he warned that the situation will become "somewhat more serious" if the planned 0.5‑percentage‑point tax cut next year goes ahead, which would reduce revenue by nearly 14 percent.

items.title: Bulgaria’s Former Interim PM Andrey Gyurov Confirms Presidential Bid
items.summary: Former interim prime minister ends months of speculation over his presidential ambitions, meaning he will likely be the main rival to Iliana Iotova in the October polls.
items.body_text:
Bulgaria’s Former Interim PM Andrey Gyurov Confirms Presidential Bid
After months of speculation, Bulgaria’s former interim Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov announced on Tuesday that he will run in the presidential elections on October 25. He will likely be the main rival to acting President Iliana Iotova who will be seeking a full mandate.
“The answer is yes, I will run, but the more important question is ‘why’… I don’t dream of a career, I dream of us leaving our children a united, honourable and modern Bulgaria, which is centred around the economy of knowledge and its biggest asset – the people,” said Gyurov.
“We can’t let our differences turn us into mutual enemies. Bulgaria can do so much better,” he added.
His two-month stint as caretaker prime minister in early 2026 was marked by a crackdown on fraudulent voting ahead of the general elections in April and the signing of a cooperation agreement with Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky in March.
Gyurov will run with the former chief secretary general to the Interior Ministry, Georgi Kandev, as his designated vice-president.
The duo – expected to lead a pro-EU and reformist campaign in opposition to the government of current Prime Minister Rumen Radev – announced their campaign in their common home town of Gotse Delchev in south-west Bulgaria, named after a revolutionary Ottoman-era hero celebrated in both Bulgaria and North Macedonia.
The announcement ended months of speculation over their political futures. Rumours started as early as April, while Gyurov was still interim prime minister, with his name widely mentioned as a potential presidential candidate by analysts and fellow politicians.
Since his caretaker term, Gyurov has been noticeable for his carefully curated social media and public presence: from visiting festivals and endorsing cultural events to running in marathons and reuniting with his baseball youth team – moves seen as aimed at engaging pro-EU, liberal, urban voters.
Born in 1975, he built a career spanning banking and financial academia, moving from work as an analyst and credit-risk expert in Vienna to lecturing and directing financial programmes in Bulgaria.
He entered parliamentary politics in November 2021 as a member of the reformist and then newly-founded We Continue the Change party, which the won the general elections. He left the party in 2023 and was then appointed deputy governor of the Bulgarian National Bank.
In 2026, he left that position to become interim prime minister, chosen by President Iliana Iotova – herself in a new role after Rumen Radev left the president’s office to successfully run in the general elections with his Progressive Bulgaria party.
Now, Gyurov and Iotova, supported by Progressive Bulgaria and the Bulgarian Socialist Party, will be the main opponents in the 2026 presidential elections.
Gyurov’s designated vice-president, Kandev – also born in 1975 – has held various positions in the Interior Ministry since 1999. He left his last position as chief secretary in June, claiming he had been subjected to political pressure by Radev’s office, but the issue was ultimately left unexplained.
A month and a half before the elections, it’s unclear whether the two men will be supported by the otherwise fragmented centre-right. The Democratic Bulgaria party and Gyurov’s former partners from We Continue the Change have previously stated that they will support their bid.
The lack of a candidate from the longstanding dominant party GERB might also be to their benefit, but Boyko Borissov’s party has yet to make its opinion public.

items.title: Russian Suspected of Triple Homicide in Montenegro Dies by Suicide
items.summary: Police say a Russian national suspected of shooting dead three Montenegrins at a firing range killed himself after being located in a wooded area in Herceg Novi.
items.body_text:
Russian Suspected of Triple Homicide in Montenegro Dies by Suicide
Montenegro police officer. Photo illustration: EPA/Boris Pejovic.
A Russian citizen suspected of killing three people at a shooting range in Danilovgrad, central Montenegro shot himself dead on Tuesday after opening fire on police when he was found near the coastal town of Herceg Novi, authorities said.
The victims, killed by the Russian national on Monday, have been identified as Podgorica residents Nemanja Kapor, 20, and Petar Globarevic, 24, and Danilovgrad resident Momir Radonjic, 67.
Police identified the suspect as 30-year-old Russian citizen Mikhail Nikolaevich Shabunin.
Police Director Lazar Scepanovic said on Tuesday that officers had located Shabunin in a wooded area above the Topla neighborhood of the coastal town of Herceg Novi.
“After the suspect was surrounded and found himself in a hopeless situation, he opened fire in the direction of police officers and then committed suicide using a firearm,” Scepanovic said.
Police said Shabunin had visited the Ceska Zbrojevka shooting range in Danilovgrad in the days before the killings.
“He carried out a test shooting at the range, entered the building and committed the killings,” Scepanovic said. “After that, he drove away in one of the victims’ vehicles.”
Police later found the vehicle that Shabunin allegedly used to leave the crime scene in Rogami, near Podgorica. They believed Shabunin later travelled by taxi from Podgorica toward Herceg Novi.
Scepanovic had described the suspect as dangerous and said he had taken a firearm and ammunition with him after the killings.
The Ceska Zbrojevka shooting club told state broadcaster RTCG that the three victims were its employees and had been at work without weapons and without the possibility of defending themselves.
Police initially urged residents to remain indoors while the suspect was at large and warned people to avoid contact with unknown persons and report any suspicious behaviour.
Authorities have not disclosed a possible motive or provided further details about the circumstances leading up to the killings.
“Police officers are continuing their activities in cooperation with the Higher State Prosecutor’s Office in Podgorica to establish all the circumstances of the incident, including its cause and motive, and to fully clarify the entire situation,” the statement said.
Prime Minister Milojko Spajic expressed condolences to the victims’ families. He said September 1 and 2 would be declared days of mourning in Montenegro.

items.title: Animals in Tirana Zoo Struggle in Sweltering Summer Heat
items.summary: A predominance of young trees and limited water resources are compounding the effects of climate change at Tirana Zoo.
items.body_text:
A white tiger plods slowly to a small pool, seeking respite from the 38-degree Celsius heat. The shade provided by trees is sparse, but it’s still better than the bear enclosure, where there is almost no shade at all. During the hottest hours, the bears retreat indoors, emerging again only in the later afternoon.
Welcome to Tirana Zoo, where captive animals are living with the discomfort of record-high temperatures and stress caused by the incessant noise of nearby building sites.
Zookeepers say they turn on sprinklers three times a day, two hours each time, but the respite they offer is not enough.
Built in the 1960s, the site of the zoo was once green, but construction is now rife. The zoo was closed in 2015 after videos circulated on social media showing the dire conditions animals were being kept in. It reopened in 2022, but shade remains insufficient to cope with the challenges of climate change.
“These are not normal temperatures,” said Ariel Vasili, an independent wildlife veterinarian who has worked in the past with the zoo.
“While we do have animals at the zoo that can handle temperatures of 34 or 35 degrees, no species in the world, only perhaps the camel, can cope with 42 degrees, though even a camel would struggle.”
“One of our downsides is that our trees are very young, so we have to wait for shade to develop,” he said. Vasili also cited limited water resources.
“We don’t have running water available, so we try very hard to conserve the water we do have; however, this isn’t just a zoo-specific problem,” Vasili said.
“You have to understand that we live in Tirana; if we kept [the sprinklers] running constantly, we would run out of water.”
Extreme heat: foreseeable animal welfare risk
 A white tiger in Tirana Zoo that was rescued from illegal captivity. Photo: BIRN.
In Britain, the BBC reported that some zoos were using paddling pools, iced water and iced fruits to keep animals cool.
Iced fruits have also been deployed at Tirana Zoo, said zoo director Evis Rrahmani.
Rrahmani said the zoo has plans to enhance its enclosures, “to make them more diverse to provide mental stimulation for the animals”.
“We intend to improve it, but it takes time,” she acknowledged.
Research-based news website The Conversation recently raised the issue with an article under the headline ‘Are Zoos Ready for the Changing Climate’. It argued that extreme heat should be treated as a “foreseeable animal welfare risk”.
“This might involve expanding shaded areas, creating climate-controlled refuges, improving ventilation, installing misting systems and water features, and monitoring temperature and humidity in real time,” it suggested.
“But infrastructure alone will not be enough. Zoos may also need to adapt their daily management practices, adjusting feeding and enrichment schedules and modifying routines to minimise heat exposure during the hottest parts of the day,” it cautioned.
“To be honest, we don’t have [enough] water in Tirana; everyone struggles to get it, not just us. But since our water consumption is higher, it stands out more in our case,” wildlife veterinarian Vasili said.
Indrit Osmani from Animal Rescue Albania, ARSA, said securing enough water and shade was only the bare minimum.
“If an animal is kept in captivity, the responsibility extends far beyond merely providing the minimum conditions for survival,” said Osmani, who stressed that ARSA opposes keeping animals in captivity.
“A modern zoo should not be judged solely by the quality of its infrastructure or the fact that the animals have access to water, food, and shade,” he said. “It must be evaluated based on whether the entire living environment is adapted to the biological, social, and behavioral needs of each species and the individual animals housed there.”
“Extreme temperatures can cause heat stress, dehydration, fatigue, and behavioural changes. Naturally, the impact varies depending on the species, age, and condition of each individual.”

items.title: National Museum Unveils Rare 16th-Century Silver Coins Found at Somló Hill
items.summary: A special exhibition titled “Thaler Hoard Discovered at the Foot of Somló Hill” opened Monday at the Hungarian National Museum. During an archaeological excavation carried out in Veszprém County in the summer of 2026 in cooperation with the institution’s volunteer archaeological team, researchers discovered 27 early modern silver thalers. The unusual archaeological finds will be […] The post National Museum Unveils Rare 16th-Century Silver Coins Found at Somló Hill appeared first on Hungary Toda
items.body_text:
The collection is particularly notable for its gold ornaments, a rarity among Conquest-era finds.Continue reading
A special exhibition titled “Thaler Hoard Discovered at the Foot of Somló Hill” opened Monday at the Hungarian National Museum. During an archaeological excavation carried out in Veszprém County in the summer of 2026 in cooperation with the institution’s volunteer archaeological team, researchers discovered 27 early modern silver thalers. The unusual archaeological finds will be on display at the museum through October 18, it was announced at the opening of the exhibition.
Gábor Zsigmond, director general of the Hungarian National Museum, said the institution considers the development of volunteer work a priority and established its Community Archaeology Department to organize and coordinate such activities through its volunteer program.
He also noted that the National Museum is hosting a three-day international numismatic conference from Monday through Wednesday.
Held for the 11th time, the conference provides leading researchers in the field with an opportunity to present their latest research in numismatics.
Historian Teréz Oborni, an associate professor at the Faculty of Humanities at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), emphasized that the exhibition is particularly interesting as Hungary has just commemorated the 500th anniversary of the Battle of Mohács. The thalers date from the period that followed the battle, including the era of the Long Turkish War.
The museum said in a statement that it has been conducting successful research in the Somló area of Veszprém County for several years.
The vast majority of the coins—18 in total—were minted by Archduke Ferdinand II of Austria, at the mint in Hall in Tirol and in Ensisheim in Alsace.
The hoard also contained three thalers issued by Holy Roman Emperor Rudolf II: two Hungarian and one Bohemian. The German territories were represented by two coins minted by the city of Lübeck, as well as one thaler each from the Palatinate, Brunswick and Brandenburg. The hoard was further complemented by a thaler from the Swiss city of St. Gallen.
The youngest coin in the hoard, known in numismatic terminology as the closing coin, is a thaler minted by Rudolf II in Kremnica in 1593. The value of the hoard and the relative proportions of the different issues suggest that it can be linked to the Long Turkish War (1591/1593–1606). The series of military campaigns that took place year after year over roughly a decade and a half extended across the entire Carpathian Basin. Hoards from this period provide direct evidence of the scale of the destruction and preserve a record of the diverse currency circulation of the era.
Via MTI, Featured image: MTI/Kovács Márton

items.title: GYSEV’s New-Generation InterCity Train Enters Testing Phase
items.summary: GYSEV’s major fleet development program has reached an important milestone: the first FLIRT InterCity electric multiple unit has left Stadler’s factory in Siedlce, Poland, and will now begin its continuous testing program. A total of 11 such electric multiple units are being built for the Hungarian-Austrian railway company, Világgazdaság reports. The trains are expected to […] The post GYSEV’s New-Generation InterCity Train Enters Testing Phase appeared first on Hungary Today.
items.body_text:
During the development process, particular emphasis was placed on maintainability, durability, and passenger comfort.Continue reading
GYSEV’s major fleet development program has reached an important milestone: the first FLIRT InterCity electric multiple unit has left Stadler’s factory in Siedlce, Poland, and will now begin its continuous testing program. A total of 11 such electric multiple units are being built for the Hungarian-Austrian railway company, Világgazdaság reports. The trains are expected to enter passenger service progressively from 2027, with the entire fleet scheduled to be completed by 2028.
The development is particularly significant because Hungary has not seen an InterCity rolling stock procurement of this scale for three decades. The new trains are not simply another version of the existing FLIRT units:
they have been specifically designed to meet the requirements of longer-distance InterCity services.
The trains will feature first- and second-class passenger areas, air conditioning, low-floor access and modern passenger information systems.
On board, passengers will have access to Wi-Fi, USB-C charging at every seat and holders for smartphones or tablets. A catering area will improve comfort on longer journeys, with food and beverage vending machines. Cyclists have also been taken into consideration: thanks to the flexible interior layout, the trains will be able to carry up to 18 bicycles on a seasonal basis.
The technical specifications are also noteworthy.
The five-car, dual-voltage FLIRT InterCity electric multiple units will be capable of speeds of up to 160 km/h and will operate not only in Hungary but also in Austria.
According to GYSEV’s plans, the new trains will primarily strengthen InterCity services on the Sopron–Budapest and Szombathely–Budapest routes.
The testing now getting underway follows extensive preparatory work. The car bodies of the trains were manufactured at Stadler’s plant in Szolnok, central Hungary, before being transported to the company’s facility in Siedlce, Poland, for final assembly. Testing will take place in several countries, followed by test runs in Hungary and the acquisition of the necessary regulatory approvals, after which the trains can enter actual passenger service.
The investment does not stop at the purchase of the trains.
GYSEV is also developing a new maintenance center in Szombathely, western Hungary, specifically designed to service the more than 100-metre-long new electric multiple units.
In addition to a workshop hall of around 5,300 square meters, more than 3,500 meters of new track equipped with overhead catenary could be built. The facility will include a three-track maintenance and repair hall as well as a separate washing hall.
The railway company’s aim is to create a complete infrastructure capable of supporting more modern, faster and more comfortable InterCity services over the long term. The Szombathely base will be capable of accommodating at least three electric multiple units at the same time, each measuring 106 meters in length.
Via Világgazdaság, Featured image: Facebook/GYSEV Zrt.

Nobel Laureate Ferenc Krausz’s open letter to Prime Minister Péter Magyar has sent shockwaves around Hungarian society. The moving, honest account of the capricious and malicious destruction of one the most promising scientific talent development initiatives by the new globalist government, titled “Requiem for the Frontiers“, is a devastating testimony to the cultural, economic and social destruction that the TISZA government is involved in.
In an article simultaneously published in Index.hu, the prominent scientist starts with expressing his deep embarrassment over being forced to explain to senior foreign scientists, who have volunteered to join the project, that it has unexpectedly been cancelled by the Magyar government. “Three North American natural scientists identified an opportunity within the program that was worth playing a role in bringing to fruition—even in a country to which, unlike the two Hungarian members of the board of trustees, they owe absolutely nothing.
They are world-renowned, pioneering researchers who turn down at least nine out of every ten invitations. It is almost unbelievable, but they made an exception for us. One year later, on this very day, August 31, 2026, the Foundation was dissolved, and with it, its Board of Trustees,”
wrote Professor Krausz.
He made no qualms about what stood behind this inexplicable decision: “Since this is a political decision, it is not my place to pass judgment on it”, he added.
The multi-year project was meant to develop indigenous scientific talent in Hungary, as well as to attract Hungarian scientists from international research institutions and universities to return back to their homeland. “This concept has been lost, along with a governing body that was exceptional even by international standards, and with them, a vision that could have strengthened Hungary’s scientific and economic competitiveness in the long term. The team—committed to the cause and having coalesced into a true community during the trials of recent months—has also been lost”, pointed out Professor Krausz.
He continues to say that “we learned of the government’s intention to terminate the contract through social media. This occurred without any substantive presentation of Élvonal’s overall professional concept, its commitments, or its achievements to date prior to the decision.”
I believe that this lack of even minimal dialogue did not serve Hungary’s interests. Nor did it show the proper respect for the matter at hand”,
he says.
In short the message the Magyar government’s vindictive purge is sending out to Hungarian or international talent is – if you were to return home, your work and person will be subjected to political criteria. And if you do not show your due loyalty within the expected channels of the newly emerging cult of personality, instead o respect and recognition, you can expect to be subjected to bullying and obstruction.
Professor Krausz’ complaints implicitly refer back to earlier unsubstantiated accusations by Péter Horváth, State Secretary for Science Policy and Innovation. On August 26, he presented the new science and innovation strategy to the National Assembly’s Education Committee, where he also spoke disparagingly about the Élvonal case. items.body_text:
Meghalt egy munkás, miután lezuhant a szegedi kormányhivatal tetejéről
Lezuhant egy ipari alpinista kedden dél körül a Csongrád-Csanád Vármegyei Kormányhivatal tetejéről, és az épület mellett található Vármegye Étterem tetejére esett, ahol életét vesztette – értesült a Szegeder. Úgy tudjuk, a munkás legalább 15 métert zuhant, és beverte a fejét, ez okozhatta a halálát.
Fotósunk helyszíni képein láthatóak az épületről lógó kötelek, amelyeken az alpinista dolgozott, valamint az, hogy a helyszínen éppen a takarósátrat állítják fel munkások.
A rendőrség a Szegeder megkeresésére elmondta, hogy az ipari alpinista eddig ismeretlen okokból esett le. Az ügyben a Csongrád-Csanád Vármegyei Rendőr-főkapitányság foglalkoztatás körében elkövetett veszélyeztetés vétsége miatt nyomozást indított, amit szakértők bevonásával végeznek.
A szerző a Szegeder újságírója. A cikk a Szegeder és a Telex együttműködésének keretében jelenik meg a Telexen is.
A Telex fontosnak tartja, hogy az egész ország területéről szállíthasson az olvasóinak sztorikat, ezért közlünk gyakran vidéki riportokat. Mivel minden térséget nem tudunk lefedni budapesti szerkesztőségünkkel, keressük az együttműködést vidéki újságírókkal, és fokozatosan országos tudósítói hálózatot szeretnénk kiépíteni. Ez a cikk is egy ilyen együttműködés keretein belül készült.

items.title: Kiszáradt a Maros összes mellékfolyója Arad megyében, a folyó vízhozama a szokásos harmadára esett
items.summary: A magyar határ közelében már csak a sokéves átlag nagyjából harmadát szállítja a Maros. Makónál mínusz 117 centiméter a vízállás. Az aszály közel 80 ezer hektárnyi vetést is károsított.
items.body_text:
Kiszáradt a Maros összes mellékfolyója Arad megyében, a folyó vízhozama a szokásos harmadára esett
Kiszáradt a Maros összes mellékfolyója Arad megyében az elmúlt hónapok csapadékhiánya miatt, maga a folyó pedig a megyei szakaszán átlagosan már csak az ilyenkor megszokott vízmennyiség körülbelül harmadát szállítja.
A négy fő Arad megyei mérőpont mindegyikén jóval a sokéves átlag alatt van a Maros vízhozama. Soborsinnál másodpercenként 63,8 köbmétert mértek, ami nagyjából a fele az ilyenkor megszokottnak. Lippánál már csak a sokéves átlag 26 százalékát, Aradnál 29 százalékát, a magyar határ közelében fekvő romániai Nagylaknál pedig 32 százalékát szállította a folyó. Utóbbi mérőpontnál másodpercenként 42,8 köbméteres vízhozamot mértek.
A Maros innen Magyarország felé tart, majd Apátfalva és Makó térségén halad keresztül, végül Szegednél ömlik a Tiszába. A magyar vízügy adatai szerint szeptember 1-jén 0 órakor Makónál mínusz 117 centiméteres vízállást és másodpercenként 36,9 köbméteres vízhozamot mértek.
A mínusz 117 centiméter önmagában is beszédes adat: 2022-ben még ez számított a valaha mért legalacsonyabb makói vízállásnak. Ezt 2025-ben több új negatív rekord is megdöntötte, október elején mínusz 124 centiméterig süllyedt a folyó. A Telexnek akkor nyilatkozó kutató szerint a Maros vízszintje 2012 óta tartósan csökken, és a vízhozama is egyre kisebb.
A román vízügyi szakemberek szerint Arad megyében nagyon nagy a baj, mert nincs utánpótlás, ugyanis a Maros valamennyi mellékfolyója kiszáradt. A folyó ugyanakkor még nincs történelmi mélyponton: a régióban mért legalacsonyabb vízhozamot 1985 januárjában jegyezték fel, akkor másodpercenként alig 15,5 köbméter vizet szállított.
A hónapok óta tartó szárazság a mezőgazdaságban is komoly károkat okozott. Mintegy 1300 Arad megyei gazda jelentett károkat az őszi vetésekben, elsősorban a búzában. Összesen 79 359 hektárnyi terület érintett, ahol a felmérések szerint 30–70 százalék közötti a kár.
Augusztus végén már írtunk arról, hogy a magyar–román határ mindkét oldalán látványosan kiégtek a földek. Akkor csak a tavaszi vetésekre 995 kárbejelentés érkezett Arad megyében, több mint 23 ezer hektárról, egyes kukorica- és napraforgótáblákon pedig 90 százalék fölötti, helyenként csaknem teljes terméskárról számoltak be. A határ magyar oldalán sem volt sokkal jobb a helyzet: az Alföldön augusztus végére a kukorica és a napraforgó jelentős része elszáradt.
A rendkívüli szárazság és a vízkészletek apadása miatt többszintű korlátozás is érvényben van. A megnövekedett fogyasztás és a tározók lassú utántöltődése miatt az Aradi Vízügyi Vállalat különböző korlátozásokat léptetett életbe: 16 Arad megyei településen éjszakai vízkorlátozás van, minden éjszaka elzárják a vizet éjfél és hajnali négy óra között, hogy a tározók nyomása és tartaléka napközbenre helyreálljon. Vannak olyan kritikus fekvésű települések a megyében, például Kiszend, ahol a felszíni patakok teljes elapadása miatt a lakosok naponta mindössze 2 órán át kapnak vizet a hálózatból. A helyi hatóságok szigorúan szabályozzák a felszíni vizek kivételét is. A kritikus vízhozam miatt a Maros menti gazdáknak korlátozták vagy megtiltották a folyóvíz közvetlen használatát öntözési célokra, megvédve a minimális ökológiai vízmennyiséget.

items.title: Két új elnökhelyettest kapott az Integritás Hatóság
items.summary: Így öttagú lesz az igazgatóság a már erősebb jogkörökkel bíró testületben.
items.body_text:
Két új elnökhelyettest kapott az Integritás Hatóság
Bozzay Erika és Nagy-Fribiczer Gabriella kerülhet az Integritás Hatóság elnökhelyettesi posztjára, az Állami Számvevőszék elnöke az ő kinevezésüket javasolta a köztársasági elnöknek – írja az MTI a hatóság keddi közleménye alapján.
Az Integritás Hatóság igazgatósága ezzel öttagúvá válik, egy elnökből és négy elnökhelyettesből fog állni. A két új helyettes Biró Ferenc elnökhöz, Dabóczi Kálmán és Holbusz Tímea elnökhelyettesekhez csatlakozik.
Mindkét új elnökhelyettes több évtizedes szakmai tapasztalattal rendelkezik. Nagy-Fribiczer Gabriella korábban az Integritás Hatóság szakmai igazgatóságán dolgozott. Bozzay Erika erős hazai és nemzetközi vezetői tapasztalattal bír a közbeszerzés, az integritás, a korrupcióellenes szakpolitikák és a közpénzügyi kormányzás terén.
Idén módosították az Integritás Hatóságról szóló törvényt, amivel bővítették a hatáskörét. Augusztus 26-án lépett életbe a változás, így már a kiemelt közjogi és kormányzati tisztségviselők és hozzátartozóik vagyonnyilatkozataihoz is hozzáférnek. Emellett a közbeszerzési eljárásokat is erősebb jogosítványokkal vizsgálhatják.

September 19: Celebrate South Africa's Heritage Braai Day in Prague
Prague Morning
On Saturday, 19 September, Prague’s Rohan Beer Garden will host Heritage Braai Day, bringing the flavors and traditions of South Africa to the city.
The event is organized by Saffa Maso.
From noon, visitors can enjoy a relaxed day of grilling, music and socializing outdoors.
Heritage Day in South Africa is a public holiday celebrating the country’s cultural diversity. It has also become closely associated with the tradition of braai, or South African-style barbecuing, with friends and family gathering around the grill to share food.
In Prague, the event is open to everyone and will feature multiple grills, allowing visitors to prepare their own food. Those who prefer to leave the cooking to someone else can use the on-site grill master service, available for an additional fee.
Standard tickets include grills, coals and all braai equipment. Visitors can also choose a braai package, which includes 500g of traditional boerewors sausage and 150g of biltong.
On-site, guests will also be able to purchase Nando’s sauces, chutney, braai spices and other South African products.
Visitors should not bring their own drinks, as a selection of alcoholic and non-alcoholic beverages will be available at the venue. Guests should bring their own plates and cutlery, although disposable options are also allowed.
Tickets are available via SMSTicket at this link. Children under 12 enter free.

Prague Philharmonic Could Begin Construction in 2028. New Visuals Reveal Design
Prague Morning
Prague has taken another step toward building the long-planned Vltava Philharmonic.
The Prague Development Company (PDS) submitting an application for planning permission and new visualizations revealing the project in greater detail.
The application covers not only the Philharmonic building but also the surrounding public spaces, transport infrastructure and connections to the existing metro, tram, road, cycling and pedestrian networks.
If the permitting process stays on schedule, the city expects to receive the necessary approval in the first quarter of 2027. A tender for the construction company would then follow, with building work potentially starting in the first quarter of 2028.
The project is planned for the Bubny-Zátory district, near the existing Vltavská metro station. The new cultural complex is expected to be completed in 2033, when trial operations could begin.
The building was designed by Danish architecture studio BIG – Bjarke Ingels Group, which won an international competition in May 2022. Preparation of the detailed permit documentation began in 2025.
The complex will have three underground levels and six floors above ground. It will contain five music halls, creative spaces, restaurants and other facilities.
The project is also intended to provide new premises for the Prague Symphony Orchestra FOK and music collections belonging to the Municipal Library of Prague. The Czech Philharmonic is also expected to gain additional facilities, addressing the limitations of its current premises.
Construction could start in early 2028
The current estimated cost of the Philharmonic building is around CZK 12.33 billion, including equipment but excluding VAT. The surrounding infrastructure and public spaces are expected to cost an additional CZK 5 billion, also excluding VAT.

items.body_text:
Tiny Steps, Big Milestones: What Really Matters When Toddlers Start Preschool
Prague Morning
For a one-year-old, starting preschool is not about learning letters or sitting through lessons.
It is about feeling safe without Mum or Dad nearby, discovering the joy of playing alongside other children, and slowly gaining the confidence to explore the world independently. At Tiny Tots in Prague, these small everyday moments are at the heart of the programme.
A favourite toy clutched tightly in one hand. A cautious look back at Mum or Dad from the classroom door. Perhaps a few tears (from either side).
For families with children aged one or two, the first experience of leaving a little one in someone else’s care can feel like a very big step.
And for the child, it is one too.
At this age, development happens through moments that can look almost insignificant to adults: reaching for a spoon without help, joining another child in play, recognising a familiar song, saying a new word, or feeling comfortable enough to wander a little further away from a trusted adult.
These are precisely the moments that Tiny Tots, a programme for children aged 1–2 at Nessie English Preschool, part of Park Lane International School, is designed to encourage.
Before learning comes feeling safe
For very young children, a good first preschool experience begins with something much more fundamental than an academic curriculum: trust.
“Parents often want to know how their child will cope with separation, whether we can follow the rhythm they are used to at home and, above all, whether their child will really be seen as an individual,” says Catalina Gonzalez-Got, who leads the Tiny Tots programme.
Catalina knows the feeling from both sides. An early-years educator with international experience, she is also a mother herself. Becoming a parent, she says, gave her a much deeper understanding of how emotional it can be to entrust a young child to somebody else for the first time.
That is why settling in is treated as a process rather than a test that a toddler is expected to pass on day one.
Some children may quickly become curious about their new surroundings. Others need more time, reassurance and proximity to a familiar adult before they are ready to explore.
Both are perfectly normal. The goal is to allow each child to find that confidence at their own pace.
For toddlers, play is serious business
Adults sometimes separate “playing” and “learning”. Toddlers do not.
When a child squishes playdough between their fingers, listens to a story, sings along to a familiar song, explores the garden or watches another toddler build something, they are constantly learning.
They are practising movement and coordination. They are discovering cause and effect. They are learning how to communicate, negotiate space with other children, manage emotions and make choices.
Tiny Tots therefore follows a play-based approach inspired by the English Early Years Foundation Stage framework, with activities designed around the developmental needs of one- and two-year-olds.
There are no miniature school desks or pressure to perform.
Instead, children encounter language, movement, music, creative activities, sensory experiences, stories and outdoor play as a natural part of their day.
The programme keeps the class to a maximum of eight children, allowing teachers to pay close attention to individual personalities, routines and developmental stages.
English without the flashcards
The same philosophy applies to language.
At one or two years old, learning English does not mean memorising vocabulary lists. Children absorb language through relationships and repetition: hearing the same words during snack time, listening to songs, following simple instructions, sharing a picture book or hearing an adult describe what is happening during play.
Tiny Tots provides an English-language environment, giving children regular, natural exposure to the language throughout their day.

items.body_text:
NBG Introduces Two-Day Wait for ‘High-Risk Transactions’ by People Over 60
As of September 1, Georgian banks and other payment service providers are required to temporarily suspend or refuse certain “high-risk” transactions initiated by customers aged over 60, under a regulation that the National Bank of Georgia (NBG) says is aimed at protecting elderly customers from “fraudulent schemes.”
The measure applies to transactions exceeding GEL 500 (approximately USD 180) that are associated with activities considered to carry a high fraud risk, including online trading (“forex”), investment schemes, gambling, and virtual assets. The regulation also covers transactions deemed to reflect “unusual behavior.”
Under a decree adopted by the NBG President in April that took effect today, payment service providers “must temporarily suspend, or where suspension is not feasible, refuse the execution of a transaction initiated by the customer if it is deemed high-risk.”
In such cases, the provider must contact the customer and provide information to “support better decision-making, thereby reducing the risk of manipulation by fraudsters,” according to the decree. Customers will then have 48 hours after initiating a high-risk and/or suspicious transaction to make a final decision on whether to proceed.
The regulation further states that if a customer refuses to allow a suspended electronic payment transaction to proceed, or if the provider is unable to contact the customer during the suspension period, it “shall not execute the corresponding payment order.” At the same time, “the customer is not restricted from re-initiating the same electronic payment transaction,” the regulation says.
The regulation currently applies only to “card-based transactions.” From May 1, 2027, it will also apply to “other electronic payment transactions.”
The NBG said the changes are intended to “strengthen safeguards for vulnerable groups, particularly customers aged over 60, and improve protection against fraudulent schemes.”
Former National Bank President and ex-opposition United National Movement lawmaker Roman Gotsiridze criticized the measure, dismissing it as “complete absurd.”
“Why should a person’s age automatically mean that they need additional ‘screening’ when managing their own money? If the goal is protection from fraud, why is age the main criterion?” Gotsiridze asked.

Illegally Detained Georgian Citizen Released From Tskhinvali Custody
An illegally detained Georgian citizen has been released from custody in the occupied Tskhinvali/South Ossetia region and transferred to Tbilisi-controlled territory, the State Security Service of Georgia (SSSG) said on September 1.
While the SSSG did not disclose the individual’s identity, in line with its recent practice, the Res news agency based in occupied Tskhinvali identified him as 31-year-old Giorgi Uznadze, detained on March 17 and accused of “illegally crossing the state border.” Res said that he was handed over to “the Georgian side” after serving a six-month sentence.
“The Georgian central government regularly raised the issue of the Georgian citizen’s unconditional release from illegal detention within the framework of the Incident Prevention and Response Mechanism (IPRM) and the Geneva International Discussions,” the SSSG said.
The agency also noted that both the hotline mechanism and all other instruments available to the Georgian side were used intensively, adding that “international partners were also actively involved in the negotiations.”
According to the SSSG’s latest annual report, 34 cases of illegal detention were recorded around the occupied Tskhinvali region in 2025, while 40 cases were recorded in Abkhazia.

items.body_text:
Court of Appeals Revokes Plea Deal With October 4 Defendant Giorgi Kirvalidze
Tbilisi Court of Appeals has annulled the plea agreement reached with Giorgi Kirvalidze, an athlete who was convicted in the October 4 election-day unrest case, as the judge and prosecutors argued the defendant failed to genuinely acknowledge his guilt. His case will be returned to the first-instance court for renewed consideration.
The ruling, issued by Judge Giorgi Keratishvili on August 31, followed a request from the Prosecutor’s Office to annul the agreement, as the prosecution argued that Kirvalidze had failed to genuinely acknowledge his guilt, which it said was a necessary condition for the plea agreement.
Kirvalidze was among 34 defendants who reached plea agreements with the prosecution out of more than 60 people tried in connection with the October 4, 2025, unrest. The athlete belonged to a group of 12 who received reduced prison sentences through a June 24 court ruling, resulting in a one-year prison sentence followed by three years of suspended sentence, meaning he was expected to be released in the autumn.
At the June 24 hearing, Kirvalidze reportedly rejected the plea deal and swore at ruling Georgian Dream party founder Bidzina Ivanishvili, but only after he had pleaded guilty, and the judge had already issued the relevant ruling, leaving the plea agreement in force, according to RFE/RL’s Georgian Service.
At the August 31 hearing, Kirvalidze told the court he had acted out of frustration in a June hearing and now regretted his actions, reaffirming his admission of guilt, RFE/RL reported, with the outlet citing the judge as saying that he “did not have an impression of [Kirvalidze’s] sincere admission of guilt.”
“The defendant sometimes admits [guilt] and sometimes doesn’t, which is not a serious attitude,” Roin Khintibidze, the prosecutor on the case, told journalists. According to him, “the judge must be certain that the defendant is genuinely admitting guilt voluntarily, rather than being driven by other motives. In this case, the judge could not be certain that the admission of guilt truly reflected the defendant’s will.”
Boris Chele Kurua, Kirvalidze’s lawyer, dismissed the ruling as “unfounded” and “unsubstantiated,” saying the Prosecutor’s Office sought to annul the plea agreement over the content of Kirvalidze’s remark, rather than because Kirvalidze himself had asked for the agreement to be cancelled. He said the defense would appeal the ruling.

items.title: The destruction of the Tbilisi Tubes — a tale of urban tensions, vendetta, and alleged corruption
items.summary: Rike’s controversial landmark is coming down, but the vices that shaped its fate remain.
items.body_text:
The destruction of the Tbilisi Tubes — a tale of urban tensions, vendetta, and alleged corruption
Rike’s controversial landmark is coming down, but the vices that shaped its fate remain.
‘Just as Bilbao made a name for itself with the Guggenheim, Rike will become one of the most beautiful tourist destinations in the world’, then-Georgian President Mikheil Saakashvili said in May 2011 as he opened a new park in central Tbilisi’s Rike area.
For Saakashvili, the Music Theatre and Exhibition Hall — two interlocking structures of glass and steel sitting at the edge of the park — were to be Tbilisi’s answer to the Guggenheim. A symbolic time capsule was buried that day, marking the start of what the then-president called an ‘epochal building’ and potentially the most ‘pride-worthy’ among his projects of the period.
The building — designed by renowned Italian architects Massimiliano and Doriana Fuksas — indeed took shape, but with Saakashvili’s party losing power in 2012 soon after construction began, it was never opened to the public, remaining empty and unfinished. Even its real name stayed largely unknown, as its distinctive shape instead earned it nicknames such as the ‘Rike Jugs’ and ‘Rike Tubes’.
‘I’m not an architect, but I think this ugliness does not belong in our beautiful capital’, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze would say in May 2025, 14 years after the now-imprisoned Saakashvili’s Guggenheim remark, as the government gave the green light to dismantle the building.
Now, as the structure is being deconstructed piece by piece, there is no shortage of interpretations of what the work and its removal will ultimately come to symbolise in the history of Georgia and its capital, including that the current leadership is punishing architecture out of hatred of its predecessor.
The structure’s past is also coming to the fore, with emphasis on the project’s unconventional design and its highly controversial location in the city’s historic centre and accusations of corruption tied to the building’s dysfunction, its sale by the state at an exceptionally low price, and subsequent resales — along with the alleged squandering of vast amounts of public money.
At the same time, residents of Tbilisi still have no idea what will be erected (through private investment) on the sizeable plot of land within the park where they stood — a question that brings the debate back to what some see as its common thread: no one is asking the people of Tbilisi what should happen to their city.
Conceiving a ‘new Georgia’
Saakashvili’s government promoted the redevelopment of Rike as a symbol of overcoming the socio-political disorder that had preceded its rule — a narrative his pro-Western United National Movement (UNM) party, which rose to power in the 2003 Rose Revolution, repeatedly invoked in defining its political identity.
Several years before the Rike Park was built, the authorities demolished the restaurants occupying the site, which had largely popped up during the crises-ridden 1990s — ‘tacky’, ‘illegal’ eateries from the ‘bad old days’, as Saakashvili called them during the 2011 inauguration of the park.
However, state intervention in the historic Rike district, on the left bank of the Mtkvari River, did not begin under the UNM. Decades earlier, in the 1970s, Soviet authorities decided to demolish the old residential neighbourhood there, citing its proximity to the river and the frequent flooding.
Afterward, the cleared site became a gathering place for public events, mainly Tbilisoba, the Soviet-introduced festival celebrating the capital. The area would later once again be filled, this time with the kind of eating houses Saakashvili had described, before being cleared once more.
By the time Rike Park opened, several landmark structures had already reshaped the area or were under construction, becoming symbols of Saakashvili’s rule — from the glass Bridge of Peace linking the park to the river’s right bank and the nearby mushroom-roofed Public
