items.title: Georgian government scraps two posts created for now-retired Mdinaradze
items.summary: Georgia’s Parliamentary Speaker Shalva Papuashvili said the posts had been created based on the former Georgian Dream leader’s ‘personal capabilities’.
items.body_text:
The Georgian government has announced plans to abolish two state posts created for a senior member of the ruling Georgian Dream party, Mamuka Mdinaradze, who recently said he quit politics. Those include the State Ministry for Coordination of Law Enforcement Agencies, which Mdinaradze briefly headed, and the State Ministry for Regional Policy, a position that had yet to be fully cemented.
Speaking to journalists in parliament on Monday, Parliamentary Speaker Shalva Papuashvili announced that the position of State Minister for Coordination of Law Enforcement Agencies, which Mdinaradze held from 21 April to 29 July 2026, will be abolished. Mdinaradze subsequently served as Minister of Regional Development until 27 August.
The position of State Minister for Regional Policy Issues, which had been announced as Mdinaradze’s latest position, will also no longer be created.
Papuashvili also said the Ministry of Regional Development and the Ministry of Infrastructure will be merged into one agency. The head of the unified structure will be Revaz Sokhadze, the current Infrastructure Minister.
Asked by journalists why the ruling party had changed its mind about creating the regional policy position, Papuashvili replied that the posts had been created based on Mdinaradze’s ‘personal capabilities’.
‘It was stated from the very beginning that the tasks that Prime Minister assigned to Mamuka Mdinaradze to coordinate law enforcement agencies at that time were based on his personal capabilities, and he performed that function very well, and this coordination is very well organised today. There was a desire to do the same in terms of coordination in the regional direction’, he said.
‘Given that Mamuka Mdinaradze decided to leave politics, there is no longer a need for this’, Papuashvili said, adding that parliament will soon discuss further government changes in its next session.
The creation of the State Minister for Regional Policy Issues position required a parliamentary vote. Given that parliament was on its summer recess, Mdinaradze was expected to take up the position in the second week of September.
On 27 August, however, Mdinaradze unexpectedly announced that he was resigning from his position and leaving politics.
His resignation came several days after imprisoned former Prime Minister Irakli Gharibashvili alleged that, ‘on the instructions of [Georgian Dream founder] Bidzina Ivanishvili’ and through Mdinaradze’s mediation, he had been pressured to confess to corruption crimes in order to prevent him from entering politics in the future.
Mdinaradze rejected the claims, saying he had never sent Gharibashvili a letter.
Mdinaradze first rose to prominence as Georgian Dream’s parliamentary leader from 2016 until 2025, becoming one of the most recognisable figures in the ruling party.
Over the past several months, Mdinaradze has held three different positions.
In September 2025, he was appointed head of the State Security Service (SSG), Georgia’s domestic intelligence agency, a position he held for more than six months.
On 21 April, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze announced that Mdinaradze would become Deputy Prime Minister and State Minister for the Coordination of Law Enforcement Agencies.
His appointment to the state ministerial post after leaving the SSG raised questions within ruling circles about a possible decline in his influence.
On 29 July, Kobakhidze announced that Mdinaradze would become State Minister for Regional Policy. The new position was scheduled to be created in September, but Mdinaradze was subsequently appointed Minister of Regional Development.

items.summary: Yerevan says it will begin exporting goods to Azerbaijan ‘in the next few days’.
items.body_text:
Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev have met on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, where they discussed the peace process and the delimitation of their shared border. On the same day, Armenia hinted that it might soon begin exporting goods to Azerbaijan.
The meeting was their first since Armenia’s June parliamentary elections and came shortly after the first anniversary of the Washington Summit, held on 8 August 2025, where the two sides initialled a peace treaty and agreed to establish the Trump Route, which would connect mainland Azerbaijan to its exclave of Nakhchivan through Armenian territory.
According to the similar readouts issued by both Azerbaijan and Armenia, Pashinyan and Aliyev discussed the progress already made in the peace process and plans for further actions.
The sides also described the export of Azerbaijani petroleum products to Armenia, which began in December 2025, as well as Azerbaijan’s role in the transit of grain and other goods originating from third countries as ‘important practical manifestations of the dividends of peace’.
They also underscored the importance of continuing the delimitation process, and discussed ‘further practical steps related to the implementation’ of the agreements and ‘underlined the significance of connectivity projects along the TRIPP’.
‘The leaders also welcomed contacts between the business communities and exchanged views on opportunities for further expanding mutually beneficial economic, trade, and energy cooperation’, the readout said.
On the same day, Armenian Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan said in an interview with Armenia’s Public TV that soon Armenian will start exports to Azerbaijan.
‘In the next few days you will learn that Azerbaijani companies bought goods from Armenian companies’, Mirzoyan said, without specifying what kind of goods would be exported to Azerbaijan.
This would make trade between the two countries bilateral — so far, it has consisted predominantly of Azerbaijani petroleum product exports to Armenia.
In January, Armenia and Azerbaijan exchanged a list of potential goods they could trade. Later, Armenian Economy Minister Gevorg Papoyan told Armenian media that Yerevan was in talks with Baku to export aluminum foil, ferromolybdenum, domesticated animals, raw materials for brandy, tobacco, textile, roses, and other greenhouse products.
The leaders’ meeting in Bishkek was followed by several other meetings between Armenian and Azerbaijani officials, including between Mirzoyan and his Azerbaijani counterpart Jeyhun Bayramov.
On the same day, newly appointed Armenian Security Council Secretary Alen Simonyan met with Hikmet Hajiyev, Aliyev’s aide and head of his administration’s foreign policy department, again in Bishkek.

items.title: Finland still has Europe's worst unemployment
items.summary: Finland, Spain and Sweden continue to have the highest unemployment rates in the EU, according to Eurostat.
items.body_text:
Finland's slow economic recovery has yet to translate into a meaningful rise in jobs.
In July, the unemployment rate stood at 10.5 percent, ahead of Spain's 10 and Sweden's 8.6 percent, according to EU number cruncher Eurostat, which released the bloc's latest jobless figures on Tuesday.
Finland moved into the undesirable position last November of having the EU's worst unemployment rate.
The rates in Finland and Spain have remained at similar levels for almost a year. In previous years, Spain's unemployment rate was much higher than Finland's.
Neighbouring Sweden also has a relatively high unemployment rate by EU standards.
More people looking for jobs
Finland's rising unemployment has partly been attributed to a growing labour force. More people are now available to work than before.
At the same time, the Finnish economy has been stuck in a downturn, with fewer jobs on offer. The result is that more people have been left without work.
Despite all this, there are some tentative signs that the labour market may be on the verge of a turnaround.

items.title: Finland answers America's Nato "loyalty test"
items.summary: The Pentagon has sent Nato allies a questionnaire probing whether they are living up to Donald Trump's vision for the transatlantic alliance.
items.body_text:
Finland has responded to a US questionnaire asking Nato allies whether they support Washington's foreign policy priorities.
The Pentagon sent the questionnaire to allies in July. Finland's response was prepared by the defence ministry in consultation with the foreign ministry, the president's office and the government.
Washington is seeking allies' views on Nato participation and on shifting more of the alliance's defence costs and responsibilities to European countries. Most of the questions focused directly on defence.
Europeans avoid antagonising US
Nato allies have sought to avoid antagonising President Donald Trump, hoping to preserve his pledge that America will continue to help defend Europe.
Some questions in the survey addressed each country's relationship with America. Finland's answers described the relationship in broad terms. One Yle source characterised the response as "fact-based, not flattering".
News network Bloomberg, which first reported on the letter in July, dubbed it a "loyalty test". The questionnaire is part of America's plans to reduce its military presence in Europe in countries Washington believes are not spending enough on their own defence or supporting American foreign policy.
Some questions also touched indirectly on America's military action against Iran and Venezuela, including the capture and transfer to the United States of Venezuela's president, Nicolás Maduro.
Finland did not answer these more politically sensitive questions directly, instead highlighting issues it wanted to emphasise.
Nato allies have previously said they would help secure the Strait of Hormuz after hostilities end and uphold the rule of law.
Finland is among the European Nato members spending the most on defence and plans to raise spending further, towards Nato's target of 3.5 percent of GDP. The country is also buying new fighter jets from America and continuing close cooperation with the US armed forces.
Yle was unable to reach Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen (NCP) for comment on Finland's response.
In July, however, Häkkänen told Yle that Finland had taken the right steps by investing in national defence, strengthening its defence industry and deepening cooperation with the US.

items.title: 54-year-olds got the biggest pension boost last year
items.summary: 2025 was the final year of higher pension accrual rates for 53- to 62-year-olds.
items.body_text:
For Finland's 54-year-olds, 2025 was a particularly good year for growing older, at least on paper. They accrued more new pension benefits than any other age group, thanks in part to the last hurrah of a more generous accrual rate.
Workers in their 50s accrued an average of 57 euros in new earnings-related pension benefits in 2025, according to an estimate by the Finnish Centre for Pensions (ETK).
It was the final year in which workers aged 53–62 accrued pension benefits at a rate of 1.7 percent, rather than the standard 1.5 percent.
The higher accrual rate meant that 54-year-olds, people born in 1971, gained the most, with their projected future pension increasing by 63 euros over the year.
ETK's estimate covers all earnings-related pension-insured people living in Finland who were not already retired.

items.title: Chef worked for more than three years in Sweden after missing Brexit deadline
items.summary: It took until April 2025 – more than five years after the UK left the EU – for Gavin Watkins to realise he should have applied for post-Brexit residency. He has since lost his job, unemployment insurance and risks deportation.
items.body_text:
Since January 2022, when he, entirely without realising it, had lost his right to live and work in Sweden, he had continued working as head chef at two restaurants at Stockholm's Gröna Lund amusement park, paying taxes, and looking after his two children.
"I was living in a bubble," he shrugs when asked how he possibly could have missed something so momentous as Brexit. "I live in a Swedish world. I speak Swedish. I work in Swedish. I talk Swedish with my kids. It just kind of washed over my head, and I didn't think about it, and I didn't think of what the outcome would be."
Watkins is at risk of being the latest British citizen to be deported from Sweden as a result of either a late application for post-Brexit residency or a failure to meet Sweden's strict interpretation of the requirements for post-Brexit residency.
According to Eurostat, Sweden has issued deportation orders to 2,500 British nationals since 2021, a third of the total number of Brits ordered to leave across the EU. The UK Foreign Office calculates fully 27.5 percent of Britons in Sweden were refused post-Brexit residency, compared to an EU average of under 4 percent.
Another British citizen, who runs a Facebook Group for British long-term residents of Sweden who, like her, have been denied post-Brexit residency, suspects there are many more British citizens Watkins who have managed to continue living and working in Sweden for years without discovering that they have lost their right to reside in the country.
"I suspect there are more, although I don't honestly know how they have navigated Swedish digital hurdles so long and are only now discovering they are 'illegal'," she says.
Watkins has been living in Sweden for over 20 years, moving over after meeting his Swedish wife at a restaurant he worked in back home in Bristol, UK. In that time, he has worked his way up from being a line chef at Gröna Lund to running Tyrol, the park's most upmarket restaurant.
He only realised the trouble he was in when he took a rare trip back to the UK and was stopped at Copenhagen Airport and asked for a residency permit card.
"I froze at that point. I had no idea and she could quite clearly see that on my face. She was kind of cocky, because she said to me, 'Oh, so you've been living in Sweden for 20 years, and you didn't know you needed a residency permit?' Actually, no, I didn't."
The border guard called over an officer who stamped his passport. "He said, if you have any problems coming back into Denmark, just show this stamp, and you'll be allowed to go on your way back to Stockholm, so that was basically where it all started."
When he got back he contacted the Migration Agency, eventually speaking to an official on the phone.
"She said, 'wait, you've been working?' I said, 'well, of course, why wouldn't I be working?' 'Oh, but you're not supposed to be working because you don't have a residency permit'." I said, 'well, this is why I'm contacting you because I didn't receive any of this information. And it just sort of went downhill after that'."

Watkins made a late application for post-Brexit residency and three months later was told he was allowed to stay in Sweden and continue working while the application was processed. When the application was rejected two months later, he applied for a spouse permit, deciding to apply from within Sweden despite the risk he might be rejected for not applying from outside the country.
The human resources department from Gröna Lund then got involved and were soon told that he had lost the right to work in Sweden.
"They told my HR department that Gavin is no longer allowed to work within Sweden. We have now taken away his residency permit has been taken away. So there and then, after 15 years of working for the same company, I lost my job, and that's also where everything started to really crash."

items.title: Swedish word of the day: förtidsröstning
items.summary: Swedes are able to vote in advance for elections, either by post or in election booths in schools, libraries and other municipal buildings. But where does the word for advance voting – förtidsröstning – come from?
items.body_text:
As with many Swedish words, förtidsröstning is a compound word – a word made up of two or more words merging to form a new one.
The first half of the word, förtid, is itself a compound word made up of the words för (before) and tid (time), and usually refers to something happening prematurely or in advance, before the time it was supposed to happen.
Someone can, for example åldras i förtid (age prematurely), and people who had to stop working earlier than expected due to an illness were previously known as förtidspensionärer (early retirees). You wouldn't say that a child born prematurely was född i förtid, though. Instead, you'd say they were för tidigt född (literally: born too early).

It's similar to the word förskott, which often refers to some sort of bill or money paid out in advance, such as förskott på lön (salary paid out in advance of work) or förskottshyra (rent paid in advance). You'll also see this word in the phrase ta inte ut segern i förskott, which essentially means you shouldn't start celebrating a win or victory before the match or battle is over.
There are a number of other words which start with för and mean variations of something happening in advance. One of these is på förhand, which you might see in the phrase tack på förhand (thanks in advance). Another is i förväg, for example in the phrase det kan man inte veta i förväg (it's not possible to know that in advance).
There's also förrän, which is more accurately translated as "before" or "until": jag kommer inte kunna träffas förrän klockan 12 (I won't be able to meet you before 12 o'clock). An interesting quirk of förrän is that you can only use it in negative phrases. To use the example above, if you could meet the person in question before 12 o'clock, you'd say innan/före klockan 12 instead.
THE LOCAL'S GUIDE: How to vote in advance in Sweden's 2026 election
Now, let's look at the second half of the word förtidsröstning, röstning. This comes from the verb att rösta, to vote, plus the suffix -ning, which gives us the noun form of the verb, voting. A suffix is a letter or group of letters, like -ly, -ing, or -ness in English, which is added onto the end of a word to form a new word.
If you think this -ning suffix in Swedish looks familiar, that's because it has the same Proto-Germanic root as the English suffix -ing, which is also often used to turn verbs into nouns.
Why is there an s between förtid and röstning, I hear you ask? That's because if the first part of a compound word is itself a compound word (förtid, in this case), you need to add an s between it and the second part of the compound word.
Make sure to remember the two dots on the ö in rösta, too. Jag har rostat means "I have toasted" or "I have rusted", not "I have voted".
Rösta in turn comes from the noun röst, which can mean both a vote and a voice. You'll see it in the word röstkort, the voting card issued to people who have rösträtt (the right to vote), but you won't see it in the word for a voting booth or polling station – this is a valbås (literally: election booth) or vallokal (election venue).
There is also a large number of compound words which include the word röst, like brevröst (postal vote), blankröst (blank vote), stödröst (a support or tactical vote, where you vote for a different party than the one you actually support, such as voting for a minor party in the same bloc in order to prevent them dropping out of parliament), and personröst, where you vote for a specific candidate rather than just voting for a party.
Although voting by post is another way of voting in advance, you wouldn't describe this as förtidsröstning, you'd call it a brevröst instead. Förtidsröstning is specifically used to describe going to an election booth before the election and voti

items.title: Politics in Sweden: The small-town demagogue aiming for a Riksdag spot
items.summary: A far-right demagogue in a medium-sized Swedish town could enter the Riksdag on the most extreme platform of any party in recent times. So who are the Örebro Party and Markus Allard?
items.body_text:
Örebro doesn't feel like an extreme place. Sweden's seventh largest city, it has a thriving university, a magnificent medieval castle and successful manufacturers. It has its problem areas, like many other places in Sweden, and last year was the scene of a deadly school shooting, but overall it remains pleasant and prosperous, like a Sweden in miniature.
Örebro is a microcosm of Sweden in other ways too: its citizens earn roughly the median Swedish salary. They also vote pretty much like the average Swede, and as a result the city is seen as a bit of a political bellwether.
So driving into the city last weekend it was a shock to be confronted by election posters from a local party polling in double figures locally:
"Ut med packet." Rough translation: "Out with the scum."
If there was any doubt which groups the poster, from Örebropartiet (the Örebro Party), was targeting, a visit to the party's website made it clear: immigrants and their Swedish-born children. In both its policies and its rhetoric the party has staked out a position far more extreme than the Sweden Democrats, currently the party furthest to the right in the Riksdag.
The party's demagogic leader, Markus Allard, has attracted rare national attention to the proceedings of Örebro's municipal council. He's an unlikely far-right rabble-rouser: he started out on the left of politics as an activist for the Left Party and his grandfather was a Social Democrat speaker of the Riksdag.
The party has received a donation worth half a million kronor from Daniel Berntsson, co-founder of Mullvad VPN. Allard says he takes frequent advice from right-wing activist Chang Frick.
Allard's invective has made national headlines – in a now notorious speech in the council chamber he called a fellow councillor "f-ing coward, f-ing fool, an out-and-out idiot". When told to moderate his tone, he replied "I'll use whatever f-ing tone I like".
Despite its name and Allard's roots in local politics, the Örebro Party has ambitions way beyond local issues; its overwhelming priority is making Sweden a "monocultural" country.
It wants to make it possible to strip citizenship, not only from immigrants but also from their children. It also wants new national censuses and the registration of fingerprints, iris scans and DNA, explicitly to identify people for expulsion.
It proposes incentives to raise birth rates among what it calls the "productive Swedish population".
There's more: the party wants to sack all judges in Sweden's Supreme Court. "The fish rots from the head," its manifesto asserts.
Now some polls hint Allard might become the first politician ever to get into parliament via a local mandate.
While parties usually need 4 percent of the vote nationally to get seats in the Riksdag, they can also enter by scoring 12 percent in a single constituency; a new poll by Novus for Örebro's local paper Nerikes Allehanda showed 15 percent of people in Örebro County plan to vote for Allard's party in the election to the regional council, held the same day as the general election.
It's certainly not nailed on for Allard – voters often vote for different parties in regional and national elections – but his entry into the Riksdag would be a sensation, not least as his platform would be easily the most extreme of any political party to reach the Riksdag in modern times. The worry for Sweden's mainstream politicians is that Örebro will be a bellwether this time too.

items.title: German word of the day: Eingewöhnen
items.summary: Even if you're a fully grown adult, September has a 'back-to-school' feel. This German word is a great one to know as you settle back into a productive routine.
items.body_text:
Got your new notebooks and pens at the ready? Or a shiny new desk planner? Or maybe you're finally gearing up to tackle that creative project?
You're not alone. All over the country, kids are starting school or getting back to the classroom, while everyone else is returning to work – or indeed the Bundestag – after the summer vacation period.
But if the first few days of the new season feel a little ungewohnt (unfamiliar), don't worry – settling in takes some time. And Germans have the perfect word for it.
What does Eingewöhnen mean?
Eingewöhnen, which sounds like this, means to settle into a new environment, routine or situation.
It is most commonly used reflexively – sich eingewöhnen. So you can 'sich in einer neuen Stadt eingewöhnen' (settle into a new city) or 'sich an einem neuen Arbeitsplatz eingewöhnen' (adapt to a new workplace).
There's also a noun to go with it: die Eingewöhnung which is often used to describe the transitional period during which a child is finding their feet at a Kita or school. You also might hear it when sports reporters are describing how new players are settling into the Bundesliga.
The word comes from gewöhnen – "to get used to" – and is combined with the handy prefix "ein". In this context "ein" gives the word a sense of settling or moving into something.
In the German language this prefix often signals you are integrating something or looking inwards. You can spot the same prefix in words such as einziehen (to move in), einsteigen (to get in/on) and eintreten (to enter).
Even though they mean similar things, it's worth noting the distinction between gewöhnen and eingewöhnen. Sich an etwas gewöhnen generally means to get used to something, while sich eingewöhnen has more of a sense of settling into or finding your feet in a new place or environment.
READ ALSO: German word of the day - Schlendrian
Use it like this:
Ich muss mich erst in meiner neuen Wohnung eingewöhnen.
I still need to settle into my new flat.
Sie hat sich in der Kita wirklich gut eingewöhnt.
She settled into the daycare really well.
Wie schnell hast du dich in deinem neuen Kiez eingewöhnt?
How quickly did you settle into your new neighbourhood?

items.title: Q&A: What are your rights while waiting for a German residence permit?
items.summary: Many foreigners need a residence permit to stay in Germany legally. Residence permits can be renewed a few weeks before expiry, but waiting times of several months or more are common. So what are your rights while you wait to hear back?
items.body_text:
Can you keep working in Germany?
Whether or not you can work while waiting for your next residence permit depends on the kind of residence permit you had previously.
Generally, if your last residence permit granted you the right to work in Germany then you can keep working until your permit is renewed or a new one is issued.
But if your last residence permit did not allow you to work in Germany, then you’ll need to receive a new one that permits employment before you can legally begin work.
Put simply: If you are already legally working in Germany you can continue to do so until your residency status is changed. If you are waiting to get approval to start working, then you will, unfortunately, have to wait.
READ ALSO: Germany's 'temporary' permits are becoming an ongoing issue for foreign residents
Can you leave Germany?
You are technically free to leave Germany while waiting for your residence permit, but it’s getting back in that may be the tricky part.
Once your residence permit has expired you’ve lost the legal right to enter Germany, so if you were stopped at the border you could feasibly be denied entry. You would then need to wait in another country until your new residence permit is granted, and that process could be complicated if you fail to appear at the immigration office where you applied.
So if you are from a country that doesn’t have a free entry agreement with Germany, you’d be advised to avoid travelling internationally until you’ve received your new visa or otherwise obtained permission for re-entry.
If you do need to travel while waiting for a new residence permit, you can usually gain permission to do so in the form of a temporary stay permit (Fiktionsbescheinigung) that allows for re-entry. Note that not all of these temporary permits allow travel beyond Germany, so make sure that yours does before leaving the country.
READ ALSO: When do foreigners in Germany qualify for an expedited residence permit for travel?
What if you come from a visa-free country?
If you come from a country that has a visa-free entry agreement with Germany, then you shouldn’t have a problem re-entering the country, even while waiting for a new visa, and then you can stay as you wait for your residence permit to be extended.
Most European countries, including those in the Schengen zone and the UK, maintain “freedom of movement” agreements with Germany. Outside of Europe the US, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Korea, Singapore, Japan, and many countries in South America also maintain free-entry agreements with Germany. You can find a complete list here.
But be aware that you may eventually need to prove that you are waiting for your residence permit to remain in the country.
Visa-free non-EU citizens entering Schengen are only allowed to stay in the bloc for 90 days out of every 180 before they require a visa. So if you're time in Germany or Europe has exceeded this limit, you may need to show that you are waiting for a residence permit. Evidence for this could include a copy of the visa application that you had turned in to immigration, as well as a note of receipt from said immigration office.
You should also keep your previous residence permit - even if it's expired - until the next one is issued.
Does this apply to me if I have a permanent residence permit?
No, this only applies to those holding temporary residence permits.
If you have a permanent residence permit and your residence permit card expires or is lost, just book an appointment at your local immigration office to have your card replaced.
What’s the timeline for receiving a new residence permit?
Temporary residence permits are valid for six months up to four years, depending on the permit and your circumstances. When your residence permit expiration date is approaching you can apply to renew it, or apply for a new one, at your local immigration authority or Ausländerbehörde.

items.title: How much should I tip in Germany?
items.summary: To assume that 'Europeans don't tip' would be a serious blunder. Here's a quick guide to tipping in Germany, from the standard amount to the cool and easy way to do so.
items.body_text:
For visitors in Germany, and foreigners just settling in, the country's tipping culture may feel like an unwritten code.
Unlike in the US, where leaving a tip is basically seen as standard, Germans insist that tips (Trinkgeld) are voluntary. But a new study suggests that, in practice, tipping is deeply embedded in everyday culture.
The latest evidence comes from TUI's 2026 tipping study, which surveyed 2,000 Germans about their tipping habits while on holiday.
Among the top findings are that Germans are among Europe's most enthusiastic tippers, and also that Germans tend to tip as much on vacation as they do in their hometowns.
Whether your visiting Germany on vacation, or trying to integrate in your new home, here's a look at how to tip like the locals.
Five to ten percent is normal
If you're looking for a simple rule of thumb, this traditional advice still holds.
According to TUI, just over half of Germans typically leave between five and 10 percent in restaurants, cafés, taxis and many other service settings. A further 21.2 percent of Germans tip 10 percent or more, while only 3.3 percent said they leave no tip at all.
Rather than leaving money on the table at the end of a meal, Germans often add the tip while paying, often instructing the server to round-up the bill.
In practice, this means that if a restaurant bill comes to €45, a customer might hand over €50 and say 'Stimmt so' (keep the change).
READ ALSO: How the 'tip button' is disrupting Germany's tipping culture
The same principle applies when paying by card. Before the transaction is processed, customers often tell the server the total amount they would like to pay, including the tip. For example, on a bill of €18.50, they might say Machen Sie 20 Euro (make it €20) or simply '20 Euro, bitte'.
This approach keeps the tip transparent and straightforward, and reflects Germany's traditional preference for modest, voluntary gratuities rather than fixed percentages.
Berliners lead Germany's tipping rankings
One of the most surprising findings from the TUI study is how much tipping habits differ across Germany.
Berlin emerged as the country's most generous state-level performer, with 35.1 percent of residents saying they tip 10 percent or more. Hamburg followed on 30 percent.
North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany's most populous state, sat almost exactly on the national average, with 21.3 percent saying they leave tips of 10 percent or more, compared with the nationwide figure of 21.2 percent.
At the other end of the scale was Saxony, where only 14.1 percent reported tipping at least 10 percent. But even here, the study found that the vast majority of people still tip, suggesting that regional differences apply to the amount given rather than a divide between tippers and non-tippers.
READ ALSO: Polite but not mandatory - The dos and don'ts of tipping in Germany
Millennials are the biggest tippers
Age appears to be one of the strongest predictors of generosity.
Among 25 to 34-year-olds, 29.1 percent reported tipping 10 percent or more. Among those aged 55 to 65, the figure was just 14.5 percent.
The authors of the study suggest several possible explanations. Millennials may place greater emphasis on service quality, for example, while many may also have recent experience working in hospitality themselves.
Interestingly, the study also found that older Germans are more likely to reward hotel housekeeping staff. Nearly eight in ten respondents aged 55 to 65 said they tipped cleaners, compared with just over half of 18 to 24-year-olds.
A culture of appreciation
The TUI study found that almost everyone tips while travelling, with only 3.3 percent saying they leave no gratuity at all.
Earlier research paints a similar picture. A 2023 YouGov study found that Germans were among the most frequent tippers in Europe, not only in restaurants but also for hairdressers, taxi drivers and hotel staff.
The survey also found that many Germans tip because they believe it is simply the right thing

items.title: RI offers US$11.86 bln infrastructure projects to Japanese investors
items.summary: The Indonesian government has offered 32 strategic transportation and infrastructure projects valued at Rp207.64 ...
items.body_text:
The project pipeline was presented during the Indonesia–Japan Transportation and Infrastructure Business Forum and Business Matching 2026, held in Tokyo on August 27–28.
Organized by the Indonesian Embassy in Tokyo in collaboration with the Coordinating Ministry for Economic Affairs, the forum brought together project leaders from nine Indonesian state-owned and regional enterprises (SOEs and ROEs) with 50 representatives from 36 major Japanese companies and financial institutions.
Deputy Ambassador of Indonesia to Japan, Maria Renata Hutagalung, highlighted that the nearly seven-decade-long investment relationship between both nations focuses on sustainable, high-quality developments such as the Jakarta MRT and Patimban Port.
"What distinguishes Japanese investment in Indonesia is never solely about value, but rather the quality of engineering, discipline in project completion, transfer of technology, and a willingness to establish long-term partnerships," Maria said in a press release issued on Tuesday.
Approximately 75 percent of the offered portfolio consists of brownfield projects with operational track records and established revenue streams, including asset monetization, expansion plans, and equity divestments.
The investment portfolio includes 12 road and toll road projects, 10 property and residential development projects, six railway and Transit-Oriented Development (TOD) projects, alongside two projects each for maritime ports, logistics, and steel fabrication facilities.
To de-risk foreign capital, the government is facilitating various investment frameworks—ranging from public-private partnerships (PPPs) and joint ventures to concessions and long-term leases—backed by government guarantees through PT Penjaminan Infrastruktur Indonesia (PII) and long-term financing via PT Sarana Multi Infrastruktur (SMI).
Deputy for Coordination of SOE Management and Development at the Coordinating Ministry for Economic Affairs, Ferry Irawan, briefed attendees on Indonesia's solid economic fundamentals, noting that first-half 2026 economic growth reached 5.61 percent with annual inflation at 3.34 percent.
Overall investment realization during the period exceeded Rp1,010 trillion (US$57.71 billion).
Major Japanese institutions participating in the business matching sessions included Toyota Tsusho, Sumitomo Corporation, Obayashi, Shimizu, Penta-Ocean, Tokyu, JR East, Tokyo Metro, Mitsubishi Electric, Mizuho Bank, SMBC, as well as official development bodies JICA and JETRO.

items.title: Indonesia targets seven percent investment growth to spur growth
items.summary: Indonesia's Finance Minister Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa is targeting investment growth of up to seven percent to help ...
items.body_text:
“To achieve six percent economic growth in 2027, we must accelerate investment growth to seven percent,” Purbaya said after meeting lawmakers in Jakarta on Tuesday.
Purbaya said the target would be pursued through cooperation among the government, private sector and Danantara, Indonesia’s sovereign wealth fund.
The government will serve as an investment catalyst, while the private sector is expected to remain the main investment driver, he said.
Danantara will accelerate productive investment, particularly in strategic and downstream sectors offering high added value, Purbaya said.
“To ensure each instrument operates effectively and complements the others, the government will strengthen coordination among fiscal, monetary and financial policies, as well as with Danantara,” he said.
Investment acceleration must also be accompanied by macroeconomic stability to provide certainty, strengthen economic confidence and encourage sustainable investment, Purbaya said.
The government plans to maintain stability through policies including inflation control to protect purchasing power, consumption and investment.
Maintaining competitive interest rates will also remain a priority to improve financing access, strengthen business confidence and encourage investment, Purbaya said.
The government will coordinate with Bank Indonesia to maintain rupiah stability, he added.
“These policies aim to strengthen economic resilience, mitigate global impacts and provide businesses with certainty for investment and expansion decisions,” Purbaya said.
He said the investment target was supported by strong economic fundamentals despite global uncertainty.
Indonesia’s economy grew 5.45 percent cumulatively in the first half of 2026, while inflation remained under control and bank liquidity was sufficient to support lending.
The trade balance remained in surplus from January through June 2026, while foreign exchange reserves reached US$145.3 billion as of July.
Positive sentiment in domestic financial markets also persisted, reflected in a stronger rupiah, gains in the Jakarta Composite Index and favorable movements in government bond yields.
Capital inflows reached 140.6 trillion rupiah (US$7.6 billion) as of August 28, 2026.

items.title: New Papuan province proposal advances with four council factions
items.summary: A discourse on forming a new autonomous region called Central West Papua Province gained traction after four factions ...
items.body_text:
West Papua DPRP Speaker Orgenes Wonggor said in Manokwari on Tuesday that the four factions had voiced a common stance on the discourse, proposed by residents of the Bomberay customary region, during Monday's plenary session.
“The aspirations conveyed through the four factions will soon be followed up with the establishment of a work committee,” he said.
Wonggor explained that the plan entails West Papua Province relinquishing the Bomberay customary region - encompassing Teluk Bintuni, Teluk Wondama, Fakfak, and Kaimana districts - to pave the way for the establishment of Central West Papua Province.
“The council’s secretariat will issue a decree establishing the work committee. Although the authority to decide to create a new administrative region rests with the central government, we remain determined to advocate for people’s aspirations,” the speaker said.
West Papua Regional Secretary Ali Baham Temongmere emphasized that any attempt to establish a new administrative region in Indonesia must comply with statutory regulations, noting that its success may depend on fulfilling requirements set by the central government.
In this regard, Temongmere cited Law No. 2 of 2021 concerning Papua’s Special Autonomy, which provides room for people in seven customary regions to pursue administrative divisions. They are Bomberay, Mamta, Saireri, La Pago, Mee Pago, Anim Ha, and Domberay.
Meanwhile, Amanat Sejahtera faction speaker at the West Papua DPRP Rachmad Sinamur highlighted that the movement advocating for a new province in Bomberay had emerged several years ago but stalled due to a moratorium on the establishment of new regions.
In January 2023, he added, the leaders of the four Bomberay districts agreed to push for the establishment of a new province, with the central government notified of the campaign.
Sinamur emphasized the need for relevant regional administrations to continue advancing the movement while preparing to meet the requirements, including the establishment of new districts.
Having been divided between Papua and West Papua provinces for decades, Indonesia’s Papua region expanded administratively with the establishment of Central Papua, Southwest Papua, Highland Papua, and South Papua in 2022.
If established, Central West Papua will become Indonesia’s 39th province, though its formation requires the creation of new districts. The 2014 Law on Regional Governments stipulates that a province must comprise a minimum of five districts or cities.

items.title: KPK Ungkap Praktik Pemerasan WNA Masih Marak di Kantor Imigrasi Pasca-OTT Silmy Karim
items.summary: Aksi pungutan liar oleh oknum petugas ini tetap marak terjadi meskipun penyidik telah menggelar OTT yang menjerat Silmy Karim
items.body_text:
OTT KPK di Kantor Imigrasi
KPK Ungkap Praktik Pemerasan WNA Masih Marak di Kantor Imigrasi Pasca-OTT Silmy Karim
Aksi pungutan liar oleh oknum petugas ini tetap marak terjadi meskipun penyidik telah menggelar OTT yang menjerat Silmy Karim
Ringkasan Berita:
- KPK mengungkap praktik pemerasan dalam pengurusan izin tinggal Warga Negara Asing (WNA) masih terus berlangsung di tingkat kantor imigrasi (kanim).
- Aksi pungutan liar oleh oknum petugas ini tetap marak terjadi meskipun penyidik telah menggelar OTT yang menjerat Silmy Karim.
- Lembaga antirasuah menemukan indikasi bahwa oknum di lapangan masih mematok biaya ekstra untuk menyetujui dokumen layanan keimigrasian.
TRIBUNNEWS.COM, JAKARTA - Komisi Pemberantasan Korupsi (KPK) mengungkap praktik pemerasan dalam pengurusan izin tinggal Warga Negara Asing (WNA) masih terus berlangsung di tingkat kantor imigrasi (kanim).
Aksi pungutan liar oleh oknum petugas ini tetap marak terjadi meskipun penyidik telah menggelar Operasi Tangkap Tangan (OTT) yang menjerat mantan Wakil Menteri Imigrasi dan Pemasyarakatan (Imipas), Silmy Karim.
Baca juga: KPK Usut Aliran Uang Pemerasan Izin Tinggal WNA usai Periksa Staf KJRI Kuching Malaysia
Juru Bicara KPK, Budi Prasetyo, menjelaskan bahwa para oknum di unit pelaksana teknis keimigrasian belum juga menghentikan perbuatan culas tersebut.
Lembaga antirasuah menemukan indikasi bahwa oknum di lapangan masih mematok biaya ekstra untuk menyetujui dokumen layanan keimigrasian.
"Pascaterjadinya peristiwa tertangkap tangan, KPK menduga bahwa praktik-praktik penerimaan uang yang dilakukan oleh para oknum di imigrasi ini masih terus dilakukan," kata Budi di Gedung Merah Putih KPK, Jakarta Selatan, Selasa (1/9/2026).
Menanggapi temuan ini, penyidik KPK langsung bergerak menyisir dan menggelar penggeledahan di sejumlah lokasi, termasuk Kanim Jakarta Pusat dan Kanim Jakarta Selatan.
Penyidik menelusuri dugaan keterlibatan para oknum yang masih berani menetapkan tarif ilegal kepada para perantara atau biro jasa pengurusan izin tinggal WNA.
Modus Operasi dan Pengembalian Uang Hasil Pungli
Budi membeberkan bahwa para oknum mematok tarif pemerasan yang bervariasi bergantung pada jenis layanan serta masa berlaku izin tinggal.
Nominal uang pelicin tersebut bergerak dinamis dari ratusan ribu hingga jutaan rupiah per dokumen.
"Tarifnya ini juga kondisional, jadi memang beragam ada yang ratusan ribu, ada yang jutaan. Karena memang kondisinya berbeda-beda, ini juga bergantung dari durasi izin tinggal tersebut," ungkap Budi.
Selain memperlambat persetujuan izin tinggal, oknum imigrasi juga memanfaatkan kewenangan penindakan.
Baca juga: KPK Sita Uang Rp 6 Miliar Dari 3 Pejabat Imigrasi Bali Terkait Kasus Pemerasan Izin Tinggal WNA
Mereka membuka ruang kompromi agar WNA yang melakukan pelanggaran hukum dapat terbebas dari sanksi administratif maupun deportasi setelah menyerahkan sejumlah uang.
Meski masih menemukan penyelewengan di beberapa tempat, KPK mendapati sejumlah kantor imigrasi lain sudah menghentikan aksi kotor tersebut.

items.title: KPK Usut Aliran Uang Pemerasan Izin Tinggal WNA usai Periksa Staf KJRI Kuching Malaysia
items.summary: KPK memanggil Tri Hernanda Reza, yang kini bertugas sebagai staf KJRI Kuching, Malaysia, untuk diperiksa sebagai saksi.
items.body_text:
OTT KPK di Kantor Imigrasi
KPK Usut Aliran Uang Pemerasan Izin Tinggal WNA usai Periksa Staf KJRI Kuching Malaysia
KPK memanggil Tri Hernanda Reza, yang kini bertugas sebagai staf KJRI Kuching, Malaysia, untuk diperiksa sebagai saksi.
Ringkasan Berita:
- KPK terus mengusut dugaan pemerasan dalam pengurusan izin tinggal warga negara asing (WNA) di lingkungan Ditjen Imipas
- KPK memanggil Tri Hernanda Reza, yang kini bertugas sebagai staf KJRI Kuching, Malaysia, untuk diperiksa sebagai saksi
- Tri diperiksa karena pernah bertugas di lingkungan Direktorat Jenderal Imigrasi ketika dugaan praktik pungutan dan pemerasan tersebut berlangsung
TRIBUNNEWS.COM, JAKARTA – Komisi Pemberantasan Korupsi (KPK) terus mengusut dugaan pemerasan dalam pengurusan izin tinggal warga negara asing (WNA) di lingkungan Direktorat Jenderal Imigrasi dan Pemasyarakatan (Ditjen Imipas).
Dalam penyidikan perkara tersebut, KPK memanggil Tri Hernanda Reza, yang kini bertugas sebagai staf Konsulat Jenderal Republik Indonesia (KJRI) Kuching, Malaysia, untuk diperiksa sebagai saksi pada Selasa (1/9/2026).
Baca juga: KPK Ungkap Uang Rp 6 Miliar dari Pejabat Imigrasi Bali Bukan Hasil Pungli, Tapi Pengembalian Saksi
Tri diperiksa karena pernah bertugas di lingkungan Direktorat Jenderal Imigrasi ketika dugaan praktik pungutan dan pemerasan tersebut berlangsung.
Pemeriksaan itu diarahkan untuk mengurai mekanisme pelayanan izin tinggal WNA sekaligus alur birokrasi dan dugaan pergerakan uang dari kantor imigrasi di daerah menuju tingkat pusat.
Baca juga: KPK Sita Uang Rp 6 Miliar Dari 3 Pejabat Imigrasi Bali Terkait Kasus Pemerasan Izin Tinggal WNA
Juru Bicara KPK Budi Prasetyo mengatakan penyidik mendalami proses internal pelayanan izin tinggal yang dalam jenis layanan tertentu membutuhkan persetujuan dari kantor pusat.
“Penyidik meminta keterangan bagaimana proses dan mekanisme di internal berkaitan dengan layanan izin tinggal bagi para WNA,” kata Budi di Gedung Merah Putih KPK, Jakarta Selatan, Selasa (1/9/2026).
Tidak Semua Izin Tinggal Diproses di Pusat
Dalam pelayanan keimigrasian, tidak seluruh proses permohonan izin tinggal WNA harus diselesaikan di tingkat pusat.
Menurut Budi, terdapat layanan yang dapat diselesaikan di Kantor Imigrasi (Kanim) daerah. Namun, sejumlah layanan tertentu memerlukan proses persetujuan atau approval dari Direktorat Jenderal Imigrasi dan Pemasyarakatan di tingkat pusat.
Perbedaan kewenangan tersebut menjadi salah satu bagian yang didalami penyidik karena diduga dimanfaatkan untuk menarik pembayaran tambahan dari pemohon.
“Sehingga dalam proses pengumpulan uang ini juga semuanya didalami bahwa untuk layanan-layanan yang memang proses approval-nya sampai ke pusat, kemudian juga diduga ada aliran-aliran uang yang disetorkan dari kanim kepada Ditjen Imipas di pusat yang melakukan approval-approval untuk layanan yang memang sampai di pusat,” ujar Budi.
Dengan kata lain, KPK tidak hanya menelusuri siapa yang menerima uang, tetapi juga bagaimana mekanisme pelayanan yang resmi diduga menjadi ruang terjadinya pungutan tambahan.
Baca juga: KPK Panggil Kepala Imigrasi Denpasar Usut Kasus Pemerasan Izin Tinggal Silmy Karim Dkk
Dugaan Praktik Berlangsung Empat Tahun
KPK menduga praktik pemerasan tersebut berlangsung dalam rentang 2022 hingga 2026. Dalam periode tersebut, penyidik mengendus nilai penerimaan yang mencapai sekitar Rp145,5 miliar.

items.title: Arsenal Cuan Ratusan Miliar di Hari Terakhir Bursa Transfer, Dua Eks Pemain Jadi Sumber Rezeki
items.summary: Arsenal dapat dana raturan miliar dari dua mantan pemainnya berkat klausul penjualan kembali sebesar 20 persen.
items.body_text:
Liga Inggris
Arsenal Cuan Ratusan Miliar di Hari Terakhir Bursa Transfer, Dua Eks Pemain Jadi Sumber Rezeki
Arsenal dapat dana raturan miliar dari dua mantan pemainnya berkat klausul penjualan kembali sebesar 20 persen.
Ringkasan Berita:
- Arsenal berpeluang mendapat sekitar £10 juta atau Rp240 miliar dari klausul penjualan kembali Brooke Norton-Cuffy dan Folarin Balogun jika keduanya resmi pindah klub.
- Norton-Cuffy hampir ke Hull City, sementara Balogun dikabarkan segera meninggalkan Monaco menuju Everton. Arsenal berhak atas 20 persen dari masing-masing transfer.
- The Gunners juga aktif melepas pemain, dengan Gabriel Martinelli dan Gabriel Jesus berpeluang hengkang pada hari terakhir bursa transfer musim panas.
TRIBUNNEWS.COM - Arsenal berpeluang mendapatkan pemasukan sekitar ratusan miliar pada hari terakhir bursa transfer musim panas pada 1 September waktu setempat.
Uang tersebut bisa datang dari dua mantan pemain mereka, Brooke Norton-Cuffy dan Folarin Balogun, yang sama-sama berpeluang berganti klub dalam waktu berdekatan.
Norton-Cuffy hampir meninggalkan Genoa untuk bergabung dengan Hull City dengan nilai transfer mencapai £11,9 juta, seperti yang dilaporkan Sportbible.
Arsenal akan ikut mendapatkan bagian dari transaksi tersebut berkat klausul penjualan kembali sebesar 20 persen yang mereka masukkan ketika melepas sang pemain ke Genoa pada 2024.
Dari kesepakatan itu, The Gunners diperkirakan menerima sekitar £2,3 juta (sekitar Rp55,2 miliar).
Sementara itu, pemasukan yang lebih besar berpotensi datang dari Folarin Balogun.
Mantan striker Arsenal tersebut dikabarkan hampir meninggalkan Monaco untuk bergabung dengan Everton dengan nilai transfer £38,5 juta.
Ketika menjual Balogun ke Monaco pada 2023 dengan nilai sekitar £34 juta, Arsenal turut menyertakan klausul penjualan kembali sebesar 20 persen.
Jika transfer ke Everton terealisasi, Arsenal berhak mendapatkan sekitar £7,7 juta (sekitar Rp184,8 miliar).
Dengan demikian, dua klausul tersebut berpotensi memberikan pemasukan sekitar £10 juta (sekitar Rp240 miliar) kepada Arsenal tanpa harus menjual pemain yang masih berada dalam skuad mereka.
Baca juga: Nostalgia Manchester City di Barcelona, Gabriel Jesus Susul Rodri dan Cancelo
Arsenal Aktif Lepas Pemain
Pemasukan tersebut menjadi tambahan bagi Arsenal yang memang cukup sibuk melakukan perombakan skuad pada musim panas ini.
Sejumlah pemain tim utama telah meninggalkan Emirates, termasuk Christian Norgaard, Jakub Kiwior, Leandro Trossard, dan Reiss Nelson.
Dari sisi perekrutan, Mikel Arteta juga telah mengeluarkan hampir £200 juta (sekitar Rp4,8 triliun).
Bruno Guimaraes, Christos Tzolis, Piero Hincapie, dan Ezri Konsa menjadi beberapa nama yang didatangkan dengan biaya cukup besar.

items.body_text:
Booyakasha or bust: The high stakes of the ‘West Staines Rudeboy,’ Ali G
If you had told me a few years ago that Sacha Baron Cohen would step back into the yellow tracksuit and oversized tinted glasses of his breakout alter ego, I would have told you it was an absolute impossibility. The culture had supposedly moved on. Yet here we are staring at the cold, hard, unyielding facts: the official trailer for ‘Ali G: Who Iz I?’ has officially dropped, and it is a massive, top-secret reality check for the year 2026.
Let us look closely at what we are dealing with. This is not a scripted narrative film like 2002’s polarizing ‘Ali G Indahouse’. Instead, Sacha Baron Cohen has chosen to pivot back to his purest, most lethal format—the hidden-camera stunt mockumentary that propelled Borat to global dominance. But more importantly, the film marks Sacha Baron Cohen’s feature directorial debut. He is not just steering the character; he is steering the entire ship.
The premise: getting off the ‘batty‘
According to the official synopsis released by Amazon MGM Studios, our favorite academically challenged “West Staines Rudeboy”, Ali G has spent the last two decades “chillin’, tokin’ and bonin'”. However, his reality is upended upon discovering that his long-term girlfriend, Julie—played here by the always funny Morgana Robinson—is eight months pregnant. Faced with an extra mouth to feed, Ali G heads to America to reclaim his former glory and make a “documentary” with real, unsuspecting people.
The official trailer reveals exactly how much the world has changed since Ali G last held a microphone. As the character himself hilariously laments: “The world went to crap. There’s been Wars. Covid. And Ed Sheeran.”
The critical question: Can the prank still work?
I have been analyzing Sacha Baron Cohen’s unique brand of social satire for quite some time now, and this project presents a fascinating, high-utility case study in comedic relevance. The immediate hurdle is obvious: the media landscape has completely shifted.
When ‘Da Ali G Show’ first aired, the internet was in its infancy and political figures were entirely unprepared for his idiocy. Today, we live in a hyper-aware, media-trained society dominated by TikTok and influencer culture. Can a 54-year-old billionaire comedian pull off hidden-camera pranks when his face is universally recognized?
Judging by the first official footage, the answer is a resounding, chaotic yes. Sacha Baron Cohen is actively weaponizing modern influencer culture against itself. The official trailer showcases outrageous, cringeworthy segments featuring:
A bewildered doctor being asked to tell a pregnant woman, “it’s probably wind or a big poo”.
High-stakes pranks on retired U.S. Army General Stewart Rodeheaver.
A bizarre festival encounter involving Canadian DJ Deadmau5.
A definitive cultural risk
Make no mistake about it, my dear readers: this is an incredibly risky gamble. If ‘Ali G: Who Iz I?’ succeeds, it proves that Sacha Baron Cohen’s raw, unvarnished satirical edge is timeless, capable of cutting through the noise of the 2020s just as cleanly as it did the early 2000s. If it fails, it will stand as absolute proof that some characters belong firmly in the nostalgic vault of pop culture history. Keep your eyes glued to the marquee on October 23. This is going to be one wild, unpredictable ride at the box office. Respect.

items.title: Haze and air quality index: Things to know
items.summary: Here's what you should know about air quality indexes and how they help identify the health risks brought by haze
items.body_text:
AT A GLANCE
- Haze is a form of air pollution caused by smoke, dust, and moisture that can lead to serious health risks, especially for individuals with respiratory diseases.
- The Department of Health lists symptoms related to haze exposure, including difficulty breathing, coughing, and chest pains, and advises affected individuals to seek medical attention.
- Air quality indexes categorize pollution levels from 'Good' to 'Emergency,' providing guidelines for public safety and recommendations for limiting outdoor exposure during high pollution periods.
MANILA, Philippines – It may look like a harmless fog blanketing the skies, but haze carries small particles in the air that can lead to serious health risks.
Here’s everything you need to know about haze, how to protect yourself from its effects, and how air quality indexes help in measuring risks.
What is haze?
Haze is smoke, dust, moisture, and vapor in the air that affects visibility. It originates from large-scale forest or land fires.
These fires create very fine particles with a diameter of 2.5 micrometers (PM2.5) or smaller that go into the air.
Unlike coarse particles that dissolve in the atmosphere within hours, fine particles can stay in the atmosphere for up to weeks and can travel for hundreds to thousands of kilometers.
These often grow in size as humidity increases and affect air quality by filling the atmosphere with high concentrations of fine particles.
This poses health risks, especially for those with respiratory diseases.
How does haze affect health?
Haze is a form of air pollution that leads to health risks when particles are inhaled.
According to the Department of Health, it could lead to the following:
- difficulty breathing
- coughing
- chest pains
- watery eyes or excessive tearing
- itchy nose
- worsening of respiratory disease
The health department advises people experiencing these symptoms to proceed to the nearest health center for treatment.
What are air quality indexes?
The Department of Environment and Natural Resources-Environmental Management Bureau (DENR-EMB) reviewed air quality indexes in compliance with the Philippine Clean Air Act of 1999.
In 2020, it formulated the PM2.5 air quality index breakpoints, which are divided into six levels from cleanest to most polluted.
It is used to inform the public about potential health risks.
Below are the air quality indexes, their corresponding colors, and cautions to follow:
- Good (Green) – air quality is clean and safe
- Fair (Yellow) – safe but with a presence of pollution
- Unhealthy for sensitive groups (Orange) – people with respiratory disease should limit outdoor exposure
- Very Unhealthy (Red) – avoid traffic-heavy areas, and people with respiratory disease should stay indoors and rest as much as possible; trips are encouraged to be postponed, and the use of vehicles is restricted
- Acutely Unhealthy (Purple) – people should limit outdoor exposure, and those with respiratory disease should stay indoors and rest as much as possible; unnecessary trips should be postponed, motor vehicle use may be restricted, and industrial activities are limited
- Emergency (Maroon) – everyone must stay indoors with windows and doors closed unless heat stress is possible; motor vehicles are only allowed for emergencies, and industrial activities (except those vital for public safety and health) are limited
How to protect yourself from the haze
Here are some tips from the health department to avoid the risks brought by haze:
- Stay indoors as much as possible.
- Wear a KN95 face mask if going outside.
- Close all doors and windows and use a wet cloth to cover their crevices.
- Use headlights or fog lights when traveling, especially during nighttime.
- Stay away from low-lying areas where smoke and suspended particles may settle.
Public events in open areas may continue but must observe air quality before deciding whether to push through or cancel.
Using masks is also encouraged in classrooms, with teachers keep

items.title: Comelec seeks bigger budget for 2027 as it prepares for 2028 elections
items.summary: Speaking at a House budget hearing, Comelec Chairman George Garcia says P9.12 billion was cut from the poll body's budget for preparation for the national and local elections
items.body_text:
AT A GLANCE
- The Commission on Elections requested a P52.66-billion budget for 2027, but the Department of Budget and Management recommended only P44.7 billion.
- Comelec Chairman George Garcia warned that budget cuts totaling P9.12 billion could compromise election preparations, leading to a shortage of election counting machines and longer voting times.
- The proposed budget also lacks funding for essential operations, including ballot printing and venue leasing for the filing of certificates of candidacy, which the Comelec aims to hold earlier in September 2027.
MANILA, Philippines – The Commission on Elections (Comelec) on Tuesday, September 1, appealed to the House of Representatives to restore its proposed P52.66-billion budget request for 2027.
The Comelec requested a higher budget in preparation for the national and local elections in 2028. The Department of Budget and Management (DBM), however, only recommended a P44.7-billion budget for the poll body in 2027.
Speaking at a House budget hearing, Comelec Chairman George Garcia said P9.12 billion was cut from the Comelec’s budget for preparation for the national and local elections.
He warned that the cuts could compromise the poll body’s preparations if the budget proves insufficient.
The Comelec estimated that there would be around 74 million voters by 2028, which would also increase the demand for a higher number of voting precincts.
The DBM also slashed P5.75 billion from the Comelec’s proposed budget for regular operations and P345 million from its other locally funded projects.
If the budget cuts were not restored by Congress, the Comelec said there would be a shortage of 9,310 election counting machines. This could increase the number of voters assigned to each polling precinct, resulting in longer lines and voting times on election day.
Garcia said the cuts would also affect the printing of ballots, forms, and voter information sheets, as well as the deployment of machines and supplies to polling places. Other affected expenses include ballot packaging, consultancy for an international certification entity, and overtime pay.
The DBM also removed the P118-million budget proposal of the Comelec for the lease of warehouses and venues. Without this, Garcia said they will not have a venue for the filing of certificates of candidacy in September 2027.
The filing of certificates of candidacy is typically held in October, but the Comelec wants to set the filing period from September 20 to 27, 2027.
The Comelec said an earlier filing of certificates of candidacy will allow the poll body to print ballots earlier.
The 2027 budget proposal also contains no allocation for the Comelec’s capital outlay, which covers physical assets such as buildings. Garcia said the commission’s lack of adequate office space has long been a problem. – Rappler.com

items.title: Purple harvest: Safeguarding the future of the ube industry
items.summary: As demand for ube surges worldwide, Leyte farmers call for laws that may help stop raw ube from being sold abroad
items.body_text:
AT A GLANCE
- Ube (purple yam) is gaining global popularity, with the market projected to grow from 455 million USD in 2024 to 943 million USD by 2035.
- Many farmers in Leyte have transitioned to ube farming, responding to increased international demand, which has led to foreign inquiries and significant orders.
- To sustain ube production, farmers require training, resources, and government support, with calls for ube to be declared a priority crop to protect local varieties.
BAYBAY CITY, Philippines — “Hulog ng Langit.” (Unexpected blessing.)
This is how Olegario Paredes Jr., a root crop farmer from Eastern Visayas, describes the rise of ube (purple yam) in global food trends.
Ube has been steadily finding its place in the global market in recent months, earning comparisons to Japan’s matcha as a distinctly Filipino product with growing international appeal.
Transparency Market Research values the global ube market at roughly US$455 million in 2024, with projections climbing to $943 million by 2035. For farmers like Paredes, it is a chance to turn a once-ordinary crop into a reliable source of income.
One of the founders of Organikong Magsasaka at Mangingisda ng Rehiyon Otso (OMMRO), Paredes previously cultivated sweet potato and cassava at the Juanito Eco Farm School for Practical Agriculture (JEFSPA) in Kananga, Leyte.
But ube changed farming for him.
“Labing pamatuod lang, ang ube ang maoy naghatag ug maayong kita sa akoa, sa JEFSPA, ug sa uban pa nga mga farmers,” Paredes says.
(More than anything, ube has provided a good source of income for me, JEFSPA, and other farmers.)
Global demand
Paredes started planting ube in 2023.
The crop that once seemed ordinary was beginning to attract an extraordinary amount of attention. Soon, the surge reached Eastern Visayas directly.
As international interest in ube spiked in 2024, the Fatima Multi-Purpose Cooperative, a cooperative that uplifts local farmers, fisherfolk, and low-income groups, began venturing into ube processing.
They reached out to Paredes for an organic supply agreement.
Soon, foreigners began visiting the region in search of ube suppliers, Paredes tells Rappler.
“Niabot sa farm, niari sa region para pagkita sa amo production area ug ang processing sa Fatima,” Paredes recalls.
(They visited the farm and came to the region to see our production area and the processing facility in Fatima.)
In March 2026, a Moroccan buyer who was looking for a steady source of ube powder visited Paredes. The buyer wanted 1,000 kilograms of ube every month for distribution across four countries.
That single order alone works out to roughly 80 tons of raw ube a month.
And that Moroccan buyer wasn’t an outlier.
Purple gold
Since he started planting ube, Paredes’ farm has fielded over 10 separate foreign inquiries.
That demand pushed him to convert more of his farmland to ube production.
As a general rule, 50 tons of ube, sold at P50 per kilo, brings in P2.5 million. However, that kind of sales, he says, is only possible with consistent monitoring and cooperative weather.
But ube farming can also be challenging.
Ube’s full production cycle—from land propagation to harvest—takes about a year, Paredes explains.
In the early days, Paredes’ crops were vulnerable to pathogens, waterlogging, and mistimed planting. All the risks are concentrated in the plant’s fragile first few months.
Starting an ube farm isn’t cheap, either. Testing and planting materials come at a cost, with each seedling running P30 to P40 which can potentially rise proportionally to the demand.
While ube is a resilient crop—which means it can handle intense weather conditions—Leyte’s frequent exposure to disruptive storms could still affect yield, particularly given that harvest season is from September to November.
Support system
To meet the demand in the long run, farmers need more than planting materials: they need proper ube production training, processing tools, and adequate funding support.

items.title: Sara Duterte trial recap, Sept. 1: Military men, DepEd's P15.5-million confidential funds
items.summary: The impeachment court on Tuesday, September 1, heard the testimonies of two military officials whose signatures are on documents the Department of Education, under then-Secretary Sara Duterte, used to liquidate its confidential funds in 2023.
items.body_text:
Sara Duterte trial recap, Sept. 1: Military men, DepEd's P15.5-million confidential funds
MANILA, Philippines — The impeachment court on Tuesday, September 1, heard the testimonies of two military officials whose signatures are on documents the Department of Education, under then-Secretary Sara Duterte, used to liquidate its confidential funds in 2023.
Duterte's trial entered its ninth week today with the prosecution's relatively brief presentation of witnesses Col. Manaros Boransing II and Col. Magtangol Panopio, as the defense chose not to cross-examine both military men.
Boransing and Panopio signed certifications that attested to the "successful" conduct of youth leadership summits and information campaigns that their Army units ran in 2023.
Tuesday's session is still on Article I, which accuses Duterte of misusing P612.5 million in confidential funds across the Office of the Vice President and DepEd; the P15.54 million tied to today's witnesses is one slice of that larger figure.
Here are the three highlights from today's proceedings:
1. DepEd didn't "release" funds to the Army, though used its summits as proof its confidential spending worked
Both Boransing and Panopio testified their units, the Army's 1st Infantry Division and 7th Infanty Division, respectively, received no funds from DepEd, the Office of the Vice President, or the Vice Presidential Security and Protection Group for their divisions' conduct of 2023 Youth Leadership Summits and information campaigns.
Sen. Bam Aquino got Boransing to confirm the Army's total operational spending across all eight summits, through a rough on-the-spot computation, likely stayed under P500,000, with local governments covering most youth participants' costs and other agencies shouldering their own expenses.
DepEd nonetheless submitted Boransing's certification to the Commission on Audit as what the agency called proof of success of an information-gathering or surveillance activity, one of its bases for P15.54 million in confidential funds it claimed went to rewards payments for informants.
Private prosecutor Reynaldo Robles, who led the prosecution's direct examination today, said the amount covered a large number of individual payments, roughly P100,000 to P200,000 each, some listed under names he described as unusual, and that the figure covered only the first two quarters of 2023.
The certificates signed by Boransing and Panopio, however, both make no mention of any amount. Under questioning from Presiding Officer Chiz Escudero, Boransing acknowledged the certificate did more than state the successful conduct of activities, as there was a sentence that the Army "successfully collaborated with the Department of Education," resulting in "zero reported [communist terrorist] recruitment." Boransing agreed that it amounted to a claim of success.
Sen. Joel Villanueva pressed the same point and argued that a certificate stating an activity was "successfully conducted" doesn't establish any link between a specific informant, the information that informant supplied, and a reward paid for it. Boransing said he had no opinion on how his certificate was used and is not qualified to weigh in, since he isn't an intelligence officer.
Boransing and Panopio both said they had only learned their certificates were submitted by DepEd to justify its confidential spending during the 2024 House good government committee hearings that sought to probe Duterte's use of secret funds.
2. DepEd's "confidential" information about student matters, which partly shaped where the Army held its summits
Boransing, under questioning from Escudero, said he could not characterize DepEd's inputs as confidential in nature. What DepEd provided, he said, was information on school schedules and permission to speak with students — details he distinguished from anything resembling intelligence work.

items.title: House panel OKs sharply reduced 2027 budget for Marcos office
items.summary: The Office of the President's proposed budget for 2027 got the House Committte on Appropriations approval within 25 minutes.
items.body_text:
House panel OKs sharply reduced 2027 budget for Marcos office
MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the President’s proposed budget for 2027 worth more than P10.15 billion passed the deliberations of the Committee on Appropriations in the House of Representatives on Tuesday, September 1.
With 37 affirmative votes and five negative votes, the committee approved the P10,155,758,000 proposed budget within the first 25 minutes of the deliberations after lawmakers extended “institutional and interbranch courtesy” to the Office of the President.
According to Executive Secretary Ralph Recto, who attended the hearing with other officials from the Office of the President, the proposed budget represents only 0.14% of the P7.2 trillion total budget proposal for 2027.
Recto added that it is also 64% lower than the 2026 budget.
Based on the publicly available General Appropriations Act of 2026 uploaded on the website of the Department of Budget and Management (DBM), the Office of the President was allocated P28,028,733,000.
Recto said the decrease in the proposed budget reflects the lower operating costs of the Office of the President’s delivery units and the completion of activities related to the ASEAN Summit, which the country hosted.
“In short, we are asking for less, while remaining fully prepared to do more,” Recto said.
After Recto’s presentation, House Minority Leader Marcelino Libanan (4Ps Party-list) made the motion to extend interparliamentary courtesy to the Office of the President and terminate further deliberations and discussions of the sought budget.
The motion was seconded by House Senior Deputy Speaker Ferdinand Hernandez (South Cotabato).
Rep. Antonio Tinio (ACT Teachers Party-list), however, objected and argued that Congress should also demand transparency from the Office of the President, the same way that it demanded the Office of the Vice President to be transparent about its budget.
“Lakas maka-demand ng kongresong ito ng transparency para sa Office of the Vice President.
Dapat ganoon din para sa Office of the President,” Tinio said, citing alleged involvement of some Cabinet officials in flood control corruption. “Kailangang magpaliwanag ang Office of the President kung bakit halos kalahati ng kanyang budget ay confidential and intelligence funds.”
(This Congress demanded transparency from the Office of the Vice President. The same should apply to the Office of the President. The Office of the President needs to explain why almost half of its budget goes to confidential and intelligence funds.)
In their manifestations, some lawmakers explained their negative votes and cited the need for transparency and accountability as reasons to oppose the “parliamentary courtesy.”
Among those who opposed were Tinio, Rep. Renee Co (Kabataan Party-list), Rep. Sarah Elago (Gabriela Party-list), Rep. Eli San Fernando (KAMANGGAGAWA Party-list) and Rep. Iris Montes (4K Party-list).

items.title: Who could succeed Gesmundo? JBC invites 5 senior justices
items.summary: Leonen and four senior SC justices were invited to apply.
items.body_text:
Who could succeed Gesmundo? JBC invites 5 senior justices
MANILA, Philippines — The Judicial and Bar Council has invited five senior Supreme Court associate justices to apply for chief justice ahead of Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo's retirement in November.
Supreme Court spokesperson Camille Ting told Philstar.com Tuesday, Septemeber 1, that the JBC invited Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen and Associate Justices Alfredo Benjamin Caguioa, Ramon Paul Hernando, Henri Jean Paul Inting and Rodil Zalameda.
Ting said the JBC has followed the practice since the early 2000s of inviting five senior associate justices to apply as a matter of courtesy and recognition of their seniority.
"What began as an informal practice has since become a standing JBC policy," Ting said.
The invitation does not guarantee inclusion in the JBC shortlist that will be submitted to the president for appointment.
Gesmundo is set to retire on Nov. 6. Applications for chief justice will be accepted until 4:30 p.m. on Oct. 13.

items.title: Sleeper bus overturns in Vietnam’s Central Highlands, killing one

items.body_text:
The Viet Tan Phat bus was traveling on the eastern bypass of National Highway 19 when it overturned in Hoi Phu Ward, Gia Lai Province, on the morning of Aug. 31.
Three people died in the crash, while several other passengers sustained injuries and were transported to local hospitals for treatment.
A representative of Hung Vuong Gia Lai Hospital said the facility received around 20 people following the accident.
Rainy and foggy conditions were reported in the area at the time of the crash.
Authorities later removed the overturned bus from the scene and are investigating the cause of the accident.
National Highway 19 stretches roughly 240 kilometers from Quy Nhon Port to the Le Thanh border crossing, running through Pleiku. It is a major east-west corridor connecting Vietnam’s Central Highlands with the central coast.
The 33-year-old driver, who lives in An Khe Ward, tested negative for alcohol and drugs. He held a valid Class D driver’s license, while the bus’s inspection certificate was valid until December 2027.
