items.title: Dockers 'know what's on the line' ahead of Hawthorn showdown: Longmuir
items.summary: Fremantle is just three wins from the club's first-ever AFL premiership, but coach Justin Longmuir dismisses suggestions he will be using that as motivation heading into the finals.
items.body_text:
Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir wants Dockers to stay in the moment ahead of Hawthorn AFL finals clash
The Fremantle Dockers may be just three wins from claiming the club's first-ever AFL premiership, but coach Justin Longmuir has dismissed suggestions he will be using that as motivation heading into the finals.
The 2026 version of the Dockers is comfortably the best-performed team in the club's history when it comes to the home-and away season.
Fremantle won 19 of its 23 games to race away with the minor premiership, earning the right to host Hawthorn in a qualifying final at Perth Stadium on Thursday night.
It has seen excitement build among the Freo faithful, who are hopeful this could be their year, having made just one grand final since the club entered the AFL in the 1995 season, losing to the Hawks in 2013.
But throughout this year's campaign, Longmuir has urged his players to stay in the moment and focus on more immediate tasks, and he insisted thinking about the ultimate goal is not what would get the job done.
"I just don't feel like we need to [lean into it]. If there's someone at the footy club that doesn't see that carrot, well then you're probably in the wrong game, right?" he said.
"All our players know what's on the line, and we just need to make sure that we use whatever motivation that gives us to give it all to your next moment.
"Everyone feels it in different ways … some players will see it as a stimulus and some players will maybe see it as a distraction, and we'll work through that.
"Everyone sees pressure as different things and we've done some work on that, and it's all about staying in the moment.
"The way to win premierships is to win games of footy, and you win games of footy by winning more moments than the opposition.
"We've just got to make sure that we give our best to each moment, and the next moment is the most important one."
Fast start wanted
Much of the talk in the build-up to Thursday's game has focused on the Dockers' home-crowd advantage, after they rode the Wharfie Time rallying cry to come from behind to win their last clash against Hawthorn at Perth Stadium.
But Longmuir is hopeful they will not have to rely on the fans to overcome another slow start.
"They're not going to get us over the line if we're not playing good footy, so we've got to give them something to cheer for, and it needs to be from the start," he said.
Key defender Brennan Cox will miss Thursday's match through injury, but Fremantle is set to welcome back the likes of Murphy Reid, Jye Amiss, Heath Chapman and the retiring Sam Switkowski.
Hawthorn is at virtually full strength for the clash, with only two players unavailable on its most recent injury list.
The Hawks enjoyed a comfortable win over West Coast at Perth Stadium in their final game of the home-and-away season.

items.title: Australia’s ‘shameful’ cocaine habit prompts $600m Pacific package
items.summary: Australia is funding a Pacific-wide plan to crack down on record numbers of narco-subs full of cocaine – many of which are headed to our shores.
items.body_text:
Australia’s ‘shameful’ cocaine habit prompts $600m Pacific package
Koror City, Palau: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will pledge $600 million for a new Pacific-wide initiative to combat the surge of illicit drug smuggling in the region, especially cocaine bound for Australia.
The major funding commitment came as Albanese pushed back against China’s Pacific envoy for threatening retaliation and lodging complaints over Taiwan’s presence at the Pacific Islands Forum in Palau, declaring it was up to Pacific nations to determine their own affairs.
Tensions between Taiwan and China escalated as officials traded barbs, with Taiwan accusing Beijing of bullying smaller nations and China accusing the self-governing territory of humiliating itself.
As they struggle to cope with a dramatic rise in transnational crime fuelling the illegal drug trade, Pacific leaders are preparing to endorse a new regional initiative known as Waqa Moana to beef up maritime patrols and intelligence sharing.
The $600m package Albanese will announce on Wednesday would fund enhanced aerial surveillance to help track suspected drug vessels and provide extra support to police in Fiji, among the nations hardest hit by the rise in drug smuggling.
The Waqa Moana initiative – named after a large, sturdy canoe – would include greater co-ordination of existing resources to combat transnational crime, including the 23 Guardian-class patrol boats Australia has given to Pacific countries.
Federal police would also increase their co-operation with South and Central American countries to target the drug trade at its source.
“The Pacific is our home and our family. That’s why it’s in Australia’s interests to work with our Pacific partners to combat organised crime,” Albanese said.
“For the good of every country in the region, including our own – we need to work together to stamp out the illicit drug trade.”
Pacific leaders are expected to officially endorse the initiative at the end of the week.
Australian Federal Police Commissioner Krissy Barrett declared in May that “it is our nation’s shame that Australians consume too many illicit drugs and pay high prices for them”.
At the same time, Barrett revealed that 17 tonnes of illicit drugs, mostly cocaine, had been seized by authorities in the Pacific since January, up from less than five tonnes in all of 2025.
Barrett warned that “greedy and ruthless narco-gangs are trying to make more money by identifying new ways to traffic illicit drugs”, including by sending semi-submersible vehicles (widely known as narco-submarines) to cross the Pacific.
“The magnitude and endless maritime trafficking of illicit drugs to, and through the Pacific, has become a serious national security threat for the Pacific and Australia,” she said.
A multinational police investigation implicating 11 Fijian police officers in collusion with drug traffickers was also handed over to prosecutors in May.
A month later, Fijian police confirmed that 76 parcels that washed up in the country had been found to contain cocaine.
Pacific Minister Pat Conroy said: “Drug trafficking is having a devastating impact on Pacific communities.
“This initiative responds to the calls of regional leaders to do more, and to step up regional coordination to address this scourge.”
Speaking after the forum’s opening ceremony, China’s special envoy for the Pacific Qian Bo said he had “serious concerns” about the level of access being granted to Taiwan, a self-governing island that China claims as an integral part of its territory.
“We have made our position very clear to the government of Palau and the secretariat,” he told reporters.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun doubled down on Tuesday, telling reporters in Beijing that Taiwan “has no standing whatsoever” to participate in PIF activities.
“By sending ‘Taiwan independence’ separatists like [Taiwan Foreign Minister] Lin Chia-lung around to scheme for attention and clout, the Taiwan authorities will only end up brin

items.title: Dean Cox won’t rule out suspended five returning to the Swans this season
items.summary: Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, James Jordon and Riley Bice are serving season-long suspensions for breaching behavioural standards.
items.body_text:
Dean Cox won’t rule out suspended five returning to the Swans this season
Updated ,first published
In today’s AFL Briefing, your wrap of footy news:
- Swans coach Dean Cox didn’t rule out Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, James Jordon or Riley Bice from returning to the club this season.
- Carlton’s Ben Ainsworth has been working on his mindset this season with Richmond premiership great Alex Rance.
- Max Holmes is firming to return for the Cats’ knockout final against Carlton.
Sydney coach Dean Cox has not ruled out the five suspended players making a return to the club before the end of the season.
As the second-placed Swans prepare to embark on a finals campaign with massively reduced external expectations on them after the five – Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, James Jordon and Riley Bice – were banned for breaching the club’s behavioural standards, Cox revealed there is uncertainty about how long they’ll be absent from the club.
“I think things are changing by the hour and the day,” Cox said on AFL 360 ahead of Saturday’s qualifying final against the Brisbane Lions at the SCG.
“[With] people upstairs [at the club], and I’m privy to some of those conversations [and the focus] has been about how we best manage our football team at the minute and make sure that we can focus as heavily as we possibly can on this weekend’s game, whilst also supporting those players whilst they aren’t at the club.
“There’s no timeframe on when they will return. We’ll keep talking about it each day, and assess the situation from there.”
The five players have begun appointing different lawyers to represent them as police investigate the allegation of sexual assault at the Pullman East Melbourne that was made last month. The five have denied any criminal wrongdoing, according to a source with knowledge of the matter.
There are at least three separate counsels for the five players, whose interviews with Victoria Police loom after the alleged assault at the hotel where the Swans were staying for their round 23 clash with Essendon.
The players’ legal moves come as further details emerge about the early morning events at the hotel and how one of the women came to be in the foyer with Swans staff including Cox. No Swans officials are accused of inappropriate behaviour.
Cox confirmed he was maintaining contact with the players.
“One thing I’ll always do is support my players – I’m staying in dialogue with those five players whilst they’re away from the football club.
“I speak about their welfare, how they’re going, if we can support [them] in any way.
“We need to understand that that’s one thing I’ll always do.
“I haven’t spoken to them at all about the police investigation, and also I think we need to understand that there’s still an investigation in process.
“We need to get all the facts on that before we make any assumptions.
“It’s purely about support, and I’ll continue to do that.”
Separate to the police investigation, the players received club-imposed bans for the rest of the season for drinking, staying out late and inviting women back to the team hotel.
When the Pullman Hotel incident became public last month, Swans chairman Andrew Pridham conceded that the sanctions imposed by Sydney could “torpedo” their premiership hopes.
“They shouldn’t have been in that situation of being out that late, and the only way we can deal with it is to put our foot down incredibly hard, which we’ve done,” Pridham said at the time.
“I think a very important point to make is that we, as a football club, that is our business, and to effectively torpedo our season by making a decision such as this just tells you how seriously we are taking it.”
Cox said he hadn’t spoken to Pridham about those comments.
“Certainly in my conversations with Andrew there has been not one suggestion that he’s lost any belief in this playing group, and what it can still do,” he said.
“I think through this his support and guidance, not only for me but for all players and all st

items.title: Sydney records warmest winter on record as Melbourne equals previous hottest temperatures
items.summary: New South Wales, Victoria and Tasmania just experienced their warmest-ever winters – and BoM says above-average temperatures expected to continueGet our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcastAustralia’s two biggest cities had their hottest and equal hottest winters on record, with three eastern states also breaking temperature records.The Bureau of Meteorology’s (BoM) spring outlook shows above average daytime and night-time temperatures are expected to continue for much of the coun
items.body_text:
Australia’s two biggest cities had their hottest and equal hottest winters on record, with three eastern states also breaking temperature records.
The Bureau of Meteorology’s (BoM) spring outlook shows above average daytime and night-time temperatures are expected to continue for much of the country, with an increased chance of unusually high maximums.
Dr Simon Grainger, a senior climatologist at the bureau, said Sydney had its warmest winter on record, with the mean temperature of 15.3C at Observatory Hill breaking the previous record of 15.0C set in 2013. Average maximum and minimum temperatures at the same site were also the warmest on record.
Melbourne equalled its 2005 record for winter mean temperature of 12.2C, while Canberra recorded its warmest winter maximum, with an average maximum temperature of 14.7C.
New South Wales, Victoria and Tasmania had their warmest winters on record, and all other states and territories except the Northern Territory were in their top 10 warmest winters on record since 1910.
Australia’s mean temperature was 1.45C above the 1961–1990 average for winter, the equal third-highest on record since national observations began in 1910.
Grainger said much of the south-east’s experience was driven by “relatively warm nights and a lot fewer cold nights”, with several factors at play.
“The local weather patterns certainly assisted. For large parts of this winter we had high pressure systems sitting in the Tasman sea,” he said.
“That allowed a lot of warmer air to come down from the tropics over eastern Australia – places like Sydney, Canberra, Melbourne – with fewer outbreaks of cold air getting in.”
Grainger said the developing strong El Niño had also set up weather patterns that tended to be favourable for high daytime temperatures across southeastern Australia.
“Finally of course, all of this is occurring against the background of a globally warmer climate,” he said.
“Daily [global] land temperatures and daily ocean temperatures during August have been close to or above the historical records that were set only in 2024.”
Australia’s national annual average temperature is about 1.5C higher than in 1910, according to the BoM, and the climate crisis, driven by the burning of fossil fuels, has increased the frequency and severity of extreme weather events.
The record-breaking winter data was released as federal resources minister Madeleine King and Northern Territory chief minister Lia Finocchiaro celebrated turning on the tap that will feed the first fracked gas from the Beetaloo Basin into the territory’s power grid.
It follows a horror northern hemisphere summer of record-breaking heatwaves, drought and wildfires in Europe and North America, and intense rain and typhoons in Asia.
The national average rainfall for winter was 8% above the 1961–1990 average, driven by high rainfall in southern inland Australia. Grainger said parts of inland NSW, Victoria, South Australia and parts of the Northern Territory had above average rainfall, with parts of far-western NSW near the SA border experiencing their wettest winter on record.
SA recorded its sixth wettest winter on record. In contrast, rainfall was below average in parts of the east coast and south-western Australia.
The BoM’s long-range forecast shows below average rainfall is expected to continue through parts of southern and eastern Australia through spring, while above average rainfall is expected in large parts of the west from October.
Grainger said a continuation of above average daytime and night-time temperatures was likely for much of the country “and with that there’s [a] chance of unusually high maximum and minimum temperatures”.
He said the BoM’s models showed the El Niño in the Pacific Ocean would continue to strengthen through spring, likely peaking in late spring or in summer.

items.body_text:
More than 1,000 dead from catastrophic Nepal-China floods as rescuers search for survivors
Thousands still missing, including hundreds believed trapped in tunnels
The death toll from catastrophic flooding in Nepal and China passed 1,000 on Tuesday, authorities said, as rescue teams worked to reach communities cut off by the disaster.
Nepal's disaster agency said Tuesday that 987 deaths had been counted there, with 3,916 people missing, including 583 foreigners. Chinese authorities, in their latest update on Sunday, reported 16 deaths and 546 people still missing.
At least 11,814 people have been rescued so far, according to Nepalese authorities. Emergency crews have been using helicopters and other aircraft to reach stranded communities in areas where roads and bridges have been destroyed by the flooding and landslides.
The disaster began Wednesday with a chain of events high in the Himalayas. A glacial collapse sent large amounts of rock, ice and meltwater into valleys below, triggering powerful floods downstream.
Scientists studying satellite imagery said the collapse appears to have involved the failure of bedrock beneath a glacier in the Himalayan region. The rockfall was powerful enough to register as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event.
The resulting surge of water and debris entered rivers that flow through valleys in Tibet and Nepal, causing them to rise rapidly. Floodwaters swept away homes, buildings, roads and bridges and carried mud and rocks downstream.
Authorities are still searching for thousands of people who remain unaccounted for on Tuesday. Rescue teams are also working to provide assistance to survivors in areas where roads and other transportation routes have been damaged or cut off.
- Rescuers search for thousands following deadly Nepal-China flood
- Hundreds feared stuck in hydropower tunnels in Nepal
For rescuers, the immediate priority remains finding at least 900 workers who are missing from 12 hydropower projects damaged by the flash floods, about 500 of whom are believed to be trapped inside tunnels.
Visuals released by Nepal's army showed rescue teams entering dark, debris-filled tunnels, wading through mud and water and climbing over rocks as they searched for signs of life.
Bimal Sharma, a helicopter pilot who has been flying rescue missions since the disaster began, said he was shocked to see the devastation in Timure, a border town close to Tibet that he has known for years.
"It felt like I was flying over an entirely different landscape," he said.
Sharma said he has had little opportunity to speak with the people he rescued, but their expressions told him how deeply the disaster had affected them.
"I can see the pain in their eyes. It's heartbreaking," he said.
Filmmaker and drone pilot Manish Maharjan crossed into Nepal from Tibet through Rasuwagadhi, a border crossing closest to where last week's catastrophic flooding began, two days before the disaster. Returning home, little did he know he would be using his professional skills to help with rescue efforts along a route he has known intimately from years of travel for work.
As authorities mobilized dozens of rescue and relief teams, Maharjan joined the Nepal army's rescue efforts a day after the flash floods.
He said drones were effective in locating people who were stranded on hillsides and in isolated places, including caves.
"We used microphone speakers to call out to them. In some places, we even played songs and then waited for a response. That worked in a few cases and helped us locate people," Maharjan said.
While drones have helped him rescue some stranded people in open areas, the tunnels present an entirely different challenge, he said.
"We found tunnels were filled with mud like toothpaste in a tube," Maharjan said. "There was no hollow or empty space inside."

items.title: Russian air attacks kill 12 in Kyiv region on 6th day of strikes
items.summary: Russian air attacks killed 12 people and injured several more in Kyiv and the surrounding region early on Tuesday, authorities said, in the sixth consecutive day of strikes on the Ukrainian capital.
items.body_text:
Russian air attacks kill 12 in Kyiv region on 6th day of strikes
Swarms of drones over Ukraine capital and nearby areas kill residents, damage homes
Russian air attacks killed 12 people and injured several more in Kyiv and the surrounding region early on Tuesday, authorities said, in the sixth consecutive day of strikes on the Ukrainian capital.
Russia, which began its full-scale invasion of its smaller neighbour in 2022, has escalated its air attacks against Ukraine in recent months, as its progress has slowed dramatically on the battlefield.
Swarms of drones have plagued Kyiv and nearby areas in the last five days, killing residents, damaging homes and warehouses. Many of them are newer versions, powered by jet engines, making them harder to intercept. The near round-the-clock attacks have upended daily routines for millions with hours-long air-raid alerts.
More explosions were heard in the capital on Tuesday morning, a Reuters witness said.
Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Russian drones and ballistic missiles had targeted residential areas and railway infrastructure in the heavy overnight attacks.
He called on Ukraine's allies to increase economic pressure on Russia, and to renew discussions about using Russia's frozen assets overseas to provide funding for Ukraine's war effort.
"It is time to signal [to] the Kremlin that imitating diplomacy does not work anymore," Sybiha said in a post on X. He urged allies to provide Ukraine with more air defences, as it runs critically low on the U.S.-made Patriot interceptors capable of stopping Russia's ballistic missiles.
In Kyiv, eight people were killed and fires broke out in different locations around the capital, emergency services said on the Telegram messaging app. Russian ballistic missile strikes on a railway depot and other railway facilities killed six employees, said the head of Ukrzaliznytsia state rail group, Oleksandr Pertsovskyi.
In Boryspil outside Kyiv, four people were killed and a further 13 injured in an attack that hit a residential building and other sites, Gov. Tymur Tkachenko said on Telegram.
An Indian citizen was among those killed in Ukraine overnight, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
The overnight barrage included a "significant number" of jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles, Zelenskyy said.
Ukraine's air force said it had been able to shoot down five ballistic missiles. Kyiv recently received a small batch of Patriot interceptors.
The Russian strikes also targeted a border crossing with NATO-member Romania in the Black Sea region of Odesa, where repeated attacks on ports and ships have brought Ukraine's vital agricultural exports to a virtual halt, pressuring global food prices.
Thousands of families there were left without electricity, Zelenskyy said.
Estonia's defence forces said drones used in a Ukrainian strike against Russia had briefly entered Estonian airspace. Estonian Defence Minister Hanno Pevkur said the incident — the latest of a series in recent months — showed how important it was to support Ukraine with air defence assets.
Russia's Defence Ministry said Moscow hit military and energy facilities in Kyiv and Odesa overnight, as well as regions surrounding these cities.
Ukraine has also increased its attacks on Russia, targeting oil facilities and logistics infrastructure to undermine Moscow's ability to wage war.
Local governors said air attacks caused a fire in the port area of Ust-Luga, a major export outlet in the northwest, and damaged civilian facilities in the Samara region, home to a number of major oil refineries some 800 km southeast of Moscow.
Four people were killed and three more wounded by a wave of Ukrainian drone attacks on Tuesday in the Russian-controlled part of Luhansk region in eastern Ukraine, the region's Russian-installed governor, Leonid Pasechnik, said.
A civilian was also killed in an attack on Russia's Belgorod region, which borders Ukraine, the acting governor said.

items.title: Olivia Rodrigo's music festival raises $20M US for charities that help women and girls
items.summary: Tens of thousands of music lovers descended on Great Park in Irvine, Calif., over the weekend to scream along to their favourite artists — part of a history-making event to raise funds for women's health, reproductive rights and ending gender-based violence.
items.body_text:
Olivia Rodrigo's music festival raises $20M US for charities that help women and girls
Daisy Chain Fields featured a star-studded lineup ranging from Doechii to Bikini Kill
Tens of thousands of music lovers descended on Great Park in Irvine, Calif., over the weekend to scream along to their favourite artists — part of a history-making event to raise funds for women's health, reproductive rights and ending gender-based violence.
Daisy Chain Fields is the inaugural charity festival spearheaded by pop darling Olivia Rodrigo, following in the footsteps of the 1990s' trailblazing Lilith Fair with its all-women lineup.
The event brought together stars new and old, with queer pop star Chappell Roan and rapper Doechii featured alongside legacy punk and rock acts like Bikini Kill and Garbage.
Prior to the start on Saturday, Rodrigo announced that they had raised $10 million US for the festival's 10 non-profit partners, including Planned Parenthood, the National Institute for Reproductive Health and Black Mamas Matter Alliance — a figure which was then matched by Melinda French Gates to bring the total to $20 million US.
Rodrigo first announced the festival in June, sharing that stars would perform for free, with all net proceeds going "to charities dedicated to advancing and advocating for women and girls."
The 23-year-old paid homage to those who paved the way, performing Landslide with Stevie Nicks and bringing two Canadian icons out onstage during her set.
Alanis Morissette made a surprise appearance in place of Karen O, lead vocalist of the Yeah Yeah Yeahs, who was unable to make the event. Morissette performed her hit Ironic with Rodrigo, updating one lyric from "his beautiful wife" to "his beautiful husband," a change that sparked cheers in the crowd.
Lilith Fair founder Sarah McLachlan also joined Rodrigo onstage for several songs during her headlining set. The Canadian musician, who originally hails from Halifax, created the wildly successful all-women festival in 1997 at a time when filling a lineup with just women seemed like a fantasy.
"She was actually the first person I called when I started thinking about doing this," Rodrigo said of McLachlan at a Friday news conference.
"At the time of Lilith Fair, women were told that they couldn't lead a festival ... and those women proved everyone wrong."
Rodrigo said the name "Daisy Chain" was inspired by the idea of individual parts coming together "to create something strong and unbreakable."
The concert comes at a time when reproductive rights are under attack in the U.S. Since the overturning of Roe v Wade in 2022, which ended the federal right to abortion, reproductive rights have been dismantled in many states.
U.S. President Donald Trump is currently attempting to overhaul the nation's only federally funded family planning program — which allows clinics to provide birth control, treat sexually transmitted infections and provide other non-abortion sexual health services to low-income Americans — to force providers to align their programs with his administration's priorities.
This means providers would have to end diversity programs, cease offering gender-affirming care to transgender patients and discourage contraception, or run the risk of losing this federal funding. More than 20 states filed to sue his administration last week over the changes.
Rodrigo said Friday that while "it's easy to be discouraged by all of the sadness and regression of women's rights in our world today," the artists and activists who joined her for Daisy Chain Fields give her hope.
Benefit concerts are a common way to raise funds for everything from refugee relief to health-care support. After fires swept through Los Angeles, a FireAid concert in January 2025 featuring more than 30 artists raised an estimated $100 million US, while a virtual benefit concert organized by Lady Gaga in 2020 for health-care workers and COVID-19 relief raised $127.9 million US.

items.title: UN food agency to halve West Bank food assistance due to severe funding shortages
items.summary: World Food Programme warns it may be forced to make further cuts in Gaza, where it supports 1.5 million people
items.body_text:
The United Nations’ food agency said Tuesday it is halving food assistance in the Israeli-occupied West Bank because of severe funding shortages and warned it may be forced to make further cuts in Gaza, where it supports 1.5 million people.
The UN World Food Programme said it will reduce assistance in the West Bank from 400,000 people to 200,000 beginning this month. In Gaza, it reduced the value of cash assistance by 40 per cent for 375,000 people in July and said additional cuts will be unavoidable unless it secures new funding.
WFP said it urgently needs an additional US$386-million over the next six months to assist an estimated 2 million food-insecure people across Gaza and the West Bank.
The world’s leading authority on food insecurity, the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, said in July the situation in Gaza had improved since famine was declared in parts of the Palestinian territory last year, but warned conditions were still at crisis levels.
Also in July, the WFP cautioned that funding shortages and what it described as donor fatigue could force deeper reductions in Gaza and said it needed more than US$420-million to sustain operations in Gaza and the West Bank through the end of the year.
In the West Bank, WFP estimated in its Tuesday report that 900,000 people are food insecure. The agency said increased violence, displacement and economic deterioration have disrupted livelihoods and deepened hunger, while food needs have more than doubled since 2023.
“Families who were once thriving and earning a living from their land are now unable to afford enough food,” Shaun Hughes, WFP’s country director, said in a statement Tuesday. He added the agency was being forced to prioritize the most vulnerable households while cutting assistance to others despite widespread need.
According to WFP’s latest food security analysis, 76 per cent of households in the West Bank have experienced a significant decline in income. One-third cannot afford a nutritious diet, while food and fuel prices remain among the highest in the Middle East. Rural communities and the southern West Bank are among the hardest hit, the agency said.
Humanitarian conditions also remain severe in Gaza. According to recent UN figures from aid agencies, about one in five families ate only one meal a day, while half reported running out of food entirely at least once in the previous month. Aid agencies say cash shortages and soaring food prices have made it increasingly difficult for families to obtain basic necessities.
According to WFP, three-quarters of households in Gaza had difficulty accessing markets in August. The UN and its partners recently collected hundreds of pallets of food, fuel and other supplies through the Kerem Shalom crossing and distributed food parcels and wheat flour to more than 600,000 people during the August aid cycle.
Despite a ceasefire signed by Israel and Hamas in October, 2025, ongoing hostilities and security restrictions continue to hamper movement and recovery efforts, according to UN agencies.
The UN says more than 2 million people have been displaced during the war and that much of Gaza’s civilian infrastructure, including homes, hospitals, schools and water facilities, has been damaged or destroyed.

items.title: Iran urges U.S. to honour June interim deal, says it would reciprocate
items.summary: Tensions remain high after Trump threatens Tehran with further strikes
items.body_text:
Iran said on Tuesday it would reciprocate if the United States honoured its commitments under a June interim deal on halting their conflict, but tensions remained high after U.S. President Donald Trump threatened Tehran with further strikes.
Oil prices rose after the first exchange of direct attacks since late July, and following reports of two tankers coming under fire leaving the Strait of Hormuz, the global oil supply waterway that Iran has effectively closed to shipping.
The six-month-old conflict had shifted into an economic standoff before a U.S. attack on Iran’s Larak Island on Sunday, which Iran responded to by launching missiles overnight at two U.S. air bases in Jordan.
“We’re going to hit them hard ... There will be a response,” a Fox News reporter quoted Trump as telling the channel on Monday, although the president separately told reporters that the renewed strikes did not signal a return to full-scale war.
A senior Iranian source told Reuters the exchanges of fire were a “limited and contained confrontation” but said Tehran would deliver a harsh response if attacked again.
While neither side appears to want a return to all-out war, their pledges to respond to further attacks highlight how quickly a conflict that has increasingly been fought through sanctions, blockades and economic pressure could spill back into military action.
Fears that Iran conflict could go on
Tehran has repeatedly said it will allow free navigation through the Strait of Hormuz only if Washington implements the terms of the Memorandum of Understanding that was signed by both sides in June but quickly unravelled.
The MOU declared an end to fighting but deferred many of the most difficult issues and paved the way for a broader 60-day negotiation period – which passed without further agreement.
“I am stating clearly that if the U.S. returns to its commitments under the Memorandum of Understanding, the Islamic Republic of Iran will immediately reciprocate,” Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said.
He was speaking in Bishkek, capital of Kyrgyzstan, during a summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, whose members also include Russia, China, India and Pakistan.
He had also said on Monday that war was in no one’s interest and that Tehran was still open to a negotiated solution.
But there has been no sign of a breakthrough and the heightened tensions this week have renewed fears of oil supply disruptions from the world’s key crude-producing region, with Brent futures rising another 1.3 per cent on Tuesday.
“The tit-for-tat missile exchanges between the U.S. and Iran bring validation to those who believe that even if not a ‘forever war’, this conflict will run and run,” said PVM analyst John Evans.
Highlighting such concerns, two supertankers carrying Saudi oil were struck by unknown projectiles within minutes of each other while transiting outbound through the Strait of Hormuz late on Monday, according to data from shipping intelligence and tracking firms Marisks and Kpler.
Economic pressure
Thousands have been killed in the conflict, mainly in Iran and Lebanon, since it began with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb. 28. Washington has increasingly relied on economic pressure to try to force Tehran to stop blockading the Strait and end the conflict.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has warned that countries doing business with Iran could face U.S. sanctions and said secondary sanctions are likely to be unveiled weekly in the effort to pressure Iran, with an initial focus on banks.
Iran’s central bank governor, Abdolnaser Hemmati, said on Tuesday that Tehran had sufficient foreign currency reserves.
The central bank was ready to inject up to US$2-billion into the foreign exchange market to calm recent volatility, Hemmati was quoted as saying by the semi-official Tasnim news agency.
“I am telling the president of the United States: Iran has [foreign] currency and it has enough,” he said.

items.title: Marc-Olivier Fortin: Quebec goes ‘elbows up’ — CAQ could ride anti-Trump voters to victory
items.summary: Christine Fréchette is shamelessly copying Mark Carney's playbook
items.body_text:
Marc-Olivier Fortin: Quebec goes 'elbows up' — CAQ could ride anti-Trump voters to victory
Christine Fréchette is shamelessly copying Mark Carney's playbook
Hannibal ad portas. “Hannibal is at the door.”
Trump is the imminent danger “at the door” that Christine Fréchette, CAQ leader and Quebec premier, is using to rally-round-the-flag against, in an attempt to rescue her government from what had seemed certain defeat in October’s election.
Recommended Videos
Sounds familiar? It is a very similar to the strategy that Mark Carney used for his own election against Pierre Poilievre.
A key figure from former premier François Legault’s government, Fréchette was handpicked by party apparatchiks and won a leadership race after Legault resigned this past winter. In power since 2018, Legault was at one time the most popular, and later the least popular, premier of the province this century.
Trump might not be about to sack Quebec City, but Fréchette is behaving as if he is. In her first campaign news conference on Thursday, she declared with all seriousness, yet could not help but crack a little smirk: “My opponent is named Donald Trump. He’s the real adversary.” The similarity with the Carney campaign is almost uncanny.
It is not a secret though that her campaign manager, Brigitte Legault, a former federal Liberal, is very close to Carney’s entourage. This association is even more remarkable considering the Liberal Party of Quebec still exists. The Coalition Avenir Québec is using the same playbook in an egregious way, considering Fréchette isn’t even leading trade talks. At least Carney could claim direct responsiblity for dealing with Trump.
The premier is not an outsider, and her resume is far from being in the same weight class as Carney’s. But, as we say in politics, the first rule is to choose your adversary, and chose she did. A recent Abacus Data poll showed that Donald Trump and his administration is the main issue of concern for Quebec voters at 63 per cent.
-   Kevin Paquette: Quebec Conservative Éric Duhaime’s moment is here
-   Michael Higgins: Trade war was never about sovereignty
- Advertisement 1Story continues below
Fréchette is moving away from “how well the CAQ has governed” to “who do you trust to protect Quebec from Trump?” Only one of these questions requires the government to defend its record.
Fortunately, not everybody is falling for this dog and pony show. Two polls released in the first week of the campaign still show the CAQ in fifth place among 18-34 years old and fourth place among 35 to 54 years old. Most of the party’s support, comes from voters 55 and older, where we find most of the “elbows-up” crowd. Fréchette is leadeing this group by a wide margin.
Overall, poll aggregator Qc125 on Aug. 30th has the PQ at 29 per cent and the CAQ at 25 per cent, with the Quebec Liberals at 21 per cent. The latter were once at 32 per cent back in April. The Conservative Party of Quebec sits at 15 per cent and the progressive Quebec Solidaire at 10 per cent
In this current election, younger voters tend to support political parties that support change, nationalism, address the economy, the cost of living, housing, health care, immigration, the more bread-and-butter issues younger generations are facing. To these voters, though the tariffs’ impact is real and Trump poses a significal challenge to Canadian exports, Quebec needs to control what it can control and get its own house in order. Unfortunately, this does not describe a large part of the electorate, particularly among older voters.
An age divide along such drastic lines has rarely been seen in Quebec. It is not only a difference of opinion, but also a divergence of where these two different electorates get their political information from. Older generations still rely mostly on traditional media such as television. items.title: I’m a good listener but no one ever asks about me. Am I missing something? | Ask Rebecca
items.summary: The right thing to do is try the Salad Test at your next lunch. Before the bill comes, point to their full plates and ask, 'See anything interesting here?'
items.body_text:
I'm a good listener but no one ever asks about me. Am I missing something? | Ask Rebecca
The right thing to do is try the Salad Test at your next lunch. Before the bill comes, point to their full plates and ask, 'See anything interesting here?'
We independently select everything we recommend. Buying through us may earn us a commission, which supports our work.
Ask Rebecca is smart, honest advice to readers’ questions about life, family and relationships by columnist Rebecca Eckler. Got a question for Rebecca? Submit it anonymously on the form here. You can also send an email to NPadvice@postmedia.com.
Dear Rebecca:
I have so many people in my life who express what a good listener I am and what a great time or conversation we have together. These comments leave me feeling confused. About a year ago, I started to pay attention to whether our dialogue, whether one-to-one or in a group, was reciprocal. It is not. No one asks me a single question. If I ask, “Would you like to hear about my darling, or my grandchildren, or where my time is spent?” they will say “yes.” However, no one, and I mean no one, asks.
I ask about everything and keep the conversation moving. I care about all these people, yet I am no longer interested in one-way talk streets. And if I don’t organize us getting together, we don’t. I am truly wondering what value there is for me to continue in these relationships.
I don’t think they would miss me, and I wonder if I would miss them. Or am I the one missing something entirely? — Always Waiting For My Turn
Dear Always Waiting For My Turn:
Being a good listener is a bit like being too good at washing dishes. Once people find out, you’re somehow always expected to do them.
I understand why people tell you you’re a good listener. You make people feel interesting and comfortable enough to tell you things. It’s a lovely quality. People love people who make them feel fascinating.
But, as you’ve discovered, it can also be exhausting.
Being a good listener seems to have turned into being the one who does all the listening. You say you’re a good conversationalist. The irony is you barely get to converse.
I understand why that hurts. You feel invisible and unappreciated. It’s hard not to wonder if your friends value you or simply value being cared for by you.
You can spend two hours over lunch learning that your friend’s sex life is dead, her cat has gastrointestinal issues, she’s increased her Ozempic dosage and why she will never fly Air Canada again, only to realize when the cheque arrives she never once asked, “So, what’s up with you?”
Now, salad.
About a decade ago, I developed a completely unscientific way to measure whether a conversation is reciprocal: the Salad Test. If my friend finishes lunch and my plate is still full, I did most of the talking. If hers is untouched, she did. If we finish at roughly the same time, congratulations. We’ve achieved that increasingly rare social phenomenon known as a conversation.
Try it at your next lunch. Before the bill comes, point to her full plate and ask, “See anything interesting here?”
But you’re not asking me why your friends don’t ask you questions. You’re asking if you stopped doing all the listening and organizing, whether these friendships would still exist.
Maybe a better question is whether you still value these friendships enough to work this hard at them.
I also noticed how emphatic you are that no one asks you questions. “No one, and I mean no one.” When the same pattern shows up in every friendship, it’s worth looking at your own role. Do you automatically become The Listener? Fill every silence with another question? Wait to be asked before sharing?
I’m not letting your friends off the hook, but I’m not letting you off either. You’ve spent years expecting them to notice something you haven’t actually told them.
You mention asking your friends if they’d like to hear about your “darling or your grandchildren.” Stop doing that.

items.title: Étienne A. Beauregard: Could generation Z help save western civilization?
items.summary: The cohort rejects the nihilistic progressive project as much, if not more, than their elders
items.body_text:
Étienne A. Beauregard: Could generation Z help save western civilization?
The cohort rejects the nihilistic progressive project as much, if not more, than their elders
What happens when a society loses the traditions, institutions and shared obligations that once gave people a sense of belonging and purpose? In this adapted excerpt from Anti-Civilization: The Collapse of Society and the Case for the Common Good — now available from Sutherland House Publishing — Étienne-Alexandre Beauregard examines what this loss has meant for Generation Z, the first generation to come of age fully within this new landscape.
Generation Z — those born from 1997 to 2012 — are reaping the fruits sown by the baby boomers, the “sixties generation,” who, in their libertarian fervour, broke the chain of transmission without realizing that the cultural and moral heritage they had received was precisely the condition of their freedom.
As generations succeed one another, the traces of this precious heritage fade and young people are orphaned of the civilizational transmission they desperately need. The idea that culture, established customs and civilization are burdens for human beings ultimately proves to be the greatest of “luxury beliefs.” Because we took these treasures for granted and neglected to maintain them, we sorely miss them today.
The breakdown of value systems and social relationships has left behind a field of ruins. Several studies conducted among young Americans at the forefront of Western trends, point to a worrying impoverishment of social ties. They have fewer close friends and see them less often than before. Love is also in decline: young people have less sex than their elders did at the same age, and young people in relationships are sleeping together less often. It seems that “social distancing,” a term coined during the pandemic, has become an established reality. Unsurprisingly, a desocialized civilization is also one that has fewer children and where people become parents later, now after 30, in most of the Western world.
Has this “open society” made them happier? On the contrary, Generation Z is swept away by a nihilistic temptation, more inclined to believe that life has no meaning, to doubt themselves and to have a pessimistic view of the future. It would seem that individualism has created a need for identity, belonging, and reference points that have not been fulfilled by the void that has been offered to their generation.
The impoverishment of general culture, which, at present, dismisses the great works of the Western canon, goes hand in hand with a closing of the mind and horizons, making us incapable of communing with what came before us. As French essayist and politician François-Xavier Bellamy writes,“Our ignorance renders statues mute, images indecipherable, texts incomprehensible; the signs we have inherited lose their meaning.”
This “precariousness of all spheres of existence” logically translates into a “demand for protection, measure and limits” to serve as a guide in an unknown and strange world to which they have been deliberately denied the keys. Left to fend for themselves in a labyrinth without a map to guide them, young people have every right to hold this new world accountable for abandoning them.
Increasingly, observers are realizing that the younger generations reject the progressive project as much, if not more than their elders, and are among the most enthusiastic supporters of the populist shift to the right. In the 2024 U.S. election, no less than 56 per cent of men and 40 per cent of women under the age of 30 cast a Republican ballot, whereas in 2008, 66 per cent of young people had voted for Barack Obama.

items.title: Déreconstruire
items.summary: Que nous devons-nous les uns aux autres quand tout est en morceaux?
items.body_text:
Il tient dans les mains. Un bol cassé dont les morceaux ont été recollés par des veines d’or. La technique a un nom, kintsugi, et une règle que l’Occident a mis des siècles à entendre : pour réparer la cassure, on la dore. L’objet brisé tend ainsi sa fêlure vers des paumes futures. Chaque fois que je prends ce bol imaginaire, je me dis que nous sommes exactement là : un monde en morceaux dans les mains, et deux gestes qui doivent être revus.
Le premier : déconstruire. Ce geste fut absolument nécessaire. Il fut même, pendant un demi-siècle, la définition de la lucidité. Mais un geste critique qui triomphe devient une habitude, une habitude devient une tradition et une tradition peut devenir un dogme.
La déconstruction, née pour ébranler les orthodoxies, est parfois devenue la nôtre. Mais pendant que dehors les ruines s’accumulent — écologiques, démocratiques, intimes —, la question aujourd’hui semble moins être « Qu’est-ce qui est encore à défaire ? », mais plutôt « Comment fait-on pour vivre dans ce qui est défait ? ».
Le second geste guette alors, et il est plus dangereux encore : restaurer. C’est la grande tentation de notre époque, et elle porte plusieurs costumes : la nostalgie des formes anciennes dans nos arts, la nostalgie des ordres anciens dans nos parlements, la promesse — toujours criée, jamais tenue — d’une grandeur retrouvée. Car la restauration ment. Elle ment sur l’objet, dont elle maquille l’histoire, et elle ment sur nous, qu’elle invite à désapprendre ce que la casse nous a appris.
Nous ne pouvons plus simplement déconstruire, car le geste s’est épuisé en système. Et nous ne pouvons pas restaurer : le geste s’est disqualifié en déni. C’est ce nœud qu’il faut dénouer. Non pas en faisant l’arbitre entre les deux gestes, mais en nommant un troisième geste qui les traverse et les excède. Déreconstruire ?
Le néologisme est laid. Il ne se laisse pas prononcer d’un trait. Il faut le décomposer pour l’entendre — dé, re, con, struire — et cette décomposition est son mode d’emploi. Le radical dit le chantier : construire. Les préfixes disent l’histoire sédimentée dans le chantier : ce qui fut construit fut défait (dé-), et ce qui fut défait demande à être repris (re-), mais repris sans que l’aspect défait soit gommé, puisque le dé- demeure, inscrit dans le mot comme la veine d’or demeure dans le bol. Déreconstruire, c’est rebâtir avec et par les marques du délitement. Ni détruire ni restaurer : reconstruire en maintenant visible, dans la forme reconstruite, portant la trace de la fêlure.
Du côté du patrimoine bâti, deux églises brûlées le disent mieux que moi. À Dresde, on a rebâti la Frauenkirche en réintégrant dans la pierre claire les blocs noircis par les bombes : elle enseigne sa catastrophe. Notre-Dame de Paris, à l’inverse, fut relevée à l’identique, l’incendie rendu invisible. Deux relèvements : l’un tend la fêlure, l’autre l’efface.
Ici, dans Okinum, Émilie Monnet fait tenir ensemble l’anishinaabemowin, le français et l’anglais dans la même partition : la fracture coloniale y est audible et tendue dans la langue même.
Ce que j’appelle déreconstructivisme n’est ni un style, ni une école, ni une période. C’est une pragmatique de l’adresse réparatrice. Et le geste déreconstructif ne loge ni dans l’œuvre, ni dans le sujet, ni dans une communauté. J’avance qu’il loge dans ce qui les engendre tous les trois : la scène d’adresse.
À mon sens, un geste est déreconstructif quand quelqu’un, depuis les décombres, reprend un matériau brisé, le dévie dans la reprise même, et le tend vers l’autre, dont il attend la réponse et le soin. C’est une phrase adressée à des mains qui ne l’ont pas encore tenu.
Que peut une adresse ? Que peuvent une parole, une forme, un geste, quand ils reprennent ce qui est cassé — une langue, une institution, une convention du vivre-ensemble, un je — et le tendent, fêlure visible, vers quelqu’un ? À quelles conditions cette adresse répare-t-elle au lieu d’orner, enseigne-t-elle au lieu de surplombe

items.title: La crise en éducation préoccupe bien peu les électeurs
items.summary: Les défis sont pourtant nombreux dans les écoles, les cégeps et les universités du Québec.
items.body_text:
Écoles qui débordent et manquent d’entretien, pénurie d’enseignants qui entraîne le recours à du personnel non légalement qualifié, cégeps et universités aux prises avec un manque de financement : les problèmes en éducation et en enseignement supérieur sont grands. Mais les partis politiques pourraient y accorder une place bien mince dans leurs promesses électorales, à l’image de l’importance qu’y accordent les Québécois.
Selon les résultats de deux sondages menés au début et à la fin du mois d’août auprès de quelque 1000 Québécois par la firme Synopsis pour le compte de La Presse, l’éducation se trouve dans l’ombre de trois « grands défis » qui accaparent l’attention des électeurs. Il s’agit, en ordre, du système de santé, de l’inflation et du coût de la vie, puis des défis liés au milieu de l’habitation.
Suivent l’instabilité créée par la guerre commerciale que mène Donald Trump avec le Canada, puis une série d’autres sujets qui rejoindraient moins les électeurs, dont l’état de nos routes, le niveau des taxes et des impôts… et l’éducation.
« Notre crainte, c’est vraiment qu’on ne parle pas du tout d’éducation pendant cette campagne », indique en entrevue au Devoir le porte-parole du Regroupement des comités de parents autonomes du Québec, Sylvain Martel. « D’habitude, quand ce n’est pas en haut de la liste [des priorités des électeurs], il y aura peut-être des questions là-dessus dans un débat, mais on ne passera pas des jours à en parler, c’est sûr », entrevoit-il à regret.
Evelyne Brie, professeure adjointe en science politique à l’Université de Montréal, constate elle aussi que, lorsqu’on demande aux électeurs de trier leurs priorités, quelques dossiers « vont tout écraser », avec pour résultat qu’une série d’autres sujets se partagent des miettes.
Pourtant, souligne-t-elle, les Québécois sont préoccupés par les nombreux problèmes que rencontre notre réseau de l’éducation, qui comprennent son manque de financement, le haut taux de roulement du personnel et les problèmes de violence et d’intolérance dans les écoles. « Il y a comme un consensus sur le fait que ça ne va pas très bien en éducation au Québec », poursuit l’experte.
Néanmoins, certaines questions, comme celles entourant le réseau de la santé, touchent une plus grande partie de la population — vieillissante — du Québec, note-t-elle. Les parents d’élèves qui fréquentent une école primaire ou secondaire représentent pour leur part une minorité de la population, tandis que les étudiants des niveaux collégial et universitaire votent en moyenne moins que leurs aînés. Ce sont là autant de facteurs qui pourraient limiter la place que les partis politiques accorderont à l’éducation et à l’enseignement supérieur pendant cette campagne électorale, analyse Mme Brie.
« C’est un peu inquiétant, parce que, selon nous, c’est un pilier. L’éducation, c’est ce qui amène tout le reste, que ce soit une meilleure santé de la population ou une meilleure situation économique au Québec », indique pour sa part M. Martel, qui ne cache pas sa déception devant le manque d’intérêt des Québécois pour ce dossier.
De multiples défis
Ce manque d’intérêt pour les problèmes que vit le réseau de l’éducation survient d’ailleurs alors que ceux-ci n’ont cessé de s’accumuler ces dernières années. En plus de la pénurie de personnel et du mauvais état des bâtiments, la présidente de l’Association montréalaise des directions d’établissement scolaire, Kathleen Legault, souligne les conséquences de « l’école à trois vitesses », « qui menace l’équité » et « nuit à la réussite de nos jeunes ».
« Ça crée beaucoup d’injustices, d’inégalités. items.title: Fierce storm downs trees and damages shopping malls in Guadalajara, with more rain on the way
items.summary: The Jalisco capital's metropolitan zone, which also includes Zapopan and Tlaquepaque, was battered hard Sunday by heavy rain and strong wind gusts. The post Fierce storm downs trees and damages shopping malls in Guadalajara, with more rain on the way appeared first on Mexico News Daily
items.body_text:
The intense storm that struck the Guadalajara Metropolitan Area (ZMG) Sunday afternoon left behind downed trees, pooled water on roadways and damaged shopping centers in both Guadalajara and Zapopan.
In Zapopan, Civil Protection and Fire Department authorities reported that at least 13 trees had fallen, mostly in the city center. One went down on Patria Avenue, near the urban forest of Los Colomos, blocking traffic.
In Guadalajara, initial reports counted another seven fallen trees. The affected areas include Pablo Neruda and Circuito Madrigal intersections; Terranova and Buenos Aires; Manuel Diéguez and José María Vigil; and Patria and Alberta.
Authorities worked to remove branches and trunks, clear streets and reduce risks for pedestrians and motorists.
The storm also caused damage to shopping centers.
Andares, a shopping mall in the high-end residential area of Puerta de Hierro, Zapopan, reported that water leaked through the roof of a department store, damaging merchandise.
Meanwhile, gusts of wind caused glass panels to detach and fall from the roof in Midtown, a shopping mall located along López Mateos Avenue in Guadalajara. Debris fell onto the food court, where diners and visitors were taking shelter from the storm. However, no injuries were reported as a result of the incident.
In addition to fallen trees and damage to shopping centers, Sunday’s storm reportedly caused power outages in several neighborhoods in the ZMG, where power didn’t return until Monday morning.
More rain was expected today across the city, with the National Water Commission (Conagua) anticipating an 80% chance of rain in Guadalajara and 40% in Zapopan.
Despite the severe storms that have occurred this year in Jalisco, rainfall has not generated a significant recovery in the level of Lake Chapala, the main source of water supply for the ZMG. Data from Conagua revealed that the lake’s water capacity currently stands at 69% — up 6% compared to the beginning of June.
Josué Sánchez Tapetillo, a specialist in water resource management, told the local newspaper El Informador that the lake has recovered approximately 46 centimeters during the current rainy season. He noted that although the recovery rate has been slow compared to previous years, there is no cause for alarm as the rainy season is not over yet.
With reports from Telediario and El Informador

items.title: In Coatepec, INAH discovers ceremonial plaza and stele with never-before-seen features
items.summary: The stele features engravings alluding to a symbolic event in which two elite figures, seated and wearing elaborate attire, receive a fluid from a divine entity holding a vessel on a higher plane. The post In Coatepec, INAH discovers ceremonial plaza and stele with never-before-seen features appeared first on Mexico News Daily
items.body_text:
A civic-ceremonial plaza and a monolithic stele featuring atypical characteristics for the region were discovered in the area of Coatepec, Veracruz, in a find that could provide new clues about the societies that lived there prior to the Conquest.
Both the structure and the sculpture, which are reminiscent of those from nearby Maya settlements, were found in a good state of preservation.
The National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) said in a statement that the find offers the opportunity to explore a unique regional expression that has been little studied and that is challenging to connect definitively with the established traditions of the Gulf Coast.
In an interview with newspaper La Jornada, INAH archaeologists Lino Espinoza García and Alberto Vázquez Domínguez said that the settlement dates back some 1,500 years before the Christian era, coinciding with the beginning of the Campo Viejo settlement.
According to the archaeologists, “from that time onwards, there was a continuous population [inhabiting the area] until the colonial era,” which began in the early 1500’s.
The findings on the platform and the stela, however, could date back to the Protoclassic period, ranging from 200 B.C. to 200 A.D.
A discovery with features never seen before
The discovery occurred on a private residential property as part of an archaeological salvage operation led by INAH archaeologists in the San Lucas subdivision, near the Campo Viejo archaeological zone.
The findings consist of a platform — 30 meters long by 12 meters wide — built with white slabs and blocks of dressed limestone, with a texture similar to plaster, which would have been selected or worked to create a specific visual finish.
The ornamentation features square-like figures and circular stones on two of its sides, attributes that are not typical of the region and had not been previously recorded there.
The monolithic sculpture measures 1.88 meters high, 1.47 meters wide at its widest point and 0.68 meters wide at its narrowest. With a thickness that ranges from 22 to 25 centimeters, it features engravings alluding to a symbolic event in which two elite figures, seated and wearing elaborate attire, receive a fluid from a divine entity holding a vessel on a higher plane.
Lino noted that “the entire stele, made of andesite stone, references themes of fertility and cultivation of the land.”
Field excavations conclude this month, and specialists will proceed with laboratory analyses, which will extend until early 2027.
Mexico News Daily

items.title: Mexican-built particle detector slated to help global scientists illuminate the birth of the universe
items.summary: If all goes according to plan, the Mexican team, under UNAM physicist Antonio Ortiz Velásquez, will contribue to an international project at the famous atom-smashing CERN Large Hadron Collider. The post Mexican-built particle detector slated to help global scientists illuminate the birth of the universe appeared first on Mexico News Daily
items.body_text:
A Mexican physicist was recently chosen to lead the development of a particle detector for one of the world’s largest scientific projects: an underground atom smasher in Europe that is helping scientists understand the universe shortly after the Big Bang.
The proposed detector would be built in Mexico and installed at the European Organization for Nuclear Research (CERN), home of the Large Hadron Collider beneath a portion of the French-Swiss border.
The Mexican-built device, called the Muon Identifier Detector (MID), is planned for ALICE 3, a future version of one of the collider’s four main experiments.
If built and approved, it would give Mexican institutions responsibility for a central subsystem of ALICE 3.
The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) is a particle accelerator and collider covering a circular circuit of 27 kilometers, or 17 miles, near Geneva, Switzerland. It speeds beams of protons or electrically charged atomic nuclei to within a whisker of the speed of light — about 1.08 billion km/h, or 671 million mph — before steering them into head-on collisions.
Collisions involving heavy atomic nuclei can briefly create matter thought to resemble conditions in the universe’s earliest moments.
The Mexican project is still not guaranteed to reach CERN.
While the MID is included in the reference design for ALICE 3, the Mexican team must obtain funding, finish the design and construction work and clear technical reviews before it can be installed. Operations are targeted for 2036.
The Mexican project is headed by Antonio Ortiz Velásquez, a senior researcher at the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM) whose appointment was approved by the ALICE Collaboration Board, UNAM said Aug. 13.
UNAM said Ortiz, a physicist at UNAM’s Institute of Nuclear Sciences, is the first Mexican scientist chosen to direct development of a strategic ALICE 3 subsystem.
Mexico has already worked with ALICE for years, helping build and operate earlier detector equipment and analyze collision data, but the new project goes even further.
The Mexican-built device would track muons, small particles that can pass through much of the detector after a collision. Their paths can help researchers study a fleeting, superheated state of matter that scientists believe filled the universe immediately after the Big Bang.
“We are recreating tiny droplets from the early universe and studying them through the traces they leave in particle detectors,” Ortiz said.
The team hopes to begin construction in Mexico in 2028. It includes researchers from UNAM, the Center for Research and Advanced Studies, the Benemérita Universidad Autónoma de Puebla, the Autonomous University of Sinaloa and the National Technological Institute of Mexico, along with partners in the United States, Hungary, the Czech Republic and Pakistan.
With reports from La Jornada, MxPA and Space Daily

items.title: Editorial: EU: ¿el verdadero narcoestado?
items.summary: El Comité de Supervisión de la Cámara de Representantes de Estados Unidos investiga a la Administración de Control de Drogas (DEA, por sus siglas en inglés) por una polémica táctica policial que permitió que “cantidades asombrosas de fentanilo mortal” llegaran a las calles cuando las autoridades federales buscaban armar casos antidrogas de mayor envergadura. items.body_text:
l Comité de Supervisión de la Cámara de Representantes de Estados Unidos investiga a la Administración de Control de Drogas (DEA, por sus siglas en inglés) por una polémica táctica policial que permitió que “cantidades asombrosas de fentanilo mortal” llegaran a las calles cuando las autoridades federales buscaban armar casos antidrogas de mayor envergadura. De acuerdo con informantes de la agencia entrevistados por funcionarios de Nuevo México –entidad considerada el epicentro de la crisis del fentanilo–, sus jefes les ordenaron hacerse a un lado en lugar de incautar cientos de miles de pastillas de fentanilo, en posible violación de normas del Departamento de Justicia destinadas a proteger a las comunidades.
Hace dos meses, Associated Press reveló que entre 2023 y 2025, en medio de la epidemia de drogas más mortífera en la historia de Estados Unidos, agentes de la DEA permitieron que más de 3 millones de pastillas de fentanilo llegaran a las calles con el presunto propósito de fortalecer casos penales. En Albuquerque, la ciudad más poblada de Nuevo México, los elementos de la DEA se mantenían al margen y observaban desde helicópteros y vehículos de vigilancia cómo distribuidores de droga entraban a hoteles con mochilas que se creía que llevaban hasta 100 mil pastillas de fentanilo. De acuerdo con la propia agencia, siete de cada 10 pastillas contienen suficiente droga para provocar la muerte por sobredosis a un adulto promedio, es decir, que por cada mochila que dejaban pasar se hacían cómplices de 70 mil homicidios. Por supuesto, es absurdo suponer que cada dosis derive en una muerte, pero la DEA y la Casa Blanca usan esa métrica al hablar de los “terroristas” que trafican los estupefacientes.
Quizá el público estadunidense pueda sorprenderse al conocer las tácticas cuestionables de sus corporaciones de combate a la delincuencia, pero en México y América Latina es bien conocido el doble rasero de Washington. De este lado del río Bravo, la sociedad recuerda el operativo Rápido y furioso, el esquema perverso con el cual, entre 2009 y 2011, la Oficina de Alcohol, Tabaco, Armas de Fuego y Explosivos de Estados Unidos permitió de forma deliberada la venta y el tráfico ilegal hacia México de más de 2 mil armas de fuego, a sabiendas de que los compradores eran grupos del crimen organizado y de que esos dispositivos serían usados contra policías y civiles mexicanos. La hipocresía se extiende al ámbito financiero: hace un año, el Departamento del Tesoro forzó el cierre de dos bancos y una casa de bolsa mexicanos por “facilitar el envenenamiento de innumerables estadunidenses al mover dinero para los cárteles”; de acuerdo con los señalamientos, las entidades manejaron en conjunto menos de 17 millones de dólares de procedencia ilícita. En contraste, el mismo Tesoro impuso una multa irrisoria de 125 millones de dólares y permitió que continúe operando UBS Financial Services, pese a que esta filial del grupo financiero suizo realizó transferencias internacionales de más de 10 mil millones de dólares sin monitorear el posible origen ilícito de los recursos.
Este patrón de conducta confirma que a Washington no le interesa combatir el crimen organizado dentro de sus fronteras ni evitar que las drogas lleguen a sus ciudadanos, sino usar el narcotráfico como pretexto para interferir en otros países. En los hechos, hay una protección sistemática y bipartidista al multimillonario negocio de los estupefacientes.
Desde la organización del trasiego de la cocaína para financiar la guerra contra el gobierno nicaragüense en la década de 1980, hasta el auge de la siembra de amapola durante la ocupación de Afganistán; desde el indulto al narcotraficante y ex presidente de Honduras Juan Orlando Hernández, hasta el programa de recompensas a los llamados testigos protegidos, resulta inocultable que durante el último medio siglo Estados Unidos ha sido un verdadero narcoestado.

items.title: Anuncian fechas para la compra de boletos en el regreso de la NFL a México
items.summary: Los boletos para el partido entre los Vikingos de Minnesota y los 49ers de San Francisco, que marcará el regreso de la NFL a México, se podrán adquirir en tres etapas a partir del 14 de septiembre, informó la liga y la plataforma Ticketmaster.
items.body_text:
Martes 1º de septiembre de 2026, p. a12
Los boletos para el partido entre los Vikingos de Minnesota y los 49ers de San Francisco, que marcará el regreso de la NFL a México, se podrán adquirir en tres etapas a partir del 14 de septiembre, informó la liga y la plataforma Ticketmaster.
La primera será el lunes 14 de septiembre a las 10 horas, con una preventa exclusiva para tarjetahabientes de American Express, quienes podrán adquirir hasta seis boletos por comprador.
El jueves 17, a la misma hora, comenzará la preventa para clientes de Banorte, con un límite de cuatro entradas por operación.
La venta general se abrirá el martes 22 de septiembre a las 10 horas y estará disponible para todos los aficionados que no hayan participado en alguna de las dos preventas anteriores.
De acuerdo con la información difundida por Ticketmaster México, los precios que aparezcan en el mapa de asientos ya incluirán los cargos por servicio, por lo que no cambiarán durante el proceso de compra. A la cantidad correspondiente a las entradas se añadirá un cargo de procesamiento de 50 pesos por orden.
La plataforma también hizo algunas recomendaciones para quienes busquen conseguir entradas. Entre ellas, pidió a los usuarios no actualizar la página mientras permanezcan en la fila virtual, debido a que podrían perder su lugar o ser identificados como bots y quedar fuera del proceso de compra.
Ticketmaster señaló que la disponibilidad de lugares podrá modificarse conforme otros usuarios completen sus operaciones. Por ello, el mapa de asientos se actualizará automáticamente durante la venta y los lugares disponibles podrán variar en tiempo real.
El encuentro entre Minnesota y San Francisco se disputará el domingo 22 de noviembre en el estadio Banorte, y representará el regreso de la temporada regular de la NFL al país después de cuatro años de ausencia.
El llamado Mexico City Game 2026 será el primer partido de temporada regular de la liga en México desde 2022, cuando los 49ers enfrentaron a los Cardenales de Arizona en el estadio Azteca.

items.body_text:
¿Oportunismo o doble personalidad? // ¿Dónde está su “odiado hegemón”? // “Nunca daremos paso a la traición”
istante quedó –no en tiempo, sino en forma y fondo– la entonces vicepresidenta de Venezuela (cuando, el 28 de septiembre de 2019 y a nombre de su país, participó como oradora en la Asamblea General de la Organización de Naciones Unidas, ONU) comparada con la actual “presidenta encargada” tras el ilegal secuestro estadunidense de Nicolás Maduro (3 de enero de 2026). Desde luego se trata de la misma persona, Delcy Rodríguez, pero a ciencia cierta no se sabe si ella tiene problemas de doble personalidad o de plano es políticamente oportunista.
Lo anterior, porque en aquella cumbre de la ONU tomó el micrófono “en nombre de la única Venezuela, de la Venezuela digna, la valiente, la que no se arrodilla ante poder imperial alguno”, y desde la principal tribuna de la Asamblea General transmitió “un saludo bolivariano en nombre del presidente Nicolás Maduro y del espíritu de nuestro comandante Hugo Chávez”; denunció las sucias prácticas “del hegemón del mundo –Estados Unidos– y sus satélites” en contra de su país, y subrayó que “el proyecto bolivariano es intrínsicamente contrario al proyecto monroísta que pretende hacer ver que toda nuestra América es un patio trasero de Estados Unidos”.
Todavía el 3 de enero de 2026 (tras el secuestro de Maduro y su designación como “presidenta encargada” de Venezuela, que rápidamente fue reconocida por la Casa Blanca) Delcy Rodríguez subrayó que su país “no va a ser colonia de nadie, de ningún imperio viejo ni nuevo, y la respuesta será unitaria, organizada y consciente, defendiendo la soberanía con dignidad; el único presidente de Venezuela es Nicolás Maduro y exijo su liberación inmediata junto a su esposa, Cilia Flores”.
No se sabe con exactitud cuál de ese par de discursos debe darse por válido (28 de septiembre de 2019 o 3 de enero de 2026), pero lo cierto es que –con Maduro ilegalmente preso en Nueva York– ambos son descartables, pues en apenas ocho meses, si no es que menos, como por arte de magia se fue apagando la retórica del “rechazo” al “proyecto monroísta”, “la defensa de la soberanía” y la denuncia del “patio trasero”, para dar paso a la acelerada cuan descarada entrega de las reservas petroleras venezolanas a su “odiado hegemón del mundo”, disfrazando el saqueo por ella autorizado de “pacto binacional que tendrá un impacto significativo en el renacimiento nacional”, con todas las de ganar para el barón Trump (para él, 71 por ciento de las ganancias por la venta de oro negro ajeno durante, cuando menos, 25 años), a quien reiteradamente denunció por su injerencismo y el cúmulo de sanciones aplicadas a la nación sudamericana que “pretenden apropiarse de todos nuestros recursos”.
En las dos décadas recientes, Delcy Rodríguez (hija del fundador de la Liga Socialista de su país y dirigente del Movimiento de Izquierda Revolucionaria, asesinado por el gobierno en el primer periodo presidencial de Carlos Andrés Pérez, el mismo que en 1975 nacionalizó el petróleo venezolano, sólo para reprivatizarlo en 1990 durante su segundo mandato) de forma ascendente recorrió todo el escalafón burocrático-político –siempre dentro del movimiento chavista– hasta llegar a ser la “presidenta encargada”, toda vez que su “hegemón” predilecto secuestró a Maduro, y ya en esa posición comenzó a “desandar” el movimiento bolivariano.
Fue ministra del Despacho de la Presidencia (con Hugo Chávez en el cargo), de Comunicación e Información, de Relaciones Exteriores, de Economía, Finanzas y Comercio Exterior, así como de Hidrocarburos. Fungió de primera y duodécima presidenta de la Asamblea Nacional Constituyente y de ahí a ser “presidenta encargada”, y parece que rápidamente olvidó de qué se trataba todo ello, pues más tardó en recorrer ese escalafón que en entregar el petróleo venezolano a su “odiado enemigo” (en el discurso).
