items.title: Ratko Mladić is still viewed as a hero by many Bosnian Serbs. It’s a reminder how divided my country remains today
items.summary: Bosnia remains a country divided by contrasting histories and narratives about the war. Mladić is a symbolic reminder of this.
items.body_text:
I was a 19-year-old living in Banja Luka, the second-largest city in Bosnia, when Yugoslavia began falling apart. What I remember most is the shock and speed with which my normal life and those of my friends abruptly ended.
At the time, I wasn’t following politics or watching the news much, so I had no idea what was to come – a full-blown war and genocide of the Bosniak (Bosnian Muslim people), led by Ratko Mladić, the Bosnian Serbian general and convicted war criminal, who died this week in a prison in The Hague.
Ethnicity was not something my friends and I ever talked about growing up. Two of my best friends were non-Serbs, which I only realised when they suddenly left Bosnia in April and May of 1992.
Soon after, I learned I was to be drafted into the Serbian territorial defence, not knowing what that even was. I went to pick up my uniform and boots, and that’s when my parents put me on the bus to leave the country. I didn’t know where I was going.
This was how I left my country, on my own, for the first time in my life: in haste, without goodbyes, not knowing if or when I would see my family again.
I was not the only one. Almost two million Bosnians were displaced during the war.
Now, with Mladić’s death, these memories of the war are flooding back, juxtaposed with the disheartening scenes of Mladić being celebrated by Serbs in Bosnia as a hero.
He was not a hero; nor is it helpful to refer to him simply as a “madman” or a “butcher”. Mladić is a symbolic reminder of the unresolved legacies of the war – the continued divisions among Bosnians and selective memories that many have about the atrocities that occurred.
Swift rise up the ranks
Mladić was a career military officer in the Yugoslav army. His rise through the ranks was accelerated at the beginning of the Bosnian war when he was named commander-in-chief of the Bosnian Serb army.
It’s important to understand this newly created army inherited all of its armour from the former Yugoslav army. It had all the weapons and military infrastructure in Bosnia, and was led by an experienced professional officer in Mladić.
Mladić’s army quickly took over 70% of the country, laying siege to the capital, Sarajevo. More than 100,000 people died in the war from 1992–95. At least 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were killed by the Bosnian Serb Army in the genocide in Srebrenica in July 1995.
Mladić was the face of this ruthless military campaign, and the rise of Serb nationalism at the time.
In my research, I’ve reviewed the accounts of Serbian soldiers and wartime leaders, and I’ve spoken extensively with Biljana Plavšić, the former president of the Bosnian Serb Republic and the only woman to be indicted by the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia. Plavšić worked closely with Mladić and knew him very well.
Serbian soldiers and leaders – and, unfortunately, many Serbs themselves – admired him for his perceived courageousness, his extraordinary self-confidence and his expressions of power.
This is why, to this day, many Serbs still see him as their protector – as a saint, who defended Serbs during the war. He has a special place in Serb mythology, due to the way generations of young Serbs have been indoctrinated by the narratives of his heroism during the war.
When the war was over in 1996, Mladić went into hiding for nearly 16 years, living in rural Serbia until he was arrested. He was tried in The Hague and convicted of war crimes, and sentenced to life in prison in 2017.
Understanding Mladić, the man and war criminal
As a scholar of mass atrocities, I think we need to be careful how we try to understand or explain the actions of the perpetrators of these crimes.
The media portrays Mladić as a monster, a madman, and the “Butcher of Bosnia”. But I believe it’s important to note he was not a psychopath.
Characterising him that way diminishes his criminal responsibility, as well as the structures that made his crimes possible. It paints him as someone detached from humanity

On August 26 a glacier collapsed in the Langtang region of Nepal near the China border, triggering an ice and rock avalanche. This apparently entered the Lhende Khola, a tributary of the Bhote Koshi river, where it either caused or contributed to a temporary blockage. When this burst, a catastrophic flash flood travelled almost 100 kilometres downstream.

Did warm conditions play a role?
There is increasing interest in the role of unusually warm conditions and glacial permafrost instability. Warming can increase meltwater penetration into the crevasses of glaciers and weaken ice-rock bonds. British Antarctic Survey researchers reported unusually high ground temperatures two days before the collapse.

items.summary: Iran president offers olive branch even as US restarts attacks Submitted by MEE staff on Tue, 09/01/2026 - 10:31 Masoud Pezeshkian says his country would be willing to reciprocate if the US returns to the June interim deal Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian arrives for a SCO+ format meeting of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek, 1 September 2026 (Vyacheslav Prokofyev/AFP/Sputnik) Off Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has offered an olive branch to US President Donald
items.body_text:
Iran president offers olive branch even as US restarts attacks
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has offered an olive branch to US President Donald Trump even after several soldiers and civilians were killed in an US strike on Larak Island.
Speaking on Monday before travelling to Bishkek for a Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit, Pezeshkian said Iran was "not looking for war” but would “never sit still in the face of any aggression”.
Iran “will give a decisive response to the aggressors” if attacked again, he said, according to the Fars news agency, but also said his country would immediately reciprocate if the US fulfilled its commitments under an interim deal signed in June, state media reported.
"I state explicitly that if the United States returns to its commitments under the aforementioned memorandum of understanding, the Islamic Republic of Iran will immediately take reciprocal action," Pezeshkian said, according to the Iran presidency's website.
US forces bombed Larak Island on Sunday, the official state broadcaster IRIB reported.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
It marked Washington’s first attack on Iran since July and raised fears of another escalation in the Israeli-US war against the country.
Following the strike, Iran urged the UN Security Council in a letter to demand that Washington end its attacks.
The letter, addressed to UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres by Gholamhossein Darzi, Tehran’s deputy permanent representative and ambassador to the UN, on Monday described the attacks as a "a clear violation of the sovereignty and territorial integrity" of Iran.
Darzi also accused the US and others involved in the attacks of war crimes and crimes against humanity in the war on Iran.
He also stressed that while Iran had show restraint, its forces "would not hesitate" to respond to any further strikes.
Economic strains
The impact of the war on the global economy has been highly damaging, particularly after Iran closed off the crucial Strait of Hormuz waterway.
The number of vessels sailing through the Strait of Hormuz saw little change on Monday, with preliminary ship-tracking data from Kpler showing the transit of five commodity vessels.
Four of those vessels entered the waterway and one exited.
One of the vessels that entered was an empty handy-sized gas tanker which travelled via the Iranian route. The other three were laden dry bulk carriers.
On Tuesday, Central Bank Governor Abdolnaser Hemmati said that Iran had sufficient foreign currency reserves despite the recent ramping up of US sanctions.
"I am telling the president of the United States: Iran has (foreign) currency and it has enough," he said.
Hemmati indicated that the central bank was ready to inject up to $2bn into the foreign exchange market to calm recent volatility.
He added that the central bank was continuing to collect foreign currency receivables and had domestic reserves as well as other resources.
"I tell the people with complete honesty that economic conditions and livelihood management have become difficult, but collapse has never happened and will never happen," he stressed.
"These claims are just psychological warfare and the dust will settle soon."

Israeli attacks on Gaza have escalated, with five Palestinians killed in the last 24 hours, the Palestinian health ministry is reporting.
On Tuesday morning, at least seven air strikes hit an area west of Gaza City within a 10-minute period, killing a child, while Israeli soldiers opened fire in Deir el-Balah, killing another child.
Palestinian journalist Abdulrahman Ismail reported in a post on X that the attacks in Gaza City targeted an area "near a field hospital and thousands of tents sheltering displaced Palestinians".
"Quadcopter drones then surrounded the area, opening fire and dropping explosives at anyone moving, as the sound of clashes echoed nearby. Israeli drones simultaneously spread across Gaza City, while smoke bombs were reported over Al-Shati," Ismail said.
He added that the scenes bore "a disturbing resemblance to previous incidents involving Israeli special forces operating on the ground, but what exactly unfolded remains unclear".
Ismail said that people remain trapped in the area.
Mai Elawawda, Medical Aid for Palestine's Communications Officer in Gaza, said: “Israeli military attacks have not stopped all week. We are all constantly stressed that anywhere can be evacuated or attacked by Israeli forces at any moment.”

items.body_text:
Almost half of terrorism arrests in UK since 9/11 have come after Palestine Action ban
New data has revealed that almost half of Britian's counterterrorism arrests since 9/11 coincided with the UK government's proscription of direct action group Palestine Action.
According to Home Office data, of the 6,539 arrests for terror-related activity in the UK since the 2001 attacks on the twin towers, 3,021 were in the past year.
The surge coincides with the proscription of Palestine Action in July last year - which led to thousands of arrests of people for holding signs during silent vigils in support of the group.
The ban is subject to a continuing legal challenge, which will be heard at the UK Supreme Court in November.
In the year ending 31 March, terrorism-related arrests soared by 1,434 percent with a 3,761% increase in arrests of women and girls and a 2,306% increase in arrests of those aged 30 and over.
Raj Chada, the head of criminal defence at the law firm Hodge Jones & Allen, said: "The most common terrorist in the UK at present is a pensioner at a silent vigil holding a placard."
According to the campaign group Defend Our Juries (DOJ), more than 3,600 people have been arrested so far for alleged support of Palestine Action.
"The proscription of Palestine Action is not about protecting the British public, but about protecting the UK's relationship with Israel and protecting the arms companies who, on UK soil, manufacture and supply weapons to a genocide," A DOJ spokesperson said.
"If the government was truly aiming to proscribe violent groups targeting civilians, the IDF [Israel Defense Forces] would be first on its list."
In a statement responding to the data, Ruth Ehrlich, the director of external relations at the civil rights group Liberty, said: “The staggering increase in arrests over the past year is the clearest indicator that the UK’s counter-terror laws are not fit for purpose." She added that when without public trust "counter-terror laws simply won’t work".

Duane "Keffe D" Davis, a former Los Angeles gang leader, was found guilty on Monday by a Las Vegas court of the 1996 murder of chart-topping rapper Tupac Shakur.
Thirty years after the rap legend's death, the jury found Davis, 63, guilty of murder after just a few hours of deliberation.
"Count one, murder with use of a deadly weapon, guilty of first-degree murder with use of a deadly weapon," the foreperson of the jury announced to the court.
Davis, who faces possible life in prison without parole, addressed Judge Carli Kierny after the verdict was announced and stated his intention to appeal.
The one-time leader of the South Side Compton Crips was accused of ordering the September 7, 1996 killing of the hip-hop artist after his own nephew had been beaten by members of Shakur's entourage at a Las Vegas casino.
"Duane Davis, in the culture of gangs, could not let that stand," prosecutor Binu Palal said during closing arguments. "So what did he do? He acquired a firearm, got his group together, and went hunting for Mr Shakur."
Shakur, who was in Las Vegas for a Mike Tyson heavyweight fight, was shot about two hours after the casino confrontation by a gunman in a white Cadillac that pulled up at a red light alongside the BMW in which the rapper was riding in the front passenger seat.
According to prosecutors, Davis handed the gun to someone sitting in the back seat of the Cadillac and ordered that person to shoot Shakur, who died six days later.
Davis is the only person who was in the Cadillac that evening who is still alive.
The driver of the BMW, Death Row Records co-founder Marion "Suge" Knight, was wounded.
The killing of Shakur, also known as 2Pac, has been one of America's most famous cold cases, prompting endless debate among music fans over who did it, and why.
Davis, whose Crips were one of a patchwork of rival gangs that ran parts of Los Angeles in the 1990s, is the only person to have been charged in connection with the shooting of Shakur.
Sentencing is scheduled for October 13.
Confession
The investigation into Shakur's murder sputtered for decades because of a lack of evidence, but the case was revived when Davis's memoirs were published in 2019.
In that book, Davis recounted that he was in the front seat of the Cadillac and that he handed a pistol to those in the back seat. But he does not say who opened fire on Shakur.
Davis has repeatedly boasted over the years of involvement in Shakur's murder -- in interviews with law enforcement and media and ultimately in his autobiography, "Compton Street Legend."
He has since backtracked and pleaded not guilty to the murder charge.
Palal, the prosecutor, played clips from Davis's various alleged confessions as part of his closing arguments.
Michael Sanft, Davis's defense attorney, characterized his client's confessions as fiction and lies partly designed to promote his book.
"You're reading a book that is fiction and not fact," Sanft told the jury. "But the state wants you to believe that this is somehow a confession, that he was there and present at the time of the shooting."
Sanft said there was no evidence implicating Davis in Shakur's murder other than his own statements.
In the run-up to the trial, Davis's lawyers tried in vain to keep the book from being introduced as evidence, along with remarks he made in an interview with police in 2008.
Shakur, who was 25 when he died, was a key figure in a hip-hop rivalry pitting the US East Coast against the West Coast.
Known for hits such as "California Love" and "All Eyez on Me," Shakur -- the son of a Black Panther -- was raised in Harlem and Baltimore, but quickly became the epitome of California hip hop when he signed with Los Angeles-based Death Row Records.

items.title: Former French PM Edouard Balladur dies aged 97: family
items.summary: Balladur, who was born in Turkey, served as President Francois Mitterrand's last prime minister from March 1993 to May 1995, carrying out several major privatisations of state companies, and unsuccessfully ran for the top job in 1995
items.body_text:
Edouard Balladur
Former French prime minister Edouard Balladur died in Paris on Monday at the age of 97, his family told AFP.
Balladur, who was born in Turkey, served as President Francois Mitterrand's last prime minister from March 1993 to May 1995, carrying out several major privatisations of state companies, and unsuccessfully ran for the top job in 1995.
After a fierce campaign, he lost to his former political ally-turned-rival, Jacques Chirac, who would remain president until 2007.
President Emmanuel Macron said Balladur was a man who "had France at heart" and a "devoted servant of the nation", while former president Nicolas Sarkozy said he had lost "an example, a mentor and a friend".
"Tonight, I mourn the loss of one of the men who mattered most in my life," Sarkozy wrote on X.
His family told AFP that a private mass will be held for Balladur, without giving further details.

items.body_text:
South Africa
Social media was buzzing this past weekend when two flights flew across the DHL Stadium in Cape Town, South Africa, ahead of the Springboks and All Blacks test on Saturday.
Many media reports and people expressed how unsafe and irresponsible it was for the airline to fly just over 50 feet from the packed stadium.
Airlink, Southern Africa’s premier airline, released a statement assuring the public that the events were planned and rehearsed beforehand, and that it was approved by the Civil Aviation Authority.
Airlink said that they staged a memorable formation flyby over the Ellis Park Rugby Stadium, setting the stage for the highly anticipated match between South Africa’s Springboks and New Zealand’s All Blacks.
The flyby was performed by two of Airlink’s bespoke-liveried Embraer aircraft (ZS-YAE E190 in green, and ZS-YDE E195 in black), reflecting the colours of the two competing teams and bearing the official Tour logo.

items.title: Vietnam’s Expanding Strategic Partnerships: Why Canada Could Be Next
items.summary: Recent developments suggest that the two middle-powers are on the cusp of an important diplomatic upgrade.
items.body_text:
Vietnam organizes its foreign relations into a three-tier hierarchy: Comprehensive Partnerships (CPs) sit at the base, Strategic Partnerships (SPs) in the middle, and Comprehensive Strategic Partnerships (CSPs) at the top. This sits alongside a category of special relationships with Cold War-era allies Laos, Cambodia, and Cuba.
Hanoi’s “bamboo diplomacy,” flexible in form but firm at its roots, has expanded all three categories at a remarkable pace. As of early 2026, Vietnam has 15 CSPs, following the upgrade of relations with the European Union in January 2026, alongside 15 SPs and 17 CPs. This network now touches every continent and every major power center, from Washington and Beijing to Moscow, Brussels, London, and Canberra.
The question that naturally follows is: who is next? Vietnam has not filled every available slot on its diplomatic hierarchy, and Hanoi has made clear – through the CPTPP chairmanship it holds in 2026 and the APEC hosting role it takes on in 2027 – that it intends to keep climbing. There are three reasons why Canada may be the next nation in line for a diplomatic upgrade.
The first is structural. Vietnam’s diplomatic strategy increasingly resembles that of other “middle powers” – states too large to be ignored but not seeking hegemony, which instead build resilience through diversified, non-aligned partnerships. Analysts have already grouped Vietnam alongside Australia, Canada, the Netherlands, and Switzerland as countries capable of maintaining deep ties with rival great powers simultaneously. If Vietnam is consciously cultivating this identity, it has an incentive to deepen ties specifically with other middle powers that share its instinct for strategic autonomy rather than bloc alignment — and Canada is one of the clearest examples of that category on the world stage today.
The second reason is geographic. Vietnam’s CSP network is heavily concentrated in Asia and Europe. Of its 30 SPs and CSPs, only two are in the Americas: the United States as a CSP and Brazil as an SP. For a country pursuing “multi-directional” diplomacy and actively courting new markets to reduce its dependence on any single economy, this is a conspicuous gap. Creating a second North American SP or CSP would meaningfully reduce the imbalance and enhance Vietnam’s global footprint and give it a more credible claim to truly global reach.
Third, Vietnam already holds strategic-level partnerships with six of the seven G-7 members, namely the United States (CSP), Japan (CSP), Germany (SP), France (CSP), the United Kingdom (CSP), and Italy (SP). Canada is the only G7 economy with which Vietnam has not yet formalized a strategic-tier relationship; the two countries currently sit at the lower “Comprehensive Partnership” level. In the meantime, Vietnam’s foreign policy attaches importance to promoting relationships with “major powers and important partners.” Obviously, Vietnam sees Canada as “an important partner.”
Taken together, these three reasons converge on a single conclusion: among Vietnam’s plausible next upgrades, Canada is the most logical choice.
Indeed, what makes this more than a hypothesis is that Hanoi and Ottawa are visibly moving in this direction already. In January 2026, at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney delivered a widely noted address describing a “rupture” in the rules-based international order and calling on middle powers to cooperate more closely to protect their interests as great-power rivalry intensifies. His argument – that middle powers need to band together as the old order frays — dovetails almost precisely with the logic Vietnam has been applying to its own diplomacy.
On the Vietnamese side, the signals have been just as direct. On June 29, Vietnamese Prime Minister Le Minh Hung told Canada’s ambassador that Hanoi “always regards Canada as an important partner” and pressed for expanded cooperation in trade, artificial intelligence, quantum technology and semiconducto

items.title: Indonesia, United States Kick Off Annual Multinational Military Exercises
items.summary: Super Garuda Shield 2026 will involve more than 4,700 troops from 13 nations, and observers from a further eight others.
items.body_text:
The United States and Indonesia launched annual multilateral military exercises yesterday, which the two sides said aimed to improve interoperability and bolster deterrence in the region.
Super Garuda Shield, which has been held annually since 2007, will take place in various locations including Bandung, Lampung, Kalimantan, and the Indonesian Army’s Baturaja Combat Training Center in South Sumatra before concluding in Jakarta on September 11.
This year’s iteration will involve more than 4,743 personnel from 13 other countries including Japan, South Korea, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Canada. A further eight nations will join as observers. While the total number of troops is slightly down on last year’s iteration, which featured a record 5,400 participants, it includes more participating nations than ever, with India taking part as an observer for the first time.
Major General Patrick Ellis, the commanding general of the U.S. Army’s 4th Infantry Division, said that the exercise was critical for “building the human architecture that keeps the Indo-Pacific safe.”
“The security landscape of the Indo-Pacific is complex and readiness cannot be surged when a crisis begins,” he said at an opening ceremony at the Indonesian Armed Forces’ School of Command in Bandung. He added, “We are not just meeting for another annual training cycle. We are writing a historic new chapter in our bilateral relationship.”
TNI Commander General Agus Subiyanto, the commander of the Indonesian National Armed Forces, said that “the purpose of the exercise is, first, diplomacy, and then cooperation through the exchange of capabilities.”
The Garuda Shield exercise was established between the U.S. and Indonesian militaries in 2007 and forms a primary pillar of the two nations’ defense relationship. “Super” was added to its title in 2022, when the exercise was expanded into a multilateral format.
This year, the exercises “will include a joint staff exercise, cyber exercise, airborne operations, jungle training, and amphibious exercise,” the U.S. Army said in a statement. U.S. Navy and U.S. Coast Guard personnel will also conduct coordinated maritime training serials with the Indonesian Navy in adjacent waters in order “to strengthen joint interoperability at sea.”
Participating forces will also take part in special forces infiltration drills, cyber defense exercises, the firing of Stinger missiles, and humanitarian assistance and disaster relief operations.
The expanded exercise is the first to take place since Indonesia and the U.S. established a new defense cooperation pact in April. The Major Defense Cooperation Partnership (MDCP) will bolster cooperation in Indonesian military modernization and increase training, joint exercises, and professional military education, with the aim of “maintaining peace and stability” in Asia.
Indonesian Defense Minister Sjafrie Sjamsoeddin and U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth said at the time that they “have also committed to enhance joint special forces training,” and to expand existing multilateral exercises, including Super Garuda Shield.
The continued expansion of the annual exercise speaks to the continued good health of the U.S.-Indonesia defense partnership, which has remained stable despite the erratic nature of foreign policymaking under the second Trump administration. However, while Indonesia has welcomed closer U.S. security cooperation, it continues to hew to a policy of foreign policy non-alignment, and to maintain a balanced spread of defense engagements – including with key U.S. adversaries.
For example, on the same day that Sjafrie and Hegseth signed the MDCP agreement in Jakarta, President Prabowo Subianto was being hosted at the Kremlin by Russian President Vladimir Putin.

items.title: Myanmar’s Min Aung Hlaing to Visit Vietnam Soon, State Media Says
items.summary: All four mainland Southeast Asian states have now extended an official invitation to the general-turned-president since his inauguration in April.
items.body_text:
Myanmar’s military-appointed president, Min Aung Hlaing, will soon visit Vietnam, his fourth visit to an ASEAN member state since taking office in April, Myanmar state media reported today.
According to a report in the Global New Light of Myanmar, the former general will travel to Vietnam “in the near future” at the invitation of To Lam, Vietnam’s president and the head of the Communist Party of Vietnam. In addition to meeting with Lam, he will also meet with Prime Minister Pham Minh Chinh and Tran Thanh Man, the head of the National Assembly, and “receive representatives from economic organizations.”
“During the visit, the President will hold cordial discussions and exchange views on further consolidation of the existing friendly relations… as well as cooperation across economic, cultural, and various other sectors,” the report stated.
The announcement, which has not yet been confirmed by Hanoi, comes shortly after Vietnamese Foreign Minister Le Hoai Trung traveled to Myanmar last week, the first time that a Vietnamese foreign minister has visited the country since the 2021 coup. During talks with Min Aung Hlaing in Naypyidaw, he “discussed boosting bilateral trade and investment, as well as mutual support on the international stage,” The Irrawaddy reported, citing state media.
Trung also met Lower House speaker Khin Yi and Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe, to whom he pledged “continued support for Myanmar at the U.N., ASEAN, and other international forums.” Trung also reportedly extended a formal invitation for Min Aung Hlaing to visit Hanoi.
The trip would be the former general’s fourth to an Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) member state since taking office as president in April, after visits to Laos in early July and Thailand last month and an upcoming trip to Cambodia in early September. He has also made state visits to India and China in June, and to Russia, Belarus, and Kazakhstan last month.
All of this reflects a concerted push by Min Aung Hlaing to consolidate Myanmar’s relationship with key partners. A top priority, which he mentioned in his inauguration speech in April, is to normalize relations with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).
Since late 2021, the 11-nation bloc has excluded the country from its summits over its failure to implement the bloc’s Five-Point Consensus conflict resolution plan. This plan calls for a cessation of violence, access to humanitarian aid, and inclusive dialogue involving “all parties” to the country’s conflict.
Min Aung Hlaing’s quasi-civilian government, which was formed after flawed multi-phase elections in December and January, has taken an increasingly defiant line toward ASEAN, dismissing the Five-Point Consensus as an unwarranted “interference” in its internal affairs and demanding its full readmission to the bloc.
At the same time, it has sought to engage directly with willing ASEAN member states, particularly Thailand, which has positioned itself as a bridge between Myanmar and ASEAN. During Min Aung Hlaing’s visit to Bangkok last month, Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul “reaffirmed” Thailand’s commitment “to supporting and continuing to work closely with Myanmar for Myanmar’s full and equal participation in ASEAN mechanisms and processes.”
The fact that all four of Myanmar’s mainland Southeast Asian neighbors have now extended invitations to Min Aung Hlaing to visit reflects a growing regional fatigue with the Myanmar conflict, and a belief that “calibrated reengagement” (in Thailand’s phrase) is the best way to manage the effects of the civil war, if not to resolve it.
It also reflects a continuing divergence between ASEAN’s mainland and maritime member states on how to deal with Myanmar. Over the past five years, the mainland states have favored more engagement than maritime nations such as Singapore, Indonesia, and Malaysia, which have advocated a more robust regional response to the military coup in Myanmar. items.title: Trump running out of bullets against an intractable Iran
items.summary: President Donald Trump has entangled the United States in a war of choice with Iran that he cannot easily win or quit. items.body_text:
President Donald Trump has entangled the United States in a war of choice with Iran that he cannot easily win or quit.
The war was meant to be what Trump called “a little excursion” that would be over within a few weeks. But it is now into its seventh month, with no end in sight.
Trump has said he is willing to let the conflict continue for as long as needed to force Tehran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz (which was open to free navigation before the war) and negotiate a deal over its nuclear program (even though experts say Iran was not on the verge of developing a weapon before the war).
The two sides are now in a dangerous limbo, with periodic outbreaks of fighting.
They traded strikes this week, with the US targeting Iran’s Larak island and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) retaliating with attacks on US bases in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates.
Meanwhile, there are no real negotiations toward finding a peaceful resolution to the conflict.
Repeated claims of victory
In starting the war in late February, primarily at the instigation of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Trump and his secretary of defense, Pete Hegseth, repeatedly said it would not be long or costly. They were very damning of previous American leaders for miring the US in the long wars.
But Trump acted in a strategic vacuum. His administration underestimated the resilience and preparedness of the Iranian regime to counter the US threat. It also did not foresee Iranian society coalescing in the face of outside aggression.
Even so, Trump repeatedly claimed military triumph, proclaiming Iran’s defensive capabilities had been destroyed and the US had pummeled Iran into accepting a peace deal.
But this was premature. Tehran had not only managed to maintain and rebuild its offensive capability more quickly than expected, it also gained control over the Strait of Hormuz as a critical leverage point to pressure the US and the world.
By May, Tehran had the upper hand and was disinclined to negotiate any deal that did not meet its key demands. These included:
- a ceasefire on all fronts (including Israel’s offensive against Hezbollah in Lebanon)
- the unfreezing of billions of dollars of Iranian assets
- war reparations
- the right to manage the Strait of Hormuz
- a permanent end to any US and Israeli threat to Iran.
These demands were included in the vaguely worded memorandum of understanding Trump signed in June with the Iranian leadership, which was at this point dominated by hardliners from the IRGC. Because the deal was favourable to Tehran, Trump could not endure it for too long.
As pressure mounted from Republican heavyweights and Netanyahu, Trump backed out and launched new attacks. Tehran made no effort to try to save the deal, either – it was in its interest to inflict as much political damage on Trump as possible.
Since then, Trump has reimposed the US blockade on Iranian ports to starve the Islamic regime of oil revenue and launched periodic military strikes to intimidate Tehran. But the stalemate has persisted.
‘Economic D-Day’
With the midterm elections fast approaching, the Trump administration last week announced what it called Operation Economic Outcast, widescale sanctions intended to strangle Iran economically and isolate it globally. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called it “Economic D-Day.”
However, this policy, too, is unlikely to force Iran to capitulate for several reasons. Both China and Russia have rejected Washington’s move as unacceptable. None of Iran’s neighbouring countries – most notably, Pakistan, Iraq and Turkey – have so far said they would enforce the sanctions.
The only Gulf Arab state that has paused financial transactions and trade with Iran is the United Arab Emirates, given its close coordination with the US and Israel.
As history shows, sanctions have rarely worked as a pressure instrument. Perhaps the only time they proved effective was when they were applied uniformly against the apartheid regime in S

items.body_text:
The American response to Southeast Asia’s industrial-scale scam compounds has been vigorous, even theatrical at times, yet it remains strikingly incomplete.
In April 2026, the Justice Department’s Scam Center Strike Force seized 503 domains designed to impersonate legitimate trading platforms, restrained roughly $702 million in cryptocurrency linked to the fraud and for the first time dismantled a Telegram recruitment channel that had drawn more than 6,000 followers toward employment in Cambodian compounds.
By June, the Treasury Department and FinCEN had designated nine individuals and 26 entities connected to Cambodia’s Prince Group and moved to exclude the payment platform H-Pay from the United States financial system. Subsequent actions in July added another $25 million in forfeitures, bringing the Strike Force’s cumulative recoveries past $800 million.
To be sure, these are not trivial numbers. They demonstrate capacity and political will. They also reveal the limits of an approach that continues to treat the problem as essentially an offshore-based enterprise operating on Myanmar or Cambodian soil.
The pattern of designations and seizures has so far focused almost exclusively on international operators and a handful of Cambodian financial nodes. That framing is convenient and partly accurate. It is also insufficient.
The labor that staffs the compounds and the financial corridors that move the proceeds after they leave a victim’s account both run heavily through South and Southeast Asian economies that export workers and, in some cases, tolerate or fail to police domestic mule networks. India and Indonesia sit at the center of both pipelines.
Consider the workforce first. Indian government figures cited in early 2025 placed roughly 2,000 Indian nationals inside scam operations around Myawaddy, the Myanmar border town that, alongside Shwe Kokko, remains one of the industry’s principal hubs.
Many responded to fabricated job advertisements for computer operators or data-entry clerks circulating on Facebook groups and WhatsApp forwards, offering monthly salaries of 60,000 to 70,000 rupees.
Some were trafficked in the classic sense; others appear to have entered knowingly, or at least with eyes half-open, calculating that the risks were manageable. The distinction rarely survives media coverage, which prefers a single narrative of victims held under guard and awaiting rescue.
India has repatriated more than 2,500 of its nationals from these compounds since 2022, with recent flights continuing into late August 2026. The foreign ministry still lists dozens as unaccounted for. Yet a labor force large enough to sustain round-the-clock English-language outreach across WhatsApp, Instagram, Tinder and LinkedIn cannot be assembled solely through kidnapping.
Recruitment networks reach deep into Indian towns and cities long before any border is crossed. The Central Bureau of Investigation’s recent arrests of recruiters in Haryana and elsewhere underscore that the supply chain is domestic as well as transnational.
Indonesia’s experience compresses the same story into sharper numbers. Jakarta’s Ministry of Migrant Worker Protection recorded more than 12,000 Indonesians entangled in Cambodia’s scam economy in the first half of 2026 alone, more than double the entire previous year’s count.
The mechanics are nearly identical: fake job postings, brokers who undercut slower official channels, and workers who discover too late that the promised employment is forced cybercrime.
Cambodian authorities claim to have closed hundreds of sites and deported tens of thousands, yet Amnesty International’s mid-2026 assessment found that more than 70% of the compounds it tracked had been bypassed or quickly reconstituted.

items.title: Whisper stuff: the call Wall Street can’t put in writing
items.summary: One of the small costs of running money is that you stop having time to read the people you most want to read. For me, that is Matt Levine, whose Money Stuff column runs on Bloomberg, and who has spent a decade explaining financial plumbing better than anyone alive while making it funnier than it […] The post Whisper stuff: the call Wall Street can’t put in writing appeared first on Asia Times.
items.body_text:
One of the small costs of running money is that you stop having time to read the people you most want to read.
For me, that is Matt Levine, whose Money Stuff column runs on Bloomberg, and who has spent a decade explaining financial plumbing better than anyone alive while making it funnier than it has any right to be. I have a folder of his columns I mean to get to. It is not getting smaller.
So this borrows his machinery. A simple model, some actual rules, several worse versions of the model, and the hope that the rules do the joke for you. The idea is to discuss things in a way that does not come across as accusatory, but still allows for the expression that something may be off. We cannot think of any better way to do this than in the style of the maestro.
Unfortunately, the sentence rhythm and the footnotes can be copied. What cannot be copied is the 20 years of structured-products law sitting under every casual aside, or the instinct for which absurdity is the load-bearing one.
Programming note: This is longer than usual. There is a lot of securities law in the middle. It is also focused on US market laws, even though the whisper-impact spread — and the corresponding potential for mischief — is now global.
Finally, because we do not have access to Bloomberg’s proprietary fonts or content management system, we cannot perfectly mimic the visual experience of reading Money Stuff. You will just have to imagine the perfectly spaced block quotes and the Arial Black section headers doing the comedic work.
Everything is expectations
From first principles, you might imagine that the way to value a public company is to look at how much money it makes. If you run a company that makes boxes, and you sell US$100 worth of boxes, that is good. If you sell $103 worth of boxes, that is better, and your box company shares are worth more money.
Obviously, this is not how it works.
If you are a public company, your value is not determined by your profits. Your value is determined by the derivative of your profits against the expectations of your profits. In the simplest possible model, the math works like this:
- Analysts write down that you will make $100.
- You report that you made $103.
- Three is a positive number, so your stock goes up.
That model had a good run. It was very popular in the 1990s. But the modern version is a bit weirder. Today, you report $103 against a published consensus of $100, and your stock immediately falls 9% in four minutes.
A guy on financial television says you had a “massive beat.” A guy on a trading desk says the buy-side expectation was actually $105. Both of these people are telling the exact truth. You beat the number on the Bloomberg terminal, and you missed the number inside the hedge fund manager’s head.
One of the core themes of this column is that everything is securities fraud. But the earnings-season variant is slightly less ambitious: everything is expectations. You beat earnings, but you missed expectations. You beat consensus, but you missed the whisper number. You beat the whisper number, but you disappointed on forward guidance. There is always another number.
And the problem with the number that actually moves the stock is that it has no author, no timestamp and no methodology.1
The official number
Mechanically, the “consensus” estimate is a manufactured product. It sounds like a grand, philosophical agreement among brilliant minds, but actually it is just a data vendor scraping 30 different Excel spreadsheets, applying some proprietary inclusion rules about what the word “adjusted” means and dividing by 30.
Because it is a manufactured product, it has manufacturing defects. Here is an academic paper by Larocque, Watkins, and Weisbrod:

items.title: Ebola deaths approach 3,000
items.summary: DR Congo has recorded 6,041 Ebola cases and 2,911 deaths, according to Congolese health authorities Read Full Article at RT.com
items.body_text:
Ebola deaths approach 3,000
More than 6,000 people have been infected with Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DR Congo) since the latest outbreak began, with nearly half of confirmed patients dying from the disease, according to government figures published on Monday.
The outbreak has spread to 60 health zones across six provinces – Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uele, Bas-Uele, and Tshopo. Ituri remains the worst affected, with 28 of its 36 health zones reporting cases, followed by North Kivu with 15. The country has recorded 6,041 confirmed cases and 2,911 deaths, putting the case fatality rate at 48.2%.
The World Health Organization (WHO) warned on Friday that the outbreak continues to worsen. “Although surveillance has expanded, numbers of cases and deaths continue to rise due to sustained transmission and geographic expansion,” the agency said in a post on X.
A total of 1,366 patients have recovered, while 619 remain in isolation or hospital, according to the National Institute of Public Health. The ministry said response teams remain active across the affected provinces, with efforts particularly concentrated in Ituri, North Kivu, and Haut-Uele.
The outbreak, which was declared in May, is caused by the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola and has become the largest recorded in DR Congo’s history, surpassing the country’s 2018-2020 epidemic. There are currently no approved vaccines or specific treatments for the Bundibugyo strain.
International organizations have also stepped up in support for the response. On Monday, vehicles were handed over to health authorities and Red Cross teams in Kisangani, the capital of Tshopo Province, to help contain the outbreak. “Sustained attention and resources for the Ebola response in DRC remain essential,” Ariel Kestens, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) head of delegation, said on X.
Last week, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres called the Ebola outbreak a “human tragedy affecting families [and] communities on an extraordinary scale.”
The WHO and the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) have also previously called for greater international support to contain the outbreak.

items.title: Hundreds of Sudan paramilitary fighters defect to army
items.summary: Around 200 RSF fighters led by a senior commander have defected to Sudan’s army Read Full Article at RT.com
items.body_text:
Hundreds of Sudan paramilitary fighters defect to army
Around 200 members of Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have defected to the army, state media reported on Sunday.
The fighters reached Omdurman, across the Nile from Khartoum, where they were received by units of the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and members of the SAF-aligned Revolutionary Awakening Council, the state-run Sudan News Agency (SUNA) reported. The group was led by Abubakr Hamouda Dahloub, identified as the RSF intelligence chief in North Kordofan.
Dahloub said the group had broken with the RSF leadership and was prepared to take part in military operations alongside the army and allied forces. Anadolu Agency quoted him as saying the fighters had realized “their mistake in following the project being implemented by the RSF militia.” The RSF has not publicly commented on the reported defection.
The latest move follows other defections reported by the Sudanese authorities in recent weeks. Sudan Tribune said two groups had surrendered to the army in Northern State during the previous three weeks. Other reports said hundreds of fighters and several commanders had left the RSF in August and joined forces aligned with the military.
The war between the SAF and the RSF began in April 2023. Fighting has since spread across the country and forced millions of people from their homes.
Sudan descended into chaos in April 2023 when fighting erupted between the national army (Sudanese Armed Forces, SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). This occurred after months of tension between their commanders, army generals Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo ‘Hemedti’, respectively, over a planned transition to civilian rule. What began in the capital, Khartoum, as a power struggle has devastated the country, killing tens of thousands and displacing millions.
Regional and international peace efforts, including African Union mediation and Saudi–US talks in Jeddah, have repeatedly stalled. Sudanese officials have named Colombians and Ukrainians among mercenaries backing the RSF against the army. Officials have also accused Ukraine and the United Arab Emirates of involvement and recently claimed the European Union has an “incomplete understanding of the complex situation” in the country.
Khartoum has also accused authorities in neighboring Kenya of backing the RSF and has broken ties with the East African grouping IGAD amid mistrust of regional mediation. In July, TASIS, a political coalition aligned with the paramilitary, announced the formation of a rival government months after its members signed a charter in Nairobi. It named Gen. Dagalo as chairman of a 15-member presidential council, a move rejected by the UN and AU.
The conflict has also created a major displacement and food crisis. About 8.6 million people remained internally displaced across Sudan as of late July, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM).
The defections come as the army has reported gains on several fronts. On Friday, the SAF said it had repelled an attack by the RSF and its allied Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N) faction on Fazughli in the southeastern Blue Nile region.
The Sudanese Army recently recaptured Kurmuk in Blue Nile state and, in late July, regained several areas in North Kordofan from the RSF, including Bara, Jabra al-Sheikh, and Um Sayala. General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, commander-in-chief of the SAF and the chairman of the country’s Transitional Sovereignty Council, subsequently visited frontline positions in the region.

items.title: Libyan rivals set deadline for national elections
items.summary: Libya’s rival authorities have signed a UN-backed roadmap aimed at holding long-delayed national elections within two years Read Full Article at RT.com
items.body_text:
Libyan rivals set deadline for national elections
Libya’s rival political and military institutions have signed a UN-backed roadmap aimed at holding presidential and parliamentary elections within 24 months. The move comes after 15 years of instability triggered by the NATO-backed uprising that overthrew longtime leader Muammar Gaddafi.
The agreement was signed on Sunday at the headquarters of the UN Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL) in Tripoli, following several rounds of talks that concluded in Tunisia’s capital, Tunis, on August 20. The talks involved two representatives from each of four major institutions: the Tripoli-based Government of National Unity (GNU), the High Council of State, the eastern-based House of Representatives, and the Libyan National Army.
Walid Ellafi, the unity government’s minister of state for political affairs, said the elections would be held “within a period not exceeding 24 months” under a single executive authority and unified national institutions. The roadmap seeks to resolve longstanding disputes over electoral laws and reform the national election commission. Shibani AbuHamoud, head of the army delegation, said the participants would work with UNSMIL to establish an implementation mechanism within one month.
The House of Representatives and High Council of State have one month to approve the agreement. If they fail to do so, the parties intend to pursue its adoption as a constitutional document through broader national mechanisms and seek UN Security Council support.
The deal is the latest in a series of attempts to end Libya’s political deadlock. The North African nation descended into conflict following the NATO-backed uprising that ousted Gaddafi in 2011. The country split between rival eastern and western administrations in 2014.
A UN-backed process previously scheduled elections for December 2021, but the vote collapsed amid disagreements over electoral laws and the eligibility of leading candidates. A joint committee representing Libya’s two legislative chambers agreed draft election laws in 2023, but disagreements over forming an interim government and implementing the legislation prevented a vote.
The latest roadmap states that military personnel “shall be permitted to participate in the presidential election as candidates and voters.” Dual nationals would also be allowed to run, although a successful candidate would have to renounce any foreign citizenship before taking the constitutional oath.
The plan would also eliminate a mandatory second round when a candidate wins more than 50% of the vote, require presidential hopefuls to secure 20,000 endorsements from across Libya, and remove the existing linkage between presidential and parliamentary election results.

items.title: Cardinal Ouellet wins case against woman who accused him of abuse
items.summary: A ruling by the Superior Court of Quebec in Canada finds that Cardinal Marc Ouellet was “falsely accused” of sexual assault in connection with a class action against the Archdiocese of Quebec, and he will receive $100,000 in damages, which he will donate to organizations combating the sexual abuse of Indigenous peoples. Read all
items.body_text:
Cardinal Ouellet wins case against woman who accused him of abuse
By Salvatore Cernuzio
Canadian Cardinal Marc Ouellet, Prefect Emeritus of the Dicastery for Bishops, has won his case against Paméla Groleau, the woman who âfalsely accused him of sexual assault in connection with a class action against the Archdiocese of Quebec.â
The Cardinal, who described himself as a âvictim of defamation and slander,â will receive $100,000 in damages for the violation of his right to honour.
The decision was handed down by the Superior Court of Quebec in Canada. Published on 31 August, it ruled in the Cardinalâs favour in the defamation lawsuit he brought after the allegations of sexual assault became public in August 2022.
Justice Martin Castonguay concluded that the allegations were unfounded and ordered Groleau to pay the Cardinal the full amount he had sought.
In a statement released afterwards, Cardinal Ouellet said he would donate the money âto organizations combating the sexual abuse suffered by Indigenous peoples in Canada.â
The Cardinalâs statement
In the statement, Cardinal Ouellet said he was grateful that âthe civil justice system of my country has recognized that the allegations of sexual assault made against me were false and formulated with âextreme recklessness equivalent to malice,â and that the person concerned has been held responsible for the âinfamousâ and defamatory statements made against me and widely circulated throughout the world.â
Cardinal Ouellet thanked the lawyers of LCM Avocats and the numerous witnesses who testified for having âhelped the Court establish the facts and ensure that the truth prevailed.â
He also reaffirmed his personal âcommitment to continuing the fight within the Church and society against every form of abuse, particularly sexual abuse,â and said he unreservedly supports âsubstantiated victims in their pursuit of restorative justice.â
The case
The case dates back to August 2022, when the Cardinalâs name appeared in a class action against the Corporation Archiépiscopale catholique romaine de Québec et lâArchevêque catholique romain de Québec concerning allegations of sexual abuse committed over several decades.
Paméla Groleau, a former lay pastoral assistant, accused the Cardinal of actions allegedly committed between 2008 and 2010. She described incidents of non-consensual physical contact that were subsequently presented as acts of sexual assault.
From the outset, Cardinal Ouellet consistently rejected the allegations, âfirmlyâ denying that he had âmade inappropriate gesturesâ and describing both the interpretation and dissemination of the allegations as âdefamatory.â
He also said he would participate âactivelyâ in any civil investigation âso that the truth may be established and my innocence recognized.â
In December of that year, the Cardinal announced legal action against his accuser to restore his honour and reputation.
Pope Francis also intervened in the matter in 2022, entrusting a preliminary investigation to Jesuit Father Jacques Servais.
At its conclusion, Father Servais stated: âThere are no grounds to open an investigation into the sexual assault of person F. by Cardinal M. Ouellet.â
The Pope therefore did not authorize the opening of a canonical investigation into the Cardinal because of the absence of âsufficient elements.â
The ruling
In Mondayâs rulingâthe outcome of a trial held in Montreal in March 2026âthe Court identified inconsistencies in Groleauâs account and questioned her credibility and reliability.
The decision also noted that âthe core of the class action is based on the experiences of seven children who were victims of paedophile members of the clergy during a dark period in Quebecâs history, when religious personnel controlled the education system.â
âThis,â the ruling states, âis the infamy of which Cardinal Ouellet complains: namely, that he was associated with paedophiles in the proceedings relating to the class action.â
The decision was welcomed with gratitude

items.title: Mozambique: Cathedral of Beira hosts Day for Catechists
items.summary: Over the weekend, the Archdiocese of Beira in Mozambique hosted catechists of the diocese for Catechist Day. The Mass was presided over by Bishop Antonio Manuel Bogaio Constantino, M.C.C.I. He is the Bishop of Caia Diocese and the Apostolic Administrator of Beira. Several priests concelebrated. Read all
items.body_text:
Mozambique: Cathedral of Beira hosts Day for Catechists
Rogério Maduca - Beira
The Eucharistic celebration and dayâs event were part of the 5th National Catechetical Week (V Semana Nacional de Catequese), a nationwide commemoration established by the Episcopal Conference of Mozambique (CEM).
In his homily, Bishop Constantino explained that a catechist is not someone who transmits religious knowledge; rather, they are witnesses of Christ. Therefore, they must proclaim the Church's faith, not their personal opinions. They witness to the faith by their lives.
The special Eucharist coincided with the Churchâs commemoration of the martyrdom of Saint John the Baptist. The feast of St. John the Baptist is closely tied to catechists because his entire life and mission served as an example that pointed others to Christ.
Ministry and not a profession
Like Saint John the Baptist, the catechist should be a servant of the truth, the Mozambican prelate emphasised. At the end of his homily, Bishop Constantino encouraged the catechists in their mission. He reminded them that theirs was a ministry and not a profession.
A public lecture also marked the celebration of Catechist Day in the Archdiocese of Beira. Father Aly do Rosário introduced the new National Directory for Catechesis (Novo Diretório Nacional de Catequese). He too spoke about the catechist's noble mission.
Later, there was a moment of fellowship among the catechists.

items.title: Missionary in Haiti: 'Violence cannot discourage us'
items.summary: Maddalena Boschetti, a fidei donum missionary in Haiti since 2002, tells Vatican News how remaining in the violence-stricken country and supporting those in need when all hope seems lost is a way to respond to the violence itself. Read all
items.body_text:
Missionary in Haiti: 'Violence cannot discourage us'
By Benedetta Capelli and Guglielmo Gallone
âThe country has not improved; the country is at war. There are open fronts, there are rear areas, and there is an entire population that is suffering and trying to adapt to an increasingly complicated daily life.â
Maddalena Boschetti, a lay fidei donum missionary in Haiti since 2002, shares what life is like in the country, where violence by armed gangs continues to spread and reshape the daily lives of the population.
Going to work, travelling, praying, and obtaining food have become increasingly difficult challenges, while rising prices are worsening an already dramatic humanitarian situation.
The Kenscoff massacre
The massacre in Kenscoff, in the hills on the outskirts of the capital Port-au-Prince, has once again brought Haiti to the attention of the international community.
In the attack carried out in the night between August 23 and 24, 47 people were killed and 22 were wounded, while more than 50 others were reportedly kidnapped. According to CNN at least 13 children and women were then released.
Many children were among the victims when armed men stormed homes and attacked civilians, even killing some people who had sought refuge in a church.
On Sunday, at the end of the Angelus in Castel Gandolfo, Pope Leo XIV made a renewed appeal for the country:
âI express my prayerful closeness to the victims and their families, and I ask that all the hostages be released without delay. I make an earnest appeal to all those responsible to make a concrete commitment to guaranteeing the safety of the population and putting an end to every form of violence.â
The echo of Pope Leo XIVâs words
In Haiti, the Popeâs words were welcomed as âa comfort for all of us, not only for the missionaries, but also for ordinary people and the faithful.â
Yet what happened at Kenscoff, Boschetti warns, is anything but an isolated incident.
The massacre âlifted the veil for a momentâ on a tragedy that continues even when Haiti disappears from the news and the media, she continued. âThere is a steady trickle of deaths, continuous violence, killings, kidnappings, and sexual violence.â
The figures convey the scale of the crisis of this internal war that causes thousands of victims. According to the latest report from the United Nations Integrated Office in Haiti, between April and June 2026, more than 1,400 people were killed and around 656 wounded as a result of the violence. The number of internally displaced people has exceeded 1.4 million.
Gangs still control large parts of Port-au-Prince, and their pressure is spreading to other areas of the country.
Operations by security forces have enabled them to regain control of some parts of the capital, but, the missionary explains, the retreat of armed groups from some neighborhoods has been accompanied by their advance into the countryâs interior.
âThere are several open fronts,â from the central region to the Artibonite department, and into the northern and southern areas, not to mention the capital, Port-au-Prince, which has been besieged by gangs for years.
The gangsâ power
Even travelling around the country means having to contend with the power of the gangs. Armed groups have established checkpoints on the roads, checking documents and phones and imposing tolls.
âIt is extremely dangerous and unsafe to travel,â says Boschetti, who for the past two years has avoided travelling to the capital.
And where the gangs are not present, there remains the fragility of an almost absent state. âThere are no public security forces,â she explains, while corruption and weak institutions make life even more difficult for communities.
Against this backdrop, the prospect of returning to the polls also remains uncertain. The transitional government is supposed to lead Haiti toward new elections, but the essential prerequisite, the missionary stresses, is the restoration of security.
